World.title: I moved to Mexico City in my 20s. Here’s what I learned
World.content:
If you move to Mexico City in your 20s, I hope it becomes a home and not just a destination.

I came to Mexico at 25 thinking I was moving abroad one more time. I had already lived outside Spain, so I knew what it meant to arrive somewhere new, figure out a city, make friends and eventually find my way around. I thought Mexico City would be another chapter in that story.

A year later, I realized something else happened. I didn’t just move to Mexico; I started building a life here.

When you’re in your 20s, it’s easy to romanticize starting over somewhere else. How many of us, after a mental breakdown, have thought about leaving everything behind? Maybe moving to Paris like Blair, or finding the messy, exciting life Carrie Bradshaw had in New York City in her 30s.

I’m not saying New York or Paris won’t give you what you need to find. They might. But I found something in Mexico City that I wasn’t necessarily looking for: a place where I could become a slightly different version of myself.

Asking better questions in a new city

For me, my 20s have become less about figuring everything out and more about asking better questions. Do I want to become a mother? Will I get married? What do I want my career to look like? What kind of woman do I want to become? What do I want my future family to look like? I don’t have the answers yet. But living abroad has made me more conscious of the questions.

When I told my friends in Europe that I was moving to Mexico, some of them were worried. I wasn’t particularly afraid. My biggest concern was more mundane: I love walking, and I simply wondered whether I would be able to walk as much as I did back home. I quickly found out I could. I walk from our apartment in San Miguel de Chapultepec to Condesa to see friends, or go to a class. I walk through Chapultepec Park almost every day, and sometimes all the way to Polanco, which can take close to an hour.

One of the first things Mexico City taught me was how easily we can misunderstand places we’ve never experienced ourselves.

Before coming to Mexico, I only knew two Mexicans. They had been exchange students in Finland when I was studying there in 2020 and 2021. We weren’t friends. I just remember them being very good at beer pong and drinking rum or gin with water.

Then I arrived. And I started meeting people.

Finding kindness in the unlikeliest moments

Before Mexico, the country that completely changed my understanding of human connection was Cuba. I would need to write another article about everything that island gave me, but I truly thought nothing could surprise me in the same way again. Until Mexico did.

On my third day living in Mexico City, I was waiting in line to pay for a haircut. The woman behind me noticed what I was doing and immediately told me there was a cheaper hairdresser in the shop across the street. This act of kindness was the first one that people have shown me here. They aren’t normally dramatic moments, but they happen very often. Sometimes it is smiling in the street, starting a conversation or simply making an effort when they have no reason to.

At home, you move through your busy day surrounded by people and routines that are familiar. Abroad, you become more aware of your interactions, and they end up becoming part of what makes a place feel like yours.

There was another adjustment I was not expecting. As a European — very active and not particularly patient — I was struck by how slowly life seemed to move here. I learned that “ahorita” doesn’t necessarily mean right now. It can mean soon. It can mean later. Most of the time it’s just a polite way of saying something will happen when it happens. And you’ll get your coffee when you’re meant to get it. If you’re in a hurry, I recommend you insist a couple of times.

How different neighborhoods shape who you are

One of the things that continues to amaze me about Mexico City is how different each neighborhood feels. Polanco and Santa Fe have their own rhythm: business, luxury, restaurants, offices, polished cars and people dressed for work.

Then you go to Condesa or Roma, and suddenly you’re surrounded by leafy streets, cafes, parks and lots of dogs. I spend a lot of time in Parque México with a good friend of mine who has lived here since 2024, and we still find ourselves surprised by what we see: people dancing, doing karate, playing pickleball, learning to skate, practicing hula-hoop, someone selling poems, couples sitting on benches, foreigners taking photographs of a scene that locals barely notice because, to them, it’s simply Tuesday. That is Mexico City.

The Historic Center still leaves me speechless: the old buildings, the ruins, the Zócalo, Alameda Central, Palacio de Bellas Artes, Museo Nacional de Arte (MUNAL), the markets and the streets where centuries of history exist on top of each other.

And then there is Coyoacán, Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera, colorful markets, museums, and streets that feel completely different from the rest of the city.

The most interesting part is not just that these neighborhoods look different. They also make you feel different. You become a different version of yourself depending on where you are in the city. And in your 20s, that gives you something I have learned to appreciate: perspective.

Experiencing Mexican art and architecture

I’ve visited many museums since arriving — some of the famous ones and others that are less known. I don’t want to pretend I can explain Mexican art after a year here. But I can say that I have never experienced history through public art in quite the same way. The murals of Diego Rivera are not simply beautiful paintings. They tell stories about Mexico, its people and its history. Artists like Frida Kahlo transformed personal pain into art and became part of a cultural identity recognized around the world. I was also so impressed by Luis Barragán. Have you seen his house in San Miguel de Chapultepec? It was designed in the late 1940s, and I swear if you discover it today, you’ll want to move in there. Mexico City reminds me that contemporary doesn’t always mean new.

The joys of Mexican food

The same happened with food. Unpopular opinion: I’m not a foodie. I enjoy a latte and a cookie as much as avocado toast or a good meal at a cool restaurant every once in a while. Just give me some food when I’m hungry, and I’ll be happy. But even I have been fascinated by Mexican food. Mexican cuisine was recognized as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2010, and one of the things I’ve learned is that there is no single thing called “Mexican food.” Ingredients, dishes and traditions change so much from state to state.

Even as a vegetarian, I have found myself trying things I never expected to eat: nopal, huitlacoche and many other ingredients I did not know of before arriving.

And Mexico City is not only Mexican food. You can eat Thai, Italian, Spanish, Chinese … you name it, you’ll find it. I even discovered one of my favorite Lebanese places here in the Historic Center.

Lessons in community through Día de los Muertos

I moved to Mexico City about a year ago, just as the rainy season was ending and Independence Day celebrations were beginning. I was warned before arriving that people knew how to celebrate. “But isn’t that true everywhere?” I thought. Especially coming from Spain, where we’re always down to party. But I understood quickly that celebration here can mean something bigger than drinking late into the night. There is a sense of community, belonging and gathering together.

To this day, experiencing Día de los Muertos in Mexico has been one of the best experiences of my life. We went to the village of Malinalco, less than two hours from Mexico City, to visit family altars. We entered house after house, each one belonging to families that had lost someone that year. Every house was different. Some had large patios and modern buildings; others were old. In all of them, they replicated the profession of the person who had died through objects, decorations and food: a baker, a secretary, a police officer, a chef. The altars were filled with bright orange cempasúchil flowers and candles.

In some of them, we lit our own candles as a sign of respect. Every family gave us something to eat and drink — from tamales and tacos to mezcal, tequila or warm spiced wine. In some of them, you could really feel the presence of the person being remembered. How generous of those families, after losing their loved ones, to celebrate their lives with us, strangers to them. It was so magical. I left with tears in my eyes from the lesson in humanity I had just experienced.

Building a life together while making it your own

I’m not single, and my boyfriend and I moved here together. Some people might think moving with your partner in your 20s means you miss out on the experience. That hasn’t been our case. If anything, moving here has made us more intentional about building a life, both individually and as a couple.

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: 2 Mexico City chefs launched an international ‘Pay What You Can’ model. How did it go?
World.content:
Food is, in many ways, the greatest of social equalizers. Everyone, after all, must sit down to eat at various points in the day, and there’s no escaping the fact that we must all break bread together.

But too often, there’s an exclusivity around who gets to actually sit at the proverbial table. In a bustling metropolis like Mexico City, in particular, many residents are gatekept and unable to enjoy the city’s most sought-after offerings, largely due to massive socioeconomic barriers.

Wealth disparities shape capital dining

The gap between those who can, or can’t, access Mexico City’s jeweled offerings is wider than ever. A 2026 report from Oxfam Mexico revealed just how disparate Mexico has become as a nation, with 1% of the population hoarding 40% of the country’s wealth.

The divide is glaringly obvious in high-end neighborhoods like Mexico City’s Santa Fe. Oscar Lopez of The Guardian wrote about how “unbelievably unequal” certain areas of Mexico City actually are: “The stark contrast in this little enclave of the capital is a microcosm of a problem that has plagued Mexico for decades: rampant income inequality, with a small slice of the population living in opulence while millions of families languish in poverty.”

The irony, of course, is that the essential workers who sustain the infrastructure for opulent lifestyles in Mexico rarely — if ever — get invited to partake in it. That trickles down to something like booking a table at a popular restaurant in CDMX, which only a select few get to enjoy.

Taking that reality into account, Norma Listman and Saqib Keval — the married chef-owners of Masala y Maíz, a prominent Michelin-starred eatery in Mexico City’s historic center that serves a blend of Mexican, Indian and East African dishes — have made efforts to raise awareness around such issues in the food industry, including workers’ rights and dining accessibility for all.

A global movement for humane hospitality

This summer, they initiated a “Paga Lo Que Puedas” or “Pay What You Can” (PWYC) day, effectively opening their doors to every diner, regardless of their tax bracket or bank account. A powerful and unprecedented gesture, it triggered a wave of support among participating restaurants who joined the cause throughout Mexico, and beyond, to galvanize a movement centered on humane hospitality.

“As the city becomes more expensive and more oriented toward tourism and higher-income visitors, there are people who have lived here and built these communities who are increasingly unable to participate in the spaces around them. For us, that contradiction is important,” Listman and Keval told Mexico News Daily. “Restaurants are part of neighborhoods and communities, but they can also become spaces that feel increasingly inaccessible to the people who live there.”

The couple went on to say, “Dining out has become a privilege for many people, and as it becomes more expensive, it can become more segregated by class. That goes against how we understand hospitality and why we entered this industry in the first place. ‘Paga Lo Que Puedas’ was one small way of responding to that reality.”

In Mexico City, more than 20 restaurants — including MUX, Sin Nombre, Baldío, Cicatriz and Fideo Gordo — declared their commitment to “Paga Lo Que Puedas,” which took place Aug. 26. More than 100 dining institutions across 14 countries also joined in.

So how did it fare? Masala y Maíz, along with 12 participating restaurants, shared their experiences with us.

The origins, challenges and joys of a novel model

The concept originally emerged years ago, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when Listman and Keval — who initially opened their restaurant as a small brick-and-mortar in San Miguel Chapultepec back in 2017 — were experimenting with ways to attract customers during a challenging time for food businesses to keep their staff employed and to provide the luxury of dining out in their community.

That evolved into a regular practice, in which diners would enjoy a meal and leave whatever they could afford inside an envelope. What began as an in-house tradition ballooned into a bigger idea that would, years later, result in a global effort.

“From the beginning, we were thinking about how we could make the restaurant more accessible while also creating a tangible way to support the people around us and keep our staff working,” they noted. “It started as a small gesture, but it was also an experiment in trust: What happens when we remove the fixed price from the menu and ask people to honestly decide what they are able to pay for their meal? In Mexico City, that question felt particularly relevant because we were already seeing how quickly the cost of living was changing around us.”

Social media deepens urban segregation

In the fall of 2026, those factors had only become more urgent. In analyzing the stratification of diners in Mexico City through the increased use of social media, Guillermo Echauri of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM) found that the role and perception of food influencers in Mexico City have only exacerbated the problem of inaccessibility.

He writes that “the attributes, perspectives, and personal experiences of the foodies themselves are integrated into an environment of significant socioeconomic disparities, urban segregation, and ethnic discrimination. This shapes their representation of the culinary landscape in the Mexican capital, as digital dynamics intensify existing inequality.”

In other words, the systemic issues around dining accessibility that Listman and Keval were attuned to nearly a decade ago haven’t disappeared — they’ve arguably worsened with the rise of food influencers and rampant social media usage, among other shifts in the community and global economy at large.

By reviving the PWYC initiative in Mexico City, the founders of Masala y Maíz — and the many restaurateurs who chose to join them — are emphasizing the ongoing need for inclusivity and egalitarianism through local and international gastronomy.

Measuring turnout and financial realities

Despite logistical complications that arose through staffing and clarity around how to accept payments in a PWYC framework (in which some diners paid with non-monetary goods, such as original artwork), a survey of 12 participating restaurants unanimously confirmed a “very positive” experience and that the day “opened doors to new audiences,” with 83% of the restaurants declaring they would “definitely” participate again.

“The response we experienced was largely one of curiosity and solidarity,” Listman and Keval affirmed. “Other chefs and restaurant owners were also thinking about accessibility, rising costs, and what it means to be a restaurant within a community. We did not approach this as a model that every restaurant should adopt. Restaurants have different circumstances and different economic realities, and sustainability for the restaurant and for its workers is important. What we wanted to do was create an invitation to think differently about what hospitality can look like.”

In terms of profitable sales, the results were mixed — although that’s to be expected when the public is invited to pay whatever they wish.

Forty-two percent of the surveyed restaurants reported a “better” day of sales; a combined 33% reported either “much worse” or “about the same.” Conversely, 75% of the food businesses shared that they saw a “much higher” or “higher” turnout than an average day, while 25% believe they saw “about the same” number of diners that they would have during normal hours. In all, it seems that the restaurants saw a boom in diners, but not necessarily in income (in an act of reciprocal care, tips reportedly went up by 42%).

Building connection beyond the dining table

Importantly, 58% of the diners self-identified as first-timers at the surveyed restaurants, indicating demand and engagement from a wider range of customers than usual, and affirming the PWYC blueprint as socially equitable.

“What has stayed with us most is the sense of connection that the initiative created. For us, the success of Paga Lo Que Puedas is not simply measured by how many meals were served or how much money was collected. It is also about what happens when people feel that a restaurant is making room for them,” Listman and Keval said. “We hope that diners experience a sense of belonging and joy, and that they are able to enjoy a meal without the usual anxiety around whether they can afford to be in that space. We also hope the experience encourages people to think about the labor, care and knowledge that goes into a meal, and to recognize the workers who make that experience possible.”

Nourishing a better city

In a city as increasingly divided as Mexico City has become in the past half-decade alone — due to gentrification, mass tourism and other sociopolitical factors — PWYC is a bold, if not necessary, kind of reclamation for the people. However, that responsibility shouldn’t fall solely on small-business owners and their staff to level the playing field (or dining tables, in this case); that work should ultimately be the focus of elected officials and local governments, who should be looking for ways to support not only diners, but those who provide the city’s best dining experiences.

Without them, what would be left to nourish and feed us when we want a transcendent meal or simply a night out? Keeping local culinary arts scenes alive — and attainable for diverse residents — should be every world-class city’s priority. No matter the price.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: Does civility in politics still exist? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
I am currently spending a few days visiting family and friends in the U.S. and, being a month away from the midterms, have had the opportunity to experience firsthand the run-up to the elections in multiple states. As is always the case now, the TV ads and political speeches of the candidates are increasingly over the top.

Do I choose the candidate who wants to turn the U.S. into a communist country? Or the one who wants to further enable a dictatorship? Do I prefer the candidate who wants to put a data center in my backyard? Or the one who wants to increase my energy costs and threaten my water supply with a data center that’s not in my backyard? It’s all so silly, so anxiety-producing, so insulting to our intelligence. In Mexico, where paid political ads on radio and TV are prohibited, it’s refreshing to not be subjected to this every two years.

Mexican politics, of course, are far from perfect, but there have been some examples of real civility demonstrated lately that give many of us some hope and inspiration. And that civility comes from the tone being set from the top by President Sheinbaum. Let me explain.

The word I most often hear to describe President Sheinbaum is “classy.” The way she dresses, the way she smiles, the way she carries herself, and the way she interacts with people are all frequently mentioned. Even those who don’t agree with all of her policies are impressed by that aspect of her.

Being an American, I have found the contrast to my native country and the increasing lack of class in politics in the United States to be maddening. I can understand genuine differences of opinion on important issues and on the general direction of the country, but I cannot get past the lack of class being exhibited by politicians that we see on a daily basis. The name-calling, the put-downs and the unwillingness to acknowledge anything positive from the other side is really depressing to watch. And it’s on both sides of the political aisle. I know I am not alone in often thinking, “We pay these people to represent us, find compromise, and make decisions — why can’t they seem to actually do it anymore?”

Which brings me back to Sheinbaum. There have been three incidents in just these past few weeks that were impressive examples of civility.

1. The U.S. administration has been back at it again, attacking Mexico for supposedly not doing enough to combat the cartels. This is despite nearly daily progress on high-profile arrests, drug and weapons seizures, and a significant reduction in homicides throughout the country. Marco Rubio, the U.S. Secretary of State, again hinted that the U.S. could act unilaterally against criminal organizations in Mexico. President Trump, acknowledging progress but not wanting to be outdone, added: “However, Mexico must take additional action against the narco terrorist organizations that dominate vast areas of its territory and continue to threaten the American people,” and arrest “the many corrupt public officials” who have colluded with them.

Sheinbaum responded calmly, saying that Mexico doesn’t need to be judged “from the outside.” She went on to say that she would like to see “a report about what the U.S. government is doing in the United States” to reduce drug use and combat drug trafficking. She asked, “Where is the effort being made to stop drug cartels and distributors in the United States? What’s going on with money laundering in the United States?” Fair questions of a government that has no problem frequently questioning her and her administration.

2. Sheinbaum recently completed her second year in office and as a result, just gave her second annual “state of the union” address. She then did something similar to last year, traveling to each of Mexico’s 32 states over a period of several weeks to personally give a “state of the state” address in which she presented, in detail, what the government has accomplished for the people of the state in the past year and what is planned for the following years.

Regardless of which political party is leading the state she visited, or which candidate they voted for, she showed up and presented a business-like progress report for the state. There was no avoiding the states that didn’t vote for her. There was no minimizing the progress in states that don’t support her. But rather a consistent, fact-based, optimistic outlook on what the government is doing to improve things in the state. It’s inspiring to watch, and impressive to see her making the effort to visit every state and make the individual presentations.

3. Sheinbaum’s visits to two states in particular, Jalisco and Nuevo León, most caught my attention. These states have the second and third largest cities in the country after Mexico City, and neither state has a governor of the Morena political party that Sheinbaum is part of. It didn’t matter; Sheinbaum showed up in both states, was warmly greeted by the governors, and spoke about the progress that the federal and state governments have made working together. This was not a post-natural disaster photo op. This was a real effort to present a progress report to the people of these states and present a united front of government.

The governor of Jalisco greeted Sheinbaum along with famous singer Vicente Fernández’s wife (Doña Cuquita). In Nuevo León, she was greeted by Governor Samuel García, his wife and their two daughters. The images of Sheinbaum kissing their youngest daughter with a beaming Governor García looking on would touch even the biggest cynic of politicians.

What we are seeing lately in Mexico is a welcome reminder that politics doesn’t have to be so classless, so off-putting, so negative, so nasty. It hasn’t always been this way in the U.S. — I’m not sure how it got this bad.

I’m not saying things are perfect in Mexico. They are far from it. But seeing politicians of different political parties together, seemingly genuinely acting like polite, kind, classy people is quite inspiring and uplifting. Perhaps that is why a recent poll just put the level of national pride of Mexicans at 90%, a record high.

Let’s hope it continues for the good of the country!

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Mexico’s fastest-growing states aren’t the ones having the most children
World.content:
The 2025 Intercensal Survey by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) has revealed a paradox in Mexico’s new demographic map: The states that have seen the greatest population growth are not those with the highest fertility rates.

Mexico reached a population of 130.9 million in 2025 – the country’s highest population in history. However, the population grew at an average annual rate of just 0.7%, its slowest pace in recent decades, with growth concentrated in states in the north and southeast of the country.

Which states lead population growth?

According to INEGI, Baja California Sur led in population growth with an average annual rate of 3.4%, followed by Quintana Roo at 2.2%. Querétaro recorded 1.7%, while Nuevo León and Coahuila grew by 1.5% annually.

Population growth in Quintana Roo is a result of its population dynamics: For years, the state has recorded growth linked to an influx of people from other states and the expansion of its urban and tourist areas, among other factors.

The same pattern is observed in Baja California Sur. Meanwhile Baja California, Querétaro and Nuevo León are attracting new residents thanks to urbanization, employment and internal migration.

In contrast, Guerrero and Veracruz lost population, shrinking by -0.6% and -0.3%, respectively.

Which states have the highest and lowest fertility rate?

The states topping the growth rankings are not the same ones showing the highest fertility rates. The Intercensal Survey revealed that Chiapas had the highest fertility rate at 1.8 children per woman, followed by Guerrero (1.6) and Durango (1.5).

The contrast is particularly striking in Baja California Sur and Quintana Roo. Despite ranking at the top for population growth between 2020 and 2025, their fertility rates were among the lowest in the country — 1.2 and 1.1 children per woman, respectively.

Mexico City has the second largest population of any entity or state, despite having the lowest fertility rate (0.8). According to the survey, its population stands at 9.1 million, just behind México state, which with 17.5 million inhabitants is the most populous state in the country.

With reports from Uno TV

World.title: Mexico’s City’s chinampa restoration project Arca Tierra wins 2026 Champions of Change Award
World.content:
Arca Tierra, a Mexican sustainable agriculture initiative founded by brothers Lucio and Pablo Usobiaga, has won the Champions of Change Award 2026 by The World’s 50 Best Restaurants in Latin America.

The award honors their work to restore the chinampas of Xochimilco — an agricultural system set on man-made islands, used by the Mexica people in pre-Hispanic times. They are raised plots anchored to the lakebed, created from mud, organic matter and vegetation.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The 50 Best Restaurants (@theworlds50best)

Today they are known as a Mexico City tourist attraction due to the boat rides aboard traditional trajineras. But the Xochimilco chinampas remain part of the capital’s productive and cultural landscape

They face, however, challenges, such as environmental degradation, urban expansion, and declining profitability for those who work the land.

Arca Tierra seeks to improve their condition to create a food supply chain that is fairer, local and regenerative. Their project seeks to produce high-quality food with a lower environmental impact, preserve traditional farming knowledge, and expand access to local products for restaurants, consumers and communities in Mexico City.

“This recognition confirms that we are on the right track and inspires us to continue working hard with the farmers and producers that collaborate with us,” Lucio said in a statement.

In the capital, Arca Tierra produces around five tonnes of food per hectare per month. Its harvests supply 47 restaurants in Mexico City and reach more than 300 families through weekly baskets.

The initiative has also developed culinary and rural tourism offerings designed to connect chefs, diners, and visitors with the origins of their food. Its projects include Baldío — a Mexico City restaurant created in collaboration with British chef Douglas McMaster — which focuses on comprehensive use of ingredients and on waste reduction. For example, vegetable peels are fermented to make a traditional beverage called tepache, or repurposed into a syrup that is then diluted and fermented before being incorporated into other dishes.

Ultimately, Arca Tierra seeks to turn the spotlight to a process often overlooked by diners — the production and sourcing of local ingredients.

“In the value chain, the person who produces the food earns the least money — it’s a total contradiction because they’re the most important of all,” Pablo said.

With the mission to bring quality produce to more people, Arca Tierra has expanded its vision beyond Xochimilco and it now operates in Huasca de Ocampo, Hidalgo, and Amanalco de Becerra and Polvillos, in México state.

With reports from El Estímulo and Cool Hunter Mx

World.title: Ebrard, in Milwaukee, strikes optimistic note on USMCA talks — ‘closer every day’
World.content:
Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard remains bullish about ongoing Mexico-U.S. trade talks, saying on Thursday that he is optimistic that new agreements are in the offing.

“We are getting closer on many issues, resolving problems, and we are making progress,” he said. “Every day we are closer to reaching new agreements.”

Ebrard spoke to reporters on the sidelines of the G-20 meeting in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, after a one-hour meeting with his U.S. counterpart Jamieson Greer.

Despite U.S. President Donald Trump’s protectionist policies, his tariffs and his lukewarm attitude toward the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), Mexican exports to the U.S. continue to grow at a double-digit rate and bilateral trade is approaching US $900 billion annually.

Ebrard said his main priorities are negotiating the reduction of Section 232 tariffs, which affect Mexican exports of automobiles and other materials such as steel, aluminum and copper, and maintaining the preferential tariff treatment currently enjoyed by Mexican shipments that meet the requirements of the USMCA.

Even with the changes Washington is pushing for in its trade policy, Ebrard insists Mexico will maintain an advantageous position.

Comparing Mexico’s situation with representatives from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and other nations present at the G-20, Ebrard said “I was able to confirm that we are in a more favorable situation than they are.”

Ebrard attributed Mexico’s preferential status to President Claudia Sheinbaum’s handling of relations with Trump and to the close economic integration on both sides of their shared border.

An unnamed Mexican official cited by France 24 television network supported Ebrard’s optimism regarding the tariff talks.

“We expect to have reductions in steel and cars and aluminum,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.

When asked if a deal would be struck before critical midterm elections in the U.S. next month, the official said Mexico is content to be patient.

In addition to meeting with Greer, Ebrard took advantage of the G-20 summit to strengthen ties with the European Union, Canada, India, Japan and Argentina.

“Our primary objective here at the summit has been to … protect jobs, our companies and our interests,” he said.

He is now planning trade missions to the EU and Canada next year, while confirming that Mexico and India are poised to begin a “new stage” in their economic relationship, with discussions ranging from tequila, which is subject to a 150% tariff, to vehicles and auto parts.

With reports from El País, EFE, France 24, LatinUS and El Economista

World.title: Former Navy officer ‘Capitán Sol’ arrested in Jalisco for fuel smuggling
World.content:
Miguel Ángel Solano Ruiz, a key participant in the fuel-smuggling scheme that has tarnished the Navy, was arrested in Zapopan, Jalisco, on Thursday night.

Solano Ruiz, aka “Capitán Sol,” is a retired Marine captain and purportedly one of the main operators of the fuel smuggling network allegedly orchestrated by the Farías Laguna brothers, both of whom were high-ranking Navy officers.

El traslado de Miguel Ángel Solano Ruiz, “El Capitán Sol” o “Mike”, señalado como uno de los principales operadores de la red de huachicol fiscal que involucró a mandos de la Marina y funcionarios de aduanas, quien fue detenido en Zapopan, Jalisco. pic.twitter.com/r6nLMvLVBo — REFORMA (@Reforma) October 2, 2026

According to witness testimony, Solano recruited active-duty and retired naval personnel to participate in the network that smuggled hydrocarbons through customs without paying the corresponding taxes, a crime known in Mexico as huachicol fiscal.

He allegedly used his influence within the Navy to place these men in key positions at maritime customs offices in ports such as Tampico, Altamira, Ensenada and Guaymas, while also corrupting public officials through bribes.

The Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) says Solano, 48, is the last remaining key player of the Farías Laguna criminal organization and will face organized crime and tax evasion charges.

The corruption scheme was uncovered when authorities seized a vessel carrying 10 million liters of diesel smuggled from Texas off the coast of Tamaulipas in March 2024.

Vice Admiral Manuel Roberto Farías Laguna was arrested on Sept. 2, 2025, while his brother Fernando, a rear admiral, remained a fugitive until he was captured in Argentina in April and deported to Mexico on Aug. 21 this year.

While serving in the Navy, Solano held several positions related to intelligence at Central Command and retired in 2018 with a pension of 18,000 pesos per month.

However, investigators found that his lifestyle greatly exceeded that pension: He lost more than 52 million pesos (US $2.5 million) on gambling, while casinos and racetracks had issued 400 warnings about him to the authorities. He also owned eight properties in Veracruz and Mexico City valued at over 13 million pesos (US $714,000).

Investigations over the course of the past year led authorities to addresses in France, Greece, Monaco and Spain, before the net closed around the suspect in Jalisco.

Authorities said that following more than 300 days in pursuit of Solano, a search warrant was issued on Thursday for a property located in the Villa Verona subdivision of Zapopan, a suburb of Guadalajara.

During the search, an arrest warrant was issued and Solano was apprehended. He was transferred to the Altiplano maximum-security prison in México state on Friday.

With reports from El Economista, El País, El Financiero and Proceso

POLITICS · CHILE

Key Facts — The country Chile, where President José Antonio Kast sent his first budget bill, for 2027, to Congress on 30 September. Lawmakers have 60 days to pass it.

— What happened On 3 October deputies of the UDI, a conservative party in Kast’s coalition, objected to education cuts and proposed trimming the INDH human rights institute instead (La Tercera, Cooperativa).

— The numbers Bicentenario merit high schools lose 46.71% in real terms. Laptop grants, worth about CLP 35 billion (about US$35.6 million) in 2026, get no money (El Mostrador, 3 October).

— What it means for you Public school families could lose the seventh-grade laptop grant in 2027. Existing Bicentenario schools keep funding, but no new schools would join, El Mostrador reported.

— Still open Whether Congress moves money from the INDH, which had CLP 16.339 billion (about US$16.6 million) for 2026 (La Tercera, August). Full education detail is due on Monday 5 October.

Chile’s 2027 budget education cuts have drawn their first open challenge from inside President José Antonio Kast’s own coalition. On Saturday 3 October deputies of the Independent Democratic Union (UDI), a conservative coalition party, vowed to reverse them.

The UDI wants to save two programmes: the Bicentenario merit high schools and the laptop grants once called Yo Elijo mi PC. To pay for them, it proposes trimming the National Human Rights Institute (INDH), an autonomous state body.

What the UDI wants changed

In a public statement, the UDI deputies voiced “deep concern” at lower funding for both programmes, Cooperativa and La Tercera reported. They called the Bicentenario schools “a true beacon” for middle-class and lower-income families.

Caucus leader Flor Weisse, who sits on the Chamber of Deputies’ finance committee, focused on the laptops. “This programme must not be eliminated, it must be strengthened,” she said, according to La Tercera.

The deputies said they share the government’s goal of a leaner state and still back Kast. They promised an “exhaustive review” of budget lines to find money for education instead.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where the 2027 budget education cuts fall

The overall education budget totals CLP 18.16 trillion (about US$18.5 billion at 982 pesos per dollar, 2 October close), El Mostrador reported. That is still 0.78% more than in 2026, in real terms.

Inside that total, several lines shrink sharply. Bicentenario schools lose 46.71% in real terms and the Education Recovery Fund falls 55.2%, according to El Mostrador.

Real cuts to selected education lines in Chile's 2027 budget bill versus 2026; the overall education budget rises 0.78%. Source: El Mostrador, 3 October 2026.

The laptop grants cost about CLP 35 billion (about US$35.6 million) this year and reached 96,100 pupils. The bill contains no line for them, as the Rio Times reported in Chile 2027 Budget Drops School Laptop Scheme.

The government says committed Bicentenario projects keep their money, but no new schools would be added. Ministers argue the laptop scheme was poorly evaluated and did little for learning.

Why the INDH is in the firing line

The INDH monitors human rights in Chile and publishes an annual report. UDI deputies accuse it of political bias, citing its conduct during the 2019 protests.

On 29 September three UDI deputies, including Sergio Bobadilla, announced an amendment cutting its budget to CLP 1,000 (about US$1). They said this would force it to close until a reform of its governance passes, El Dínamo and G5 Noticias reported.

The institute had CLP 16.339 billion (about US$16.6 million) for 2026, La Tercera reported in August. The UDI now says it should not again receive close to that sum without governance changes.

The INDH has defended its spending. In August it told La Tercera a disputed CLP 250 million (about US$255,000) events contract was tendered publicly and audited.

The government has ruled out closing the body. Justice Minister Fernando Rabat backs a deep reform of its powers and make-up instead, La Tercera reported.

What the government says

Education Minister María Paz Arzola said the laptop scheme was not having the expected impact on learning. She added that Congress would decide its future, Canal 9 Bío Bío reported on 3 October.

Total spending in the bill rises 1.5% on expected 2026 spending, as covered in Kast Raises Chile’s 2027 Spending 1.5% in Budget. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz says his team reviewed more than 600 programmes.

What Is Not Yet Known

The full budget detail reaches the Chamber of Deputies on Monday 5 October. Only then can lawmakers see every line the UDI plans to review.

It is unclear whether the UDI can gather the votes to move money from the INDH to schools. A similar UDI push against the institute’s funds was dropped last year, La Tercera reported.

The INDH’s own allocation in the 2027 bill has not yet been published. No public response from the government or the institute to the UDI’s latest proposal had been reported by Saturday afternoon.

Sources: La Tercera, 3 Oct 2026; Cooperativa, 3 Oct 2026; El Mostrador, 3 Oct 2026; Nuevo Poder, 3 Oct 2026; Canal 9 Bío Bío, 3 Oct 2026; El Dínamo, 29 Sep 2026; G5 Noticias, 29 Sep 2026; La Tercera, 4 Aug 2026; La Tercera, 4 Aug 2026 (INDH response).

DISASTER RECOVERY · COLOMBIA

Key Facts — The country Colombia. A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck the west on 10 August 2026; Infobae put the toll at 335 dead and 36,327 homes destroyed on 3 October.

— What happened The Fondo Milagro reconstruction fund, announced on 12 August, had received no money by late September, CAMBIO magazine reported on 2 October, citing Finance Ministry replies.

— The numbers COP 624.7 billion (about US$189 million) was added to the 2026 budget on 17 September. A further COP 2.7 trillion (about US$815 million) was requested on 29 September.

— What it means for you The money is not lost; the Finance Ministry still holds it. Rebuilding contracts through the fund cannot start until its trust contract is signed.

— Still open The ministry has given no start date, has not named a fiduciary company, and Congress has yet to vote on the extra money.

Colombia’s Fondo Milagro, the fund created to rebuild after the 10 August earthquake, has not started operating. By late September it had received no money, according to Finance Ministry replies reported by CAMBIO magazine.

The Pereira newspaper El Diario and the news site Infobae carried the findings on Saturday, 3 October. That is 52 days after the fund was announced, and the ministry has set no date for it to begin.

What the fund was meant to do

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the fund on 12 August, two days after the magnitude 7.4 quake centred in Chocó. It was the core of his plan (see World Rushes Aid to Colombia as Quake Toll Hits 281 and Plan Milagro Begins).

It was meant to pool national and foreign money for homes, hospitals, schools, roads and airports. Decree 1379, signed on 9 September, set it up as a ring-fenced trust that creditors cannot seize.

The model was the fund that rebuilt Armenia after the 1999 earthquake. It was designed to avoid the slow contracting rules of the national disaster-risk fund and of Fondo Adaptación, a state rebuilding agency.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Colombia Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Where the money stands

On 17 September the government added COP 624.7 billion (about US$189 million) to the 2026 budget for the emergency. CAMBIO traced it to a US$200 million World Bank contingent credit that Colombia arranged in 2025.

The ministry said none of it had been moved into the trust, so the ministry still holds it. Figures here use COP 3,312 per US dollar, the close on 2 October.

Rebuild bill cited by the government, extra sum sought from Congress, sum added to the 2026 budget, and money transferred into the fund (none), in US$ billion at COP 3,312. Source: El Diario, Infobae (citing CAMBIO), Caracol Radio, 29 Sep to 3 Oct 2026.

On 29 September the ministry asked Congress for another COP 2.7 trillion (about US$815 million) for Fondo Milagro, Caracol Radio reported. It expects to raise that sum by cutting penalties and interest on overdue tax and other obligations.

The government has spoken of a rebuilding operation near COP 30 trillion (about US$9.1 billion). That echoes the damage estimate covered in Colombia Puts the Earthquake Bill at Roughly US$9.6 Billion.

Why the fund is stuck

The trust contract with a fiduciary company has not been signed, the ministry told Green Alliance lawmaker Catherine Juvinao. Without it, the board cannot be seated and the manager cannot formally take office.

On 30 September the ministry said the Fondo Milagro contracting manual was still being defined, with no draft yet. The decree gives the president five board seats; the disaster agency UNGRD gets a voice but no vote.

Official answers have not matched: UNGRD told Juvinao on 11 September that businessman Jaime Andrés Uribe had been manager since 21 August. The presidency later said it held no records on the fiduciary or board minutes.

What is still moving

Other relief continues, as Colombia’s Earthquake Reconstruction Turns to 8 Percent Mortgages and Frozen Student Loans reported. Banks have offered victims 8 percent mortgages, and the state student lender froze loan collections.

The first tranche is also already in the budget rather than pending abroad. On the ministry’s own account, the unsigned trust contract is the step holding up the board and the manager.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ministry has not said when the Fondo Milagro trust will be signed or which fiduciary company will run it. Nor has it disclosed the fee or how the company will be chosen.

It is unclear how quickly Congress will vote on the extra COP 2.7 trillion (about US$815 million). The core findings rest on CAMBIO’s investigation, which other outlets have relayed rather than independently confirmed.

Sources: El Diario (Pereira), 3 October 2026; Infobae, 3 October 2026 (both citing CAMBIO); CAMBIO, 2 October 2026; El Quindiano, 3 October 2026; Caracol Radio, 29 September 2026; Portafolio, 9 September 2026.

EDUCATION · CHILE

Key Facts — The country Chile, where President José Antonio Kast sent his first budget bill, for 2027, to Congress on 30 September. Lawmakers have 60 days to pass it.

— What happened Education Minister María Paz Arzola defended ending the Yo Elijo mi PC laptop grant but said Congress will decide, 24 Horas reported on 2 October and BioBioChile on 3 October.

— The numbers The grant reached 96,100 pupils in 2026 with about CLP 35 billion (about US$35.6 million), BioBioChile reported on 1 October. The 2027 bill assigns it nothing.

— What it means for you Families of seventh-graders in public schools should not count on a state laptop in 2027. Socialist, populist and some pro-government deputies are pushing to restore it.

— Still open Whether the government agrees to put money back. Under the constitution, Congress can cut budget spending but cannot add it on its own.

The fate of Yo Elijo mi PC, Chile’s 17-year-old school laptop grant, now rests with Congress. Education Minister María Paz Arzola defended the cut but said lawmakers would have the final word.

“We are always respectful of the discussions that take place in Congress,” she told 24 Horas in an interview published on Friday. BioBioChile reported on Saturday that she had left the programme’s future in lawmakers’ hands.

The minister keeps the cut but opens the door

The 2027 bill gives the grant no money, as reported on 3 October in Chile 2027 Budget Drops School Laptop Scheme. It reached 96,100 pupils this year with about CLP 35 billion (about US$35.6 million at 982 pesos per dollar, 2 October).

Arzola said the government is united behind the decision. The programme “is not having the impact one would expect on learning,” she told 24 Horas.

She then called the bill a proposal open to comment. “When we start the conversation, everyone will be able to put forward their arguments,” she said.

Pupils reached by Chile's Yo Elijo mi PC / Becas TIC laptop grant: about 30,000 targeted at launch in 2009, 96,100 in 2026, and no funding in the 2027 budget bill presented on 30 September. Source: BioBioChile, 1 October 2026.

In an interview with La Tercera on Saturday, she said the grant exists only through the annual budget law. “It is not that we have anything against computers,” she said, adding that money should go where impact is proven.

The ministry’s stated priority is early-childhood education, she told the paper. Overall, Kast’s bill raises spending 1.5%, as set out in Kast Raises Chile’s 2027 Spending 1.5% in Budget.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Chile Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Votes line up against the cut

Socialist deputy Juan Santana, of the lower house education committee, said his party will reject the education chapter until the money returns. Radio Universidad de Chile and estapasando.cl both reported his position on 3 October.

Deputy Zandra Parisi of the populist Partido de la Gente (PDG) also asked the government to keep the grant. The state cannot “close the education gap by widening the digital gap,” she said.

Former presidential candidate Franco Parisi called the programme one of Chile’s most meritocratic policies, estapasando.cl reported. The site argued that PDG votes can tip a closely divided lower house.

Dissent also comes from inside the coalition. Deputies of the conservative UDI, a government ally, plan to restore the grant and find savings elsewhere, BioBioChile reported on 2 October.

Why Congress cannot simply add the money

Chile’s constitution lets Congress reduce spending in the budget bill but not raise it, except for items fixed by permanent law. The laptop grant has no such law, as Arzola noted.

Restoring it would therefore need an amendment from the government itself. If Congress fails to pass the bill within 60 days, the president’s version takes effect.

There is precedent for a deal. During last year’s debate, CLP 9.8 billion (about US$10.0 million) was restored for 2026 coverage, the Rio Times reported, citing The Clinic.

Opposition to the wider education cuts has already reached the streets, as covered in Chile Students March Against 2027 Budget Cuts. Arzola said the parliamentary debate on the grant has not yet begun.

What Is Not Yet Known

The government has not said whether it would accept a partial restoration or a redesigned grant. Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz, asked about the cut, said he did not recall the specific findings against the programme, Radio Universidad de Chile reported.

It is also unclear how the PDG bloc will vote on the full education chapter. The UDI wants the money taken from misused public-sector sick leave and from the national human rights institute (INDH), BioBioChile reported.

Sources: BioBioChile, 3 October 2026; BioBioChile, 2 October 2026; BioBioChile, 1 October 2026; 24 Horas, 2 October 2026; La Tercera, 3 October 2026; Radio Universidad de Chile, 3 October 2026; estapasando.cl, 3 October 2026; Constitution of the Republic of Chile, budget-law clause.

POLITICS · MEXICO

Key Facts — The country Mexico, Latin America’s second most populous country, governed by President Claudia Sheinbaum since October 2024.

— What happened On Friday 2 October 2026, Sheinbaum set up a working group to draft a decree obliging digital platforms to detect, remove and report content that directly incites violence.

— Who is involved The president’s legal office leads, with the security and education ministries, the National Intelligence Centre, the digital transformation agency and universities such as UNAM and IPN.

— What it means for you Social media users in Mexico may see violent posts taken down faster. The government says the aim is prevention, not creating a new criminal offence.

— Still open The decree text, due next week according to Education Minister Mario Delgado, how violent content will be defined, and what platforms face if they fail to comply.

Mexico’s government is drafting a decree that would oblige social networks and other digital platforms to detect, remove and report violent content. President Claudia Sheinbaum announced it on Friday 2 October, the day after a deadly attack on a secondary school in Torreón.

Education Minister Mario Delgado said the aim is to have a draft decree ready next week. Sheinbaum stressed the aim was prevention rather than creating a new crime, and that experts would help avoid censorship.

What the government announced

At her morning press conference, Sheinbaum said she was forming a working group led by the Consejería Jurídica, the presidency’s legal counsel. “There is a part that is the responsibility of the digital platforms,” she said, according to Contralínea.

The group includes the Security Ministry, the Education Ministry (SEP) and the National Intelligence Centre (CNI), Mexico’s civilian intelligence service. It also includes the Agency for Digital Transformation and Telecommunications, which oversees the government’s digital policy.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch said the decree would require timely detection, reporting and removal of posts that directly incite violence. It would also create channels for platforms to coordinate with the authorities.

Delgado asked how platforms with so much artificial intelligence and user data could fail to spot such posts in time. Platforms “have to show us that they are safe places for minors,” he said in an Education Ministry statement.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why now: the Torreón attack

On Thursday 1 October, two brothers, both adult former pupils, attacked Secondary School No. 13 in Torreón, Coahuila, with bladed weapons. A member of the school’s leadership was killed and four people were injured, García Harfuch said.

The Rio Times reported the attack on 2 October in Mexico School Machete Attack Kills Deputy Head. Sheinbaum said investigators had found similarities between Torreón, a recent case in Querétaro state and other attacks involving contact through social networks.

She gave no further details of the Querétaro case or of how the attackers had been in contact online.

Safeguards and the censorship question

Sheinbaum said experts from the National Autonomous University (UNAM) and the National Polytechnic Institute (IPN) would help define precisely what must be removed. The aim, she said, is to work without haste so the rules do not become censorship.

García Harfuch said intelligence monitoring of social networks, messaging services and forums has been stepped up. He added that viewing certain content or posting an opinion does not, by itself, mean someone will commit a crime.

The plan also has a classroom side. The government will expand its “ABC of Emotions” programme with parent meetings, confidential reporting boxes in schools and guidance for teenagers.

Canal N said the proposal resembles rules adopted in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia and Brazil. Delgado himself pointed to measures abroad that limit minors’ access to platforms.

What Is Not Yet Known

No draft text has been published, so the definition of content that “directly incites violence” is still unknown. The government has not said what sanctions platforms would face, or which authority would enforce them.

It is also unclear how far an executive decree can bind global companies without a law passed by Congress. Sheinbaum said wider regulation of platforms would be debated later, in broader forums.

What would the decree require from platforms?

Platforms would have to detect, report and promptly remove posts that directly incite violence, the government says. They would also coordinate with Mexican authorities. The final text has not been published.

Will posting violent content become a crime in Mexico?

President Sheinbaum said the aim is not to create a new criminal offence. The obligations described so far fall on the platforms, not on individual users.

When will the decree be ready?

Education Minister Mario Delgado said on 2 October that the goal is to have a draft decree the following week. No date for publication or entry into force has been given.

Sources: Presidency of Mexico, press release of 2 October 2026; Ministry of Public Education (SEP), statement of 2 October 2026; Contralínea, 2 October 2026; Canal N, 2 October 2026.

ENERGY · UNITED STATES

Key Facts — The country The United States pledged 172.2 million barrels to the March oil stock release, the largest share, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on 19 March 2026.

— What happened About 325 million of the 400 million barrels pledged on 11 March had been released by 2 October, the IEA said. That leaves about 75 million barrels outstanding.

— The numbers Country pledges tabled on 19 March added up to 426 million barrels, including 28 million from extra output in Canada and Mexico (IEA, 19 March 2026).

— What it means for you More crude and diesel is due on the market. The G7 says its new 100 million barrels flow over four months, with diesel frontloaded in the first 20 days.

— Still open Whether the G7’s 100 million barrels include the 75 million still owed under the March pledge, or come on top. Totals would be 400 or 500 million barrels, Veja calculated.

About 325 million barrels of oil and fuel have been released since March under an emergency action of the International Energy Agency (IEA), the agency said. That is over 80% of the 400 million barrels its members pledged on 11 March.

The United States made the largest pledge, 172.2 million barrels of crude. The update followed the G7’s separate 100-million-barrel deal (G7 Frees 100 Million Barrels as Mexico Needs US Diesel, 3 October).

What the IEA Reported

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol gave the figure at the G7 leaders’ video meeting on Friday, 2 October. “Around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on 11 March have so far been released,” the agency said.

AFP, Veja and G1 carried the update on Saturday, 3 October. The IEA groups 32 member countries, including all G7 nations, which agreed the March action unanimously.

The agency said in March that members held over 1.2 billion barrels of emergency stocks. Industry held a further 600 million barrels under national obligations.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Latin America markets Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Pledged What in March

Pledges to the IEA collective action by country, in million barrels; Canada and Mexico via extra output. Source: International Energy Agency, 19 Mar 2026.

The IEA published country pledges on 19 March, totalling 426 million barrels. Public stocks made up 280 million and obligated industry stocks 119 million.

The remaining 28 million came from higher output, 23.6 million from Canada and 3.9 million from Mexico. By product, 301 million was crude and 125 million refined fuel, a split the IEA called not final.

After the United States came Japan with 79.8 million barrels, Canada with 23.6 million from extra output and Korea with 22.5 million. Germany pledged 19.5 million, France 14.6 million, the UK 14 million and Italy 10 million.

How Far the US Share Has Gone

Washington is supplying its share through exchanges, oil lent from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) and repaid later. Five earlier solicitations awarded over 133 million barrels, the Department of Energy said, Oil & Gas Journal reported.

On 29 September the department offered another 40 million barrels, with bids due by 6 October. The SPR held 283.8 million barrels in the week to 25 September, its lowest in over four decades.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the United States and Japan were delivering. “Several European member countries have released only a fraction,” he said.

How the G7 Pledge Fits

The G7 statement of 2 October commits to “a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels,” over four months. It does so “taking into account commitments that have already been fulfilled.”

It also asks the IEA to monitor “the immediate and full implementation of the March 2026 commitments.” Leaders promised talks on further diesel releases and no export curbs among G7 members.

If the 100 million barrels are extra, total releases reach 500 million barrels, Veja calculated. If they absorb the outstanding 75 million, the total stays at 400 million.

For context on the supply gap, see Oil Prices Ended the Week Near $105. Ten Million Barrels a Day Are Not Being Pumped (13 September).

What Is Not Yet Known

The G7 did not say whether its 100 million barrels include the 75 million still owed from March, AFP reported. Nor has it published a split by country or by fuel.

The IEA has not given an updated country breakdown of the 325 million barrels. The G7 asked the agency for a follow-up report within 20 days.

POLITICS · BRAZIL

Key Facts — The country Brazil elects its president, Congress, governors and state assemblies on Sunday 4 October 2026. Roraima, on the borders with Venezuela and Guyana, is its northernmost state.

— What happened On Thursday 1 October the Federal Police arrested 22 people in a Boa Vista ring paying voters R$400 (about US$77) each, G1 and O Globo reported.

— Who is involved Police records link the ring to two Liberal Party (PL) candidates, Daniel Trindade and state deputy Marcinho Belota, O Globo reported on 3 October. Belota was searched, not arrested.

— What it means for you Voting goes ahead normally on Sunday. Most of the Roraima busts began with anonymous tips to the police electoral hotline, G1 and O Globo reported.

— Still open Who paid for the cash, and whose R$4 million (about US$766,000) police seized in Caracaraí (G1, 3 October). No response from either candidate appeared in the reports.

Brazil’s Federal Police (PF) broke up a vote-buying ring in Boa Vista, the capital of Roraima state, on Thursday 1 October. Officers arrested 22 people at two houses where voters were paid R$400 (about US$77) each in cash, G1 and O Globo reported.

On Friday the PF held 21 more people. On Saturday it searched two addresses over R$4 million (about US$766,000) in cash. The busts come on the eve of Sunday’s election, with security tight nationwide: US Consulates in Brazil Halt Services Before the Vote.

How the Boa Vista vote-buying ring worked

An anonymous tip to the PF electoral hotline flagged a house in the Calungá district, O Globo reported, citing arrest records. Voters had their names checked against lists there, then were sent to a second house to be paid.

Each voter received four R$100 notes (about US$19 each), O Globo said. Two were meant for federal candidate Daniel Trindade and two for state deputy Márcio “Marcinho” Belota, who is seeking re-election.

Both men belong to the PL, the party of presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Phones were taken at the door so nobody could film the handover, according to the records.

People arrested by Brazil's Federal Police in six vote-buying actions in Roraima, 1–2 October 2026. Source: G1 Roraima, 2 and 3 October 2026; O Globo and Poder360, 3 October 2026.

One campaign worker told police he received about R$19,000 (about US$3,640) at Trindade’s campaign office. The PF indicted three alleged organisers and 19 voters for electoral corruption and criminal association.

A court released the voters without bail, citing their low incomes. Belota’s home was searched under an electoral court warrant. Trindade was arrested in a separate PF operation on 25 September, O Globo reported.

A man held that day with a voter list and R$33,720 (about US$6,460) took Thursday’s arrests to 23 (G1, Roraima 1).

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Twenty-one more vote-buying arrests on Friday

On Friday 2 October the PF arrested 21 people and seized R$78,600 (about US$15,060) in Boa Vista and Alto Alegre, G1 reported. Three of the four actions began with anonymous tips, and one came from a routine patrol.

That patrol stopped 11 people leaving a house with R$300 (about US$57) each and campaign leaflets, G1 and Roraima 1 reported. In Alto Alegre, police found R$8,007 (about US$1,530) in a car and R$17,100 (about US$3,280) in a house, Poder360 said.

A cash seizure and a candidate arrested twice

On Saturday morning the PF launched Operation Moriarty in Caracaraí, in southern Roraima, serving two search warrants, G1 reported. It follows the seizure of about R$4 million (about US$766,000) spotted during a monitored bank withdrawal.

Police see no clear reason for the cash and suspect it was meant to fund campaigns illegally.

Separately, state assembly candidate Jalser Renier (PSDB) was arrested on 24 September and again on 1 October, G1 reported. Police said a spreadsheet in his closet planned payments of up to R$500 (about US$96) to more than 12,000 voters.

Renier was released on Friday after his defence intervened. He has not been convicted of any offence.

A national clampdown, and a reporting system that works

Roraima’s vote-buying cases are part of a wider push. By 1 October the PF had opened 1,224 electoral-crime inquiries this year, seizing about R$33 million (about US$6.3 million), SBT News reported.

The Roraima cases also show the safeguards working, since citizens tipped off police in most of them. Officials are preparing elsewhere too: Amazon Drought: Brazil’s Election Court Lines Up Backup Polling Sites Before Sunday.

What Is Not Yet Known

Investigators are still tracing who financed the Boa Vista vote-buying payments, and whether other local politicians benefited, O Globo reported. No response from Trindade or Belota appeared in the reports by Saturday afternoon.

The owner of the Caracaraí cash has not been named. It is also unclear whether the 21 people held on Friday will be indicted before Sunday’s vote.

Sources: O Globo, 3 October 2026; G1 Roraima, 2 October, 3 October and 3 October, and 2 October; Roraima 1, 3 October; Poder360, 3 October; SBT News, 1 October 2026. Conversions at R$5.22 to the dollar (2 October close).

DIPLOMACY · DOMINICAN REPUBLIC

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti and takes no part in the war between Russia and Ukraine.

— What happened On Thursday 1 October a Russian embassy attaché told protesting families the mission would investigate, Listín Diario reported. No written embassy statement had appeared by 3 October.

— Who is involved A rights group said on 1 October that about 150 Dominicans were lured to Russia, 50 of them from Haina. Officials have not confirmed that figure.

— What it means for you On 25 September the foreign ministry urged anyone offered work in Russia online to check the employer, the offer and the contract before travelling.

— Still open Whether the embassy opens a formal inquiry, how many Dominicans are at the front, and whether Russia will let them leave.

A Russian diplomat says his embassy will look into reports of Dominicans recruited to fight in Ukraine, Listín Diario reported. The attaché, Alexander Agafonov, spoke on Thursday 1 October while families protested outside the embassy.

He said the mission had no earlier reports and would start from documents handed over by a human rights group. No written statement had appeared on the embassy’s website by Saturday 3 October, and other Dominican outlets have largely repeated Listín’s account.

What the embassy official said

Agafonov received documents from Carlos Sánchez Díaz of the Dominican Committee for Human Rights, a non-governmental group. He gave Sánchez his contact details and offered a meeting once the embassy has official information, according to Listín.

The paper describes a pledge to investigate, not a formal inquiry with terms or a deadline. The embassy’s own website names Alexey Seredin as Russia’s ambassador to the Dominican Republic.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Families say about 150 men are involved

Sánchez puts the number of Dominicans recruited and taken to Russia at about 150. Roughly 50 are from Haina, an industrial town near the capital, and others from San José de Ocoa and Greater Santo Domingo.

He told Listín the men answered online offers of work in Panama or cultural exchanges at Russian museums. They travelled via Panama or Istanbul to Kazan, he said, and reached the front after about two weeks of training.

El Día reported that some were promised one million roubles a month, which the paper put at about US$12,000. Relatives told Listín they can speak to the men only on Sundays, for 10 to 20 minutes.

What the Dominican government is doing

President Luis Abinader said on Friday 2 October that the foreign ministry, known as Mirex, is following the complaints. The ministry is working “to know the situation in detail,” he said, according to El Nuevo Diario.

On 25 September Mirex warned citizens about job offers in Russia and promised consular help to bring vulnerable people home. That day Abinader put those who answered at perhaps fewer than 20 (see Dominican Republic Warns of Russian Job Offers as Recruits Reach the Front).

The rights group says it has filed evidence with the Attorney General’s office, which runs the national prosecution service. No response from prosecutors had been reported by 3 October.

A diplomatic channel is now open

The attaché’s remarks give families a direct line to Russian diplomats, alongside the government’s own contacts. In September, Foreign Minister Víctor Bisonó raised the job offers with Russia’s foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, at the UN General Assembly.

In Panama, three Dominicans are detained over recruiting Panamanians for Russia, Acento reported, citing Panamanian prosecutors. Similar cases reach across the region, as in Ukraine Says Argentine Prisoner of War Answered a Facebook Job Advert.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is unclear whether the embassy will open a formal inquiry, or share any findings with Dominican authorities or families. No comment from Moscow on the Dominican cases had been reported by 3 October.

How many Dominicans recruited by these networks are now at the front, and whether any have died, remains unconfirmed. It is also unknown whether Russia will release men who say they were deceived.

Sources: Remolacha, 3 October 2026 (republishing Listín Diario); Listín Diario, 1 October and 2 October 2026; Hoy, El Día and Teleuniverso, 1 October 2026; El Nuevo Diario, 2 October 2026; Acento, 1 October 2026; Embassy of the Russian Federation in the Dominican Republic, news page, checked 3 October 2026.

SECURITY · MEXICO

Key Facts — The country Mexico’s state of Tamaulipas faces Texas across the Rio Grande, called the Río Bravo in Mexico. The Navy runs a naval sector in Matamoros, the border city opposite Brownsville.

— What happened On 3 October 2026, Mexico’s Navy and Foreign Ministry said 159 naval personnel, 11 vehicles and two drones patrol the Matamoros border strip in “mirror operations” with the US.

— Who is involved Mexico’s Navy under Operation Sable; about 500 US troops under Northern Command’s Operation Ardent Vanguard in Texas’s Rio Grande Valley, according to the joint statement of 3 October.

— What it means for you People moving between Matamoros and the Rio Grande Valley may see more patrols and drones. The statement announced no change to border crossings.

— Still open How long both deployments last, and what the US investigation into a 26 September shooting at a Coast Guard boat near Garceno, Texas, finds.

Mexico’s Navy keeps 159 personnel on the Tamaulipas border with Texas, in what officials call mirror operations with the United States. It said so on Saturday, 3 October 2026, after reports that about 500 US troops had moved into Texas’s Rio Grande Valley.

The Navy, known as Semar, and the Foreign Ministry (SRE) issued a joint statement to explain the two deployments. Both forces, they said, act in parallel and stay inside their own country’s territory.

What the Navy Has on the Border

From its Matamoros naval sector, the Navy patrols the strip under Operation Sable with 159 personnel, 11 vehicles and two drones. La Jornada and UnoTV both reported the same figures from the joint statement.

López-Dóriga Digital also reported the figures on Saturday. Semar said it “maintains” the deployment, but it did not say when the patrols began.

Personnel deployed on each side of the Rio Grande in the mirror operations: about 500 US troops in Texas, 159 Mexican Navy personnel in Matamoros. Source: Semar and SRE joint statement, 3 October 2026.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Mexico Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The US Side of the River

The statement said US Northern Command had disclosed about 500 armed forces personnel under Operation Ardent Vanguard. Northern Command is the US military headquarters responsible for defending North American territory.

Ardent Vanguard is the umbrella name for the command’s border-security mission, according to the US military’s public media archive. Its stated aims include stopping drug trafficking, human smuggling and unlawful mass migration.

Northern Command said the reinforcement, named Operation Unified Resolve, began on Friday, 2 October, as part of Ardent Vanguard. US and Mexican media linked it to an attack on a Coast Guard boat on the river. The Coast Guard said its crew came under gunfire from the Mexican side near Garceno, Texas, on 26 September and returned fire; nobody was hurt.

Univision described the troops as National Guard members, while Northern Command said they belong to its Joint Task Force-Southern Border.

How Mirror Operations Work

In mirror operations, each country acts at the same time but only on its own soil, UnoTV reported, citing Semar and SRE. Mexico watches from Tamaulipas while US forces deploy in Texas.

Semar said any information exchange runs through established institutional channels, with full respect for sovereignty. The statement listed four principles: sovereignty, shared responsibility, mutual trust and cooperation without subordination.

Why It Matters for the Border

For residents and traders, parallel patrols signal coordination between the two armed forces rather than confrontation. Mexico presented the patrols as part of an agreed joint model with Washington.

The risk is that armed incidents on the river draw larger deployments on both banks. Tamaulipas is a long-standing cartel stronghold, as shown in Mexico Arrests Alleged Gulf Cartel Money Man in Fuel-Smuggling Raids.

US migration enforcement adds pressure on the same relationship. The latest figures appear in Mexico Border Arrests Near 200,000 in Four Months.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither government has said how long the deployments will last or whether they will grow. Northern Command has spoken of hundreds of troops; the figure of about 500 comes from the Mexican statement and US media reports.

Who fired at the Coast Guard has not been established, and the incident remains under investigation. The joint statement, as reported by La Jornada and UnoTV, did not address the shooting.

Sources: Semar and SRE joint statement of 3 October 2026, as reported by La Jornada and UnoTV; López-Dóriga Digital, 3 October 2026; Univision; DVIDS, Operation Ardent Vanguard; Newsweek, 2 October 2026.
