World.title: International News: Human Rights groups urge UN to challenge ICE policy hiding detainee locations
World.content:
International News: Human Rights groups urge UN to challenge ICE policy hiding detainee locations

By Zoila Palma: Human rights organizations are asking a United Nations panel to intervene over a new U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) practice that withholds the locations of thousands of detainees facing deportation from their families and lawyers.

ICE removed the names of detainees with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System on September 15, a change that reportedly affects more than 16,000 of the nearly 69,000 people in ICE custody, AP reports.

Immigration advocates say the policy is making it more difficult for detainees to access legal representation and challenge their deportations, while leaving families unable to locate their relatives.

A coalition of more than 30 organizations petitioned the U.N. Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances, asking it to declare the practice a violation of international law and urge ICE to reverse it. More than 45 House Democrats have also called on ICE to restore the detainees’ names to the online system.

The Department of Homeland Security rejected claims that the policy amounts to making detainees disappear, saying detainees have opportunities to communicate with family members and attorneys and that the department’s procedures comply with due process.

However, the human rights coalition said the policy has obstructed lawyers from locating their clients and intervening in cases involving immigration relief, detention challenges and deportation orders.

World.title: International News: Empty nets as El Niño drives fish into cooler waters across Latin America
World.content:
International News: Empty nets as El Niño drives fish into cooler waters across Latin America

By Zoila Palma: Fishermen along Latin America’s Pacific coast are struggling with sharply reduced catches as unusually warm ocean temperatures, intensified by El Niño, push tuna, anchovies and other fish species toward cooler waters.

From Ecuador and Peru to Panama and Guatemala, some small-scale fishermen have stopped going to sea altogether as catches decline close to shore, with ocean temperatures in some areas reaching as much as six degrees Celsius above normal.

In Ecuador’s southwestern fishing port of Santa Rosa, fisherman Juan Ollague said that after spending a night at sea, he returned with just six small tuna, AFP reports.

Fellow fisherman Darwin Zambrano said catches of larger tuna such as albacore and bonito have declined significantly in recent weeks. Oceanographer Jonathan Cedeno said sea surface temperatures off Ecuador have increased by 2.5 to 3 degrees Celsius, while temperatures at a depth of 40 meters have risen by as much as six degrees over the past 10 weeks.

The effects are also being felt across Central America. In Panama, fishermen say they are traveling farther from shore, increasing expenses for fuel, food and ice needed to preserve their catch. Some have decided to remain in port because they can no longer cover their operating costs.

In Guatemala, fisherman Eliseo Ovando said it now takes three days to catch what he previously caught in one day, while in Peru, some fishermen who depend on anchovies have reportedly turned to construction work to support their families.

The decline in catches is also creating economic ripple effects in fishing communities and markets. Vendors in Panama report receiving smaller quantities of fish, while in Ecuador, prices for mahi-mahi and swordfish have reportedly doubled amid shortages.

World.title: The minute no Belizean leader has ever spoken, so this column will speak it
World.content:
The minute no Belizean leader has ever spoken, so this column will speak it

By Horace Palacio:

Spend one Saturday listening to political Belize.

The morning shows shouting over each other. The comment sections sorting every fact by jersey before asking if it is true. The same accusations, the same defenses, the same two colors playing the same match they have played since before most of the audience was born.

Now watch what ordinary Belizeans increasingly do. They turn it off. Not because they stopped loving this country, but because they are tired, bone tired, of stale political arguments that have not produced a new idea, a new megawatt, or a new opportunity in years. That fatigue is one of the most important facts in Belize today, and both parties mistake it for apathy at their peril. It is not apathy. It is an audience waiting for somebody to say something worthy of forty five years of nationhood.

So let me name precisely what is missing, because it is small enough to fit in sixty seconds and large enough to change our politics.

In four and a half decades of addresses, budget speeches, and podiums, try to recall one minute, just one, in which a Belizean leader paused mid-speech to honor an opponent. To credit the other side’s climb. To tell the nation that the rival across the aisle is proof of what a Belizean can become. Search your memory. You will not find it, and neither will I, because our politics has no grammar for grace. We have perfected the attack, the deflection, and the blame, a theater this column audited all year and scored precisely. Sixteen years of mutual accusation over energy, twelve red and six blue, produced exactly zero megawatts. Blame remains the worst performing technology in Belize.

Very well. If no leader will speak the missing minute, this column will draft it for them, free of charge, built entirely from true Belizean stories. Here it is, ready for any podium, either color.

There are thousands of Belizeans outside Belmopan who are tired of our stale arguments and are quietly moving this country forward. They believe, and I believe, that success in Belize should depend not on the accident of birth, or the accident of acquaintance, but on the strength of a person’s work ethic and the scope of their dreams. That is the creed of this land. It is how a farm kitchen in Melinda put Belizean pepper sauce on the shelves of the world. It is how three women with seventy five cents planted a movement that today holds over a billion dollars of our people’s savings. It is how a boy born with a stutter, written off by every conventional measure, became the most honored journalistic voice in the region. And it is how a Maya girl from a village in Toledo rose to the highest office in this land, where she represents every single one of us today.

That is the minute, Belize. Four true stories, sixty seconds, no attack lines. Imagine it spoken in the National Assembly, and imagine the other side rising to applaud, because every word of it belongs to both parties and to neither.

Why has it never been said? Because our tribal war has taught two generations of politicians that honoring an opponent is weakness, that the other side’s presence is itself the problem, that every election is existential. And that belief is exactly why the stale arguments never end, because when your opponent is illegitimate, the argument is the whole politics, and nothing else ever gets built. Hear the correction clearly. Grace toward a rival is not weakness. It is the supreme confidence of a leader who knows the game has rules and both teams share one country. A politics that cannot produce one minute of it is not tough. It is insecure, and the nation pays its therapy bills in blackouts and stagnation.

Meanwhile, the sentence at the heart of the missing minute is already true, and this column holds the receipts. The Belizeans moving the country forward were never at the podiums. The cattlemen who built a fifty million dollar export trade from nothing. The citizens who oversubscribed the Hydro Belize shares, queuing to own rather than to beg. The officers who pressed send at personal risk so the truth could breathe. The teachers improvising brilliance inside a broken design, the mas camp artists, the young creators, the farmers, the credit union tellers. The real Belize has been building this whole time, outside the shouting, waiting decades for its politics to grow up and notice.

But honesty is the house rule, so the creed itself must face the mirror too. Success by work ethic and the scope of dreams, is that today’s Belize? You know the ledger, because this column wrote it. The duck gets the appointment while the eagle waits. The contract follows the connection. The land speaks US dollars, and the upstairs jobs arrive on work permits. Too often, the honest Belizean sentence is that success depends on the accident of acquaintance. Our ladder stories are real and glorious, and that is exactly the problem. They are miracles. A nation is not great when it produces miracle climbs. A nation is great when climbing is unremarkable, and making the climb unremarkable, through the daylight, the schools, the megawatts, the fair rules this column demands weekly, is the entire national project hiding inside that one unspoken minute.

So, three challenges, addressed by name, as always.

To the Prime Minister. In your next national address, spend sixty seconds honoring one opponent’s climb. It costs nothing and purchases more national healing than any announcement in the speech.

To the Leader of the Opposition. Credit one thing government delivered, fully, without a but. The tired Belizeans are not waiting for total war. They are waiting for somewhere to go, and the first party confident enough to show grace will find them.

And to every citizen in a jersey, red or blue. This week, say one true and kind thing about a Belizean wearing the other color. Out loud. The repair of our politics will not begin at any podium. It begins in our mouths, at our tables, in our comment sections.

The minute is drafted now. The stories in it are true. The climbers are already climbing, the builders already building, and the Maya girl from Toledo is already in Government House, proof that the creed runs closer to reality than our arguments have ever allowed us to see.

All that remains unwritten is the delivery.

The podium is open, Belize.

Somebody go first.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: 911 – But Who Checked the Pulse?
World.content:
911 – But Who Checked the Pulse?

The views expressed in this article are those of the writer and not necessarily those of Breaking Belize News.



Nine candidates, two public tests, and the question behind the UDP emergency call

By Lennox Lamb: In The 786 Problem, I ended with a question:

What exactly is the UDP building in Belize City?

I said that conversation was still coming.

Well, it reach.

On Tuesday, the United Democratic Party lined up nine mayoral candidates at its headquarters at the foot of the BelChina Bridge and introduced its municipal campaign under one of the smartest political themes we have seen this season:

911.

Nine municipalities. One party. One country.

And, according to UDP Leader Tracy Panton, a national emergency.

Sharp branding.

Clean presentation.

But perhaps a politically weak move.

Di siren loud.

And for old UDP heads, the word pulse carries another echo.

The People’s Pulse once carried the party’s voice. Today, Belize wants to know whether the UDP still has one.

The launch showed nine faces without showing how much political strength stood behind most of them. It created the image of readiness while withholding the evidence that would allow the public to measure it.

But an emergency team does not begin by admiring the ambulance. It checks the patient’s vital signs.

And that is where the real story begins.

This time, follow the decision

The last article stood outside on Freetown Road and watched the machinery move. This one travels back to the foot of the BelChina Bridge.

Into the party structure.

Into the selection process.

Into the space between an application, a promised convention and a name appearing on a platform.

I was not sitting inside the meetings at UDP headquarters. I will not pretend I was.

But Belizeans know: if it stinks, something dead.

And when a promised convention disappears without a public explanation, the smell leads right back to the foot of the BelChina Bridge.

The UDP presented nine mayoral candidates. Of those nine, only two emerged from documented contested mayoral conventions: Dwayne Sampson in Dangriga and Yusef Guerra in Benque Viejo.

Now, let us be fair.

Three municipalities had only one reported mayoral applicant, so no contest was necessary. Fine. A party does not need to manufacture competition where none exists.

But at least four municipalities had more than one known mayoral aspirant. Only two gave supporters a documented public vote. That is not a small procedural detail. That is a political choice.

No mek we dress it up like anything else.

And the biggest unanswered case is Belize City.

Where the UDP checked the pulse

On August 9, the UDP held mayoral conventions in Dangriga and Benque Viejo.

Dangriga drew 886 participants. Dwayne Sampson received 687 votes and Christalyn Castillo received 195.

Benque drew 533 participants. Yusef Guerra received 405 votes and Danette Lee Mendez received 119.

Combined turnout:

1,419.

Both were decisive victories. Both produced a candidate. Both allowed the party to demonstrate that people were prepared to come out and participate.

Dangriga is especially important. Before the vote, an independent poll projected turnout at roughly 695. The actual participation of 886 was about 27 percent higher.

In other words, when the UDP checked the pulse, the pulse was stronger than expected.

Di pulse neva weak.

Di pulse jump.

Panton understood the importance of that moment. Speaking after the conventions, she said it was important for Belize’s democracy and for the party’s democracy to allow people to determine who they believed could best represent them.

That is not my standard being imposed on her.

That is her standard.

So the fair question is simple:

Why did the public testing appear to stop there?

The Belize City promise

On June 30, Panton publicly identified Jacqueline Willoughby and Damian Gough as the UDP’s two Belize City mayoral contenders.

Her words were direct:

“We will have a convention in Belize City to determine our slate.”

That was not a rumour. It was not an interpretation. It was a public commitment from the party leader.

On September 29, Jacqueline Willoughby walked onto the platform as the UDP’s Belize City mayoral candidate.

There was no publicly reported convention.

No public vote total.

No reported explanation of Damian Gough’s withdrawal.

I do not have a verified answer explaining what happened between the June promise and the September presentation.

So I will not manufacture one.

Maybe Gough withdrew privately.

Maybe an agreement was reached.

Maybe the Central Executive Committee made the final decision.

All are possible.

None has been publicly established in the reporting I reviewed.

The question is not whether Willoughby is qualified. The question is how a promised public contest became an unexplained selection.

Somewhere between the open convention and the open microphone, the public test disappeared.

Maybe the purpose was unity. Maybe it was control. Maybe it was simply convenience.

Whatever the purpose, the effect was the same: no turnout, no margin and no public evidence of who could actually move the UDP base in Belize City.

An unexplained selection is not proof of unity. It proves that the public was not shown the test.

A process is not the same as a test

The UDP did have a process.

Applications were received. A nominations committee conducted reviews and vetting. Recommendations went to the Central Executive Committee. We know that process had consequences because Philip Willoughby’s application for mayor was rejected while his councillor application was accepted.

So it would be false to say there was no process.

But a process conducted at the foot of the BelChina Bridge and a political test conducted among supporters are not the same thing.

A committee can determine whether a person meets the party’s requirements.

A convention can show whether that person can organise, mobilise and bring supporters through the door.

Vetting tells you who the party believes is suitable.

Voting tells you who the party’s people are prepared to follow.

A rebuilding opposition needs both answers.

The emergency inside the emergency

The UDP’s 911 message was aimed at conditions in Belize’s municipalities, not at the condition of the UDP itself.

Fair enough.

But political slogans have a way of turning around and questioning the people who created them.

In 2015, the UDP won 62 of Belize’s 67 municipal seats.

By 2021, it held two.

In 2024, it recovered to six seats, all of them in San Ignacio and Santa Elena.

That 2024 result was a small recovery, not another decline. The numbers must be stated honestly.

But six out of 67 is still nine percent.

One council out of nine.

That is not political death.

But it is an emergency.

And a party in emergency cannot measure readiness by the number of candidates standing behind a podium. It has to know whether organisation exists beneath their feet.

Nine names prove that the UDP has a roster.

They do not yet prove that it has a rescue team.

No numbers is still an answer

For four weeks, this series pulled apart PUP conventions.

We examined crowds, delegates, margins, factional alignments, unexplained ballots and even a one-vote difference.

The PUP got hammered because it opened its internal contests and produced numbers that could be tested.

The UDP should not receive a free pass because it produced fewer numbers.

No sah. Same ruler fi everybody.

The absence of a public contest is not the absence of something to analyse. It is itself the analysis.

No convention means no turnout figure.

No margin.

No visible map of support.

No way to know whether a candidate has a working political base or only the approval of headquarters.

Whether this was designed to avoid scrutiny or merely had that effect, the result is the same: the party made itself harder to measure from the outside and perhaps easier to manage from the inside.

That may protect a leadership team from an uncomfortable Monday morning.

It does not prepare a party for March.

If you refuse to test your strength, you also refuse to know your weakness.

World.title: Belize Birding Festival takes flight today in Orange Walk
World.content:
Belize Birding Festival takes flight today in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Bird lovers, today is your day.

The Belize Birding Festival is happening today, October 3, at the Orange Walk Multi Purpose Complex in Orange Walk Town.

The festival celebrates Belize’s vibrant birdlife, community and conservation, bringing together nature enthusiasts, families and anyone curious about the country’s incredible bird species.

The event is supported by the Belize Tourism Industry Association and the Belize Audubon Society.

Organizers have called it one event you will not want to miss.

World.title: Briceño: Criticizing public officials should not be a crime
World.content:
By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize’s cybercrime law is being rewritten to make sure criticism, journalism and satire are not treated as crimes.

Prime Minister John Briceño says the amendments are meant to ensure democratic debate is protected online.

“This protection is intended to ensure that democratic debate, investigative journalism, political criticism, and other forms of public discourse are not criminalized merely because they are offensive, embarrassing or critical of public figures,” Briceño said.

The bill would refocus the law on clearly defined and serious forms of technology facilitated abuse, such as fake or impersonated content passed off as real.

It also adds a safeguard. No one could be prosecuted under the Act without written approval from the Director of Public Prosecutions.

The amendments would also clarify when Belizean courts have authority to hear cybercrime cases.

The move comes as recent cases, from alleged credit card scams in the BPO sector to high profile online complaints, have shown how complex cybercrime has become as more business, communication and financial activity moves online.

World.title: East scores brace as Reggae Boyz beat 10-man El Salvador
World.content:
Jamaica's forward #12 Javon East celebrates scoring his team's second goal during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match between El Salvador and Jamaica at the Cuscatlan Stadium in San Salvador on October 2, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica returned to winning ways in the Concacaf Nations League on Friday as Javon East scored both goals in the Reggae Boyz’ 2-0 victory over host El Salvador.

El Salvador were reduced to 10 men in the 20th minute after Rudy Clavel was shown a straight red card for a challenge on East.

From that point onwards, the Boyz piled on the pressure on the Central Americans and were rewarded in the 39th minute when East volleyed home from an excellent cross by Miguel Freckleton.

East added to his tally in the 64th minute with a brilliant one-time shot after being found by substitute Jahmarie Nolan.

With the win, Jamaica sit at second place in Group B with six points, just a point behind leaders Suriname.

World.title: Strike could not have come at a worse time, says Annotto Bay Hospital CEO
World.content:
Annotto Bay Hospital via its Facebook page.

ANNOTTO BAY, St Mary – With the hospital already grappling with a shortage of doctors, the management of Annotto Bay Hospital on Friday said they were operating in emergency mode as many junior doctors across the country withdrew their services.

Chief executive officer Dale Brown told the Jamaica Observer that while the hospital had activated its contingency plan, deploying consultants and senior medical officers to critical areas, the strain was beginning to show.

“We have the MO4s [senior doctors] out manning the areas to ensure that we do not have any deaths. A few junior doctors turned up, so the amount of persons that turned up we have to utilise them to man areas in case of an emergency,” Brown explained.

He noted that routine clinics were scaled back, with only critical cases being seen. Other appointments were rescheduled. The CEO said the industrial action could not have come at a worse time as the Type C hospital was already understaffed. Annotto Bay Hospital is the main referral medical facility for the eastern parishes of St Mary, Portland and St Ann. Staff say they are bracing for an influx of emergencies while running on a skeleton crew.

The strike is expected to last one day as, in a press release on Friday, Jamaica Medical Doctors Association (JMDA) President Dr Jubilee Brown said the body “cannot guarantee normalcy from 8 am on Friday, October 2, 2026 to 8 am on Saturday, October 3, 2026.

Brown warned that if it goes beyond that, Annotto Bay Hospital’s ability to cope will be severely tested.

“It will have a negative impact on the hospital. However, we will still be able to manage emergencies. The amount of people we have will also have burnout and will require at least some time to pause. Basically, the emergency mode persons are in overdrive,” he said.

“You have to plan just in case it would be prolonged. We will be able to man the emergencies but we do not know how long we can hold out in doing such,” Brown added.

— Ingrid Henry

World.title: Hospitals hobbled
World.content:
The Health and Wellness Ministry says there were no adverse events at the island’s public health facilities Friday after junior doctors stayed away in protest over a long-running dispute with the Government relating to overtime pay.

However, checks by Jamaica Observer journalists in rural areas found long wait times at some facilities, while others showed no evidence of outpatient activity.

World.title: Underhanded insurance companies
World.content:
Government Senator Charles Sinclair his contribution to the debate on the Jamaica Consumer and Competition Authority Bill, 2026 in the Senate on Friday. (Photo: Karl McLarty)

Government Senator Charles Sinclair has ripped into what he has described as “underhanded insurance companies”, which he said only respond to third party claims when court action is initiated.

Sinclair, a veteran attorney- at-law, made the accusation in the Senate on Friday during his contribution to the debate on the Jamaica Consumer and Competition Authority Bill, 2026.

The authority will in effect be a merger of the Consumer Affairs Commission and the Fair Trading Commission. Sinclair described third parties (the victims) as being “on the other side of the coin to policyholders of motor vehicle insurance”. “Many of these third parties are not motor vehicle owners but are pedestrians or cyclists. Many are innocent passengers in a vehicle trying to get from one place to another to earn a living or just get on with their lives.

Unfortunately, an accident arises; they suffer loss or damage, leaving them challenged in many respects and in need of compensation,” Sinclair said. “The policyholder has acted properly in reporting to the insurance carrier with facts which clearly and indisputably establish negligence on his part.

He expects his policy to protect him from a court action,” Sinclair added. However, he lamented that in many instances when a claim is submitted, even in cases when attorneys are engaged, the claimant is met with total silence. He said such silence includes correspondence not responded to for months; telephone calls being screened; calls not returned; and the telephone ringing without answer until the call is disconnected. “Many of the insurance companies move to settlement when court action is brought. That is the only time you see them moving,” Sinclair charged.

He said it was the delay tactics on the part of insurance carriers that force court action to be filed, further placing burden on an overburdened court system. “They know the delay in the Supreme Court, and they know the limit on the monetary jurisdiction in the Parish Court. They know Jamaicans are not generally litigious. Many give up and suffer in silence. Many abandon parts of genuine claims just to get a little compensation,” Sinclair told his colleagues.

“Those practices are blatantly underhanded. The public needs real protection from the bodies that can correct these shortcomings,” he insisted. Sinclair reasoned that these practices, which hurt the victims of accidents, are more egregious when one takes account of the fact that insurance coverage provided by private enterprise is mandated by law under the Motor Vehicle (Third Party Risks) Act and enforced by the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

“The insurance carrier is the only business that has the Government working on its enforcement,” he said. A former mayor of Montego Bay who still sits in the St James Municipal Corporation as a councillor, Sinclair repeated a call for the minister of justice to increase the monetary jurisdiction of the parish court from $1 million to $5 million. He said this was necessary since many of the insurance carriers move to settlement when court action is filed.

“The parish court is the court which gives the small man greater access to justice, and it’s high time we make the adjustment to allow them to recover their full claim without having to abandon any part of their claim,” Sinclair argued. He noted that in other jurisdictions, legislation has been created over the past 10 years to ensure prompt settlement of claims by the creation of timelines and standards.

“We should look at what can be adopted to better fit our circumstances,” he said, while noting that the trust factor is so low between insurers and the insured that Jamaicans were referring to the entire industry as a sham, and deeming those in charge to be scammers.

World.title: Pain and agony at Mandeville Regional
World.content:
A 75-year-old outpatient showing his swollen knee while waiting without knowing whether he will be seen by a doctor on Friday at Mandeville Regional Hospital.

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — A 75-year-old outpatient was among scores of people who either left Mandeville Regional Hospital or waited in pain as most junior doctors withdrew their services on Friday.

“This is not what I am accustomed to, and a lot of the people who were here waiting along with me, they left. I even left too and returned, yet I am still sitting and waiting. I am suffering from pain right now.

I don’t know what cause it and there is nobody to tell me what it is,” the senior citizen who had a swollen left knee told the Jamaica Observer on Friday.

The doctors were protesting the delay by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) in handing down a ruling as it relates to overtime payments. Senior medical officer at Mandeville Regional Hospital Dr Everton McIntosh told the Observer that he was “hoping and praying that normalcy” would resume by late Friday or early Saturday.

“If this goes into the weekend then it becomes a lot more stressful, because the few doctors who we have won’t be able to continue indefinitely,” said McIntosh.

He warned the public of the significant delays to access health care at the already overcrowded facility manned by 24 consultants up to mid-afternoon on Friday. “If your condition is not serious, if you are not very sick, perhaps you should consider not coming to the hospital today [Friday]. Our present patient count is 315…

We still have a significant number of patients. A big part of the problem is that over the past several months, since Hurricane Melissa, we have been inundated with patients coming for admissions — particularly medical patients with complications of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, stroke, cancers, and those kinds of things. “In any hospital, the majority of the staff would be the junior [doctors], and then there are the consultants who would lead them.

We should have had a total of 133 doctors on duty but just the consultants are here, which is about 24, who are actually working,” added McIntosh. He said all departments and wards were left without adequate staff on Friday. “We can see the discrepancy there out of a total of 133.

That has grave implications for the ability for us to cover all of the areas adequately in terms of the wards, the emergency departments, the outpatients and the clinics, so it is not physically possible for the few consultants to carry that workload,” McIntosh said while pointing to a drastic scaling down of routine procedures.

“For example, our outpatient clinics where you see patients who are walk-in patients, those services have basically been suspended for the day [Friday],” added McIntosh. He said people who turned up at the hospital were given a rescheduled appointment date and/or prescriptions. “Similarly, elective surgeries [that were] planned maybe weeks or months before to do a particular surgery, those have had to be postponed as well.

We are only focusing on emergency care, serious emergencies,” said McIntosh. “The whole idea is to ensure that we have adequate coverage for persons who are very ill so that nobody will die or suffer serious complications due to lack of care. All those persons who are well enough who can wait will be asked to wait.

“Even at the wards, what we have done also to reduce the workload is to discharge those persons who are stable, and do not require high-level care, and can survive if they go home with some instructions and with medication. Some of them will be asked to come back early to the clinic to be assessed, just to ensure that they are maintaining good health,” added McIntosh.

World.title: Western health centres see fewer patients
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — There were fewer people than usual seeking medical care at State-run medical facilities in western Jamaica on Friday as members of the public appeared to heed warnings to only seek help if they had no other choice because junior doctors withdrew their services.

“Last night I told them not to come unless it is urgent or an emergency,” clinical coordinator for the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA) Dr Delroy Fray told the Jamaica Observer Friday afternoon. While he did not have supporting data to share at the time, Fray said there were fewer than usual admissions to accident and emergency (A&E) departments across St James, Hanover, Westmoreland, and Trelawny.

“We kind of control it, because we did not want the patient who needs care to suffer because of [the strike],” Dr Fray explained. At 8:00 am on Friday, junior doctors across Jamaica went on strike to protest the delay by the Industrial Disputes Tribunal (IDT) in handing down a ruling related to years of wrangling over retroactive overtime payments.

To fill the gap, senior doctors, many of them consultants, had to step up and shoulder the additional workload, particularly in A&E departments. “We assigned all the doctors from yesterday; everybody knows what they were supposed to do and they have fulfilled it,” Dr Fray stated. At Noel Holmes Hospital in Lucea, one nurse confirmed that patients stayed away. “Things are slow. [I] don’t even think the doctors see 10 people from morning,” she told the Observer.

Of the three shifts scheduled for the day, the first shift — which ended at 3:00 pm — was staffed by five of its six doctors, comprising senior and Cuban physicians. However, all 14 junior doctors assigned to the parish’s six curative clinics stayed away, according to medical officer of health for the Hanover Health Department Dr Kaushal Singh.

“Due to that, we had to reorganise services. We were supposed to have six curative clinics — meaning the six clinics where doctors are supposed to go, [and] we had to reappoint four clinics [where patients were provided with new dates within two weeks],” Singh told the Observer.

“Two clinics were operated by the senior medical officers — Lucea in the western end of the parish and Mount Peto in the eastern section. Anybody who needs a repeat prescription should go to these clinics and get their prescription filled,” Singh advised. Despite the challenges, Singh confirmed that all 18 health centres in Hanover remained open on Friday, with maternal and child health, family planning, nutrition, and oral health services running smoothly. The Observer spoke with two patients at the Lucea clinic who expressed support for the doctors.

One woman, who identified herself only as McPherson, said she understood the situation and was willing to be patient. “It not easy, but you know we always have the doctors them move fast enough with us here. If they have a delay now we just have to cope with them,” said McPherson. Another patient shared a similar sentiment, highlighting the personal toll the profession takes. “Them have family to support, them have children, and every day them have to be in the hospital.

Them can’t sleep in them bed in peace; every minute them get call,” said the patient as he recalled experiences waiting hours at the hospital due to emergency cases taking precedence. Meanwhile, a visit to Falmouth Public General Hospital in Trelawny found the usually bustling A&E Department almost empty.

“You see, them can do better. But [usually], even if them eyelash a hurt them, them come,” one member of staff said. However, at the A&E at Cornwall Regional Hospital in St James one woman, who was outside with her ailing male relative, said they were inconvenienced by the doctors’ strike.

“We have to go to Type 5 because they are on strike. We’ve been here like two hours but now we are waiting on the drive to go down there,” said the woman who did not give her name. Type 5 is the informal name for Montego Bay Comprehensive Health Centre, and indications are things went smoothly there throughout the day.

“The turnout was the [usual] amounts, nothing really different, because patients wouldn’t know who is on strike,” St James Health Services Parish Manager Lennox Wallace told the Observer. He said in preparation for the strike they had made adjustments to the opening hours on Friday. “We were not going to take the risk, even though [most of] the doctors came out on Friday.

We had to play it by ear so I had given instructions that the clinic be closed at 4:00 pm on Friday and not 10:00 pm — because we have to gauge the risk,” Wallace explained. He said they attended to all patients who turned up Friday, even if some were rescheduled for other dates.

“No patient that came here, as much as you can see that it is empty, not even one was turned away — not even one,” Wallace stressed. He said while fewer doctors showed up for work, each of the 22 health centres in the parish had a doctor present throughout the day. “We would have had like 10 doctors normally.

We had six today but we should have the full complement Saturday and Sunday,” said Wallace.

World.title: STICK OR MOVE!
World.content:
West Indies cricketer Rovman Powell

Jamaican cricketers Rovman Powell, Vitel Lawes and John Campbell are among West Indies players who have two weeks to decide whether to accept reduced contracts offered by Cricket West Indies (CWI).

Last week, the regional governing body announced that international retainer contracts would see fees cut by 25 per cent as part of a series of measures to address CWI’s current financial challenges.

CWI CEO, Jamaica’s Chris Dehring, told ESPN Cricinfo on Thursday, that the West Indies Players Association (WIPA) agreed to the changes following “multiple discussions” which started from 2025.

Dehring revealed that the international players were directly addressed at a meeting last Wednesday. “We held a Zoom call involving CWI, WIPA and both male and female players.

There were over 96 participants in that video conference, where we outlined the plans, explained the situation, and answered questions. The CWI president [Kishore Shallow], the director of cricket [Miles Bascombe] and I were on that call along with the WIPA president [Wavell Hinds] and secretary [Wayne Lewis],” he said.

Although the list hasn’t been made public, it’s understood former T20 Captain Powell, spinner Lawes and opening batsmen Campbell, who are currently part of the Windies squad for the ongoing tour of India, have all been offered retainer contracts along with Windies red ball captain Roston Chase, white ball captain Shai Hope and pacers Shamar Joseph and Alzarri Joseph.

However, Dehring admits there is no guarantee the players will accept the offer, with the option of franchise cricket on the table. “WIPA has agreed with us on the domestic side, and we informed them what we’re able to afford on the international side. So really that is now up to individual players to determine whether or not they would like to sign international contracts that have been offered to them,” he said.

“With regard to them being able to earn outside of West Indies cricket in other lucrative leagues around the world, we have always been very understanding, allowing players leeway where we can. WIPA and ourselves have also discussed various options to seek amicable compromise before coming to an agreement.”

“Of course, we would prefer them to play for the West Indies at all times as a priority, but we also understand that there are opportunities around the world for them to apply their trade.

At the same time, we believe there should be some level of obligation to give back to the institution that is West Indies cricket, which facilitated the opportunity for them to earn from cricket. We believe, by and large, the players understand that obligation.” With the India tour wrapping up on October 17, Dehring believes the players have ample time to weigh their options.

“We don’t want players to feel there is the proverbial gun to their head to sign contracts that have been offered. It’s an important and considered decision for them to make, discuss it with their agents, their lawyers, so we have given them two weeks to review and they can decide whether or not they choose to be internationally contracted players,” he said.

“That would not preclude them from being selected to represent West Indies, or making themselves available to West Indies. So, we will wait to hear from those players that have been offered international contracts as to whether they are accepting or not. And then, we will get them approved at CWI board level and announce those players.”

The Windies Women, who are currently touring Zimbabwe, will also face a 25 per cent pay cut including Jamaicans Stafanie Taylor and Chinelle Henry. — Daniel Blake

World.title: Sandals Foundation Island Challenge off to strong start in Jamaica
World.content:
Men’s Health magazine writer Andrew Tracey competes in Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica on Friday.

OCHO RIOS, St Ann — Sandals Foundation’s Island Challenge Jamaica got off to a strong start on Friday, with approximately 30 participants from the United Kingdom testing their endurance along Jamaica’s north coast.

The event forms part of a four-day fundraising effort aimed at strengthening neonatal and paediatric healthcare.

The opening day saw participants complete a 10-kilometre run from Rio Nuevo Fishing Beach in St Mary to Sandals Ochi Beach Club, before taking to the water for a five-kilometre kayak along the White River Fish Sanctuary.

The challenge, which runs from October 2 to 5, has brought together athletes, travel industry figures and community supporters, with a target of raising £100,000 to purchase essential medical equipment and strengthen paediatric and neonatal services at Falmouth Public General Hospital in Trelawny.

Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke sounded the horn to officially start Friday’s competition, sending participants off on the first leg of what is expected to become an increasingly demanding journey over the next three days.

For Clarke, however, the physical test is secondary to the lives the initiative is intended to impact. “It’s really all about raising money to buy equipment for our hospitals here in the Caribbean,” she said. “For this one, the Falmouth General Hospital is going to benefit. “We’re really thrilled to be able to support the doctors and nurses working there who are working in conditions that have not been ideal since Hurricane Melissa.”

The intensity off the challenge is expected to increase on Saturday when participants climb the world-famous Dunn’s River Falls before embarking on a 10-kilometre rainforest trek and tree-planting exercise in the Bogue 11 Forest. “This challenge is everything from running to kayaking to hiking… to Trelawny up to Blue Hope then into the Blue Mountains for a hike and sampling some great Blue Mountain coffee on Monday,” Clarke said.

On Sunday, the group will be joined by 13 local participants for a 21-kilometre half-marathon through Falmouth. The route will take them past Falmouth Public General Hospital before continuing through the historic town, Hague and on to Good Hope.

The challenge culminates on Monday in St Andrew, where participants will face a military-style endurance test in Newcastle before taking on a partial hike of the Blue Mountains, reaching approximately 4,500 feet above sea level. Among those taking on the challenge is Men’s Health magazine writer Andrew Tracey, who is participating for the second consecutive year after completing the 2025 staging in Saint Lucia.

Tracey said Friday’s opening leg provided an early indication of just how demanding the Jamaican edition could be, particularly because of the humid conditions. “It was tough, it was really tough. It was so humid,” Tracey said. “The sun came out in Saint Lucia so it was like running up a hill in a spotlight, but we were blessed with a little bit of cloud cover today. It wasn’t easy by any stretch of the imagination, but a little bit more enjoyable.”

This year’s fundraising effort has taken on added significance following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa at Falmouth Public General Hospital last October. The Category 5 hurricane caused extensive damage to the facility, including the loss of approximately 90 per cent of its roofing.

Extensive flooding also compromised electrical systems as well as diagnostic and clinical equipment. Proceeds from the Island Challenge are expected to help purchase equipment and strengthen the hospital’s capacity to provide care for newborns and children.

Peter Davenport of the Daily Mail in the United Kingdom, who is also participating in the challenge, said this year’s event has taken on even greater meaning because of the hurricane’s impact. “Every year is special in what we do, but this year is even more special because of what happened last year,” Davenport said.

“The fact that there is no paediatric care left there now… all the money we make on this trip will go towards that. That’s what it is about. It’s about saving lives.”

Jamaica is the fourth Caribbean country to host the Sandals Foundation Island Challenge, following stagings in Antigua and Barbuda in 2023, St Vincent and the Grenadines in 2024, and Saint Lucia in 2025.

The previous challenges have collectively raised more than £300,000 and benefited approximately 1,800 babies across the region.

Attention now turns to Saturday’s second day, when participants will tackle Dunn’s River Falls before completing the 10-kilometre rainforest trek and tree-planting exercise.

World.title: Two Iranians charged with alleged bomb plot against Britain’s Jewish community
World.content:
Police said the two men received instructions and materials to make a homemade bomb for possible use on Jewish targets.

Two Iranian men have been charged with terror offenses over an alleged plot to bomb Manchester’s Jewish community.

Rahman Salehi, 34, and Salam Ahmadyan, 36, appeared in a British court on Saturday on charges of preparing to commit an act of terrorism or assisting another to commit an act of terrorism.

Police said the two men, who were arrested last month on the eve of the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, had received material and instructions on how to make a bomb, identified targets and carried out reconnaissance ahead of an attack on Jewish targets.

World.title: Spaniards protest housing crisis as Sánchez weighs snap vote
World.content:
“The people on the streets once again hold the power,” she said while addressing the demonstration, insisting that their movement would “no longer tolerate inaction.”

The protests were triggered after an investment firm evicted 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the apartment where she had lived since 1956. Sánchez’s government sought to contain the discontent on Tuesday by unveiling two long-delayed bills aimed at curbing speculative practices, extending eviction protections for vulnerable tenants and automatically renewing existing contracts. But conservative lawmakers in parliament rejected both bills on Friday.

Amid the defeat, senior government figures indicated Sánchez — already under pressure over the ongoing migrant crisis in Ceuta and corruption cases involving members of his family and close political allies — was considering calling a snap election in a bid to capitalize on anger over housing.

Protesters hold a banner reading ‘towards the general strike’ along Gran Via street during a demonstration against the housing crisis on October 3, 2026 in Madrid. | Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty Images

Saturday’s protests underscored the risks of that strategy. While demonstrators slammed the conservative opposition for voting down the bills, they also accused Sánchez of failing to tackle the housing crisis since taking office in 2018.

“Eight days of people power have achieved more than eight years of progressive government,” Racu said, adding that protesters would continue pressuring politicians “regardless of who governs this country.”

Calling for a general strike to force the adoption of urgent housing measures, Racu said “the feelings of disaffection, desperation, disillusionment and sadness have been replaced by a new energy on the streets.”

World.title: Sandu slams Russia as attack debris hits Moldova in latest airspace violation
World.content:
Moldova's President Maia Sandu reacts during the Coalition of the Willing meeting, in Kyiv on August 24, 2026. | Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP via Getty Images

Three missile and two drones entered Moldovan airspace and caused collateral damage in the country, local authorities said.

Moldovan President Maia Sandu on Saturday hit out at Moscow after saying debris from five Russian air attack weapons violated the country’s airspace and exploded on the country’s territory.

“I condemn Russia’s attack on Ukraine this morning. Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova,” she wrote on X. “Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil.”

In all, three missiles and two drones flew over the country between 7.45 a.m. and 8 a.m., with fragments later found in the country’s eastern districts of Hincesti, Anenii Noi and Causeni. The police were dispatched to secure the debris, which caused a fire to break out but no casualties.

World.title: Russia hits major Kyiv bridge, logistics hub in latest attack
World.content:
Russia’s defense ministry confirmed it had carried out the attack, stating the bridge was being used to transport military cargo. It also separately said it had struck the key Hostomel logistics hub and a cargo ship crossing the Black Sea near the southern port of Odessa.

Separately, the UN-linked International Atomic Energy Agency said four strikes in recent days had threatened safety and security” at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, including reportedly disabling an off-site radiation monitoring station.

Moscow has stepped up its bombing campaign in recent weeks against Ukraine’s civil and critical infrastructure, targeting residential areas, energy facilities, sea terminals and data centers, setting the stage for a dire winter for Kyiv. In the past week alone, Russia has launched more than 190 missiles and drones, mostly targeting energy infrastructure.

The Russian foreign affairs ministry issued a statement on Saturday warning “foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel against remaining in” Kyiv.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has ordered his troops to abandon the rules of war, Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the FT this week.

Meanwhile, Ukraine is grappling with a yawning financial deficit and shortage of critical weapons. Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi this week said the country faces a $27 billion defense funding gap this year, with Kyiv hoping to cover about $7 billion domestically and looking to partners for the rest.

This article was updated.

World.title: Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act on Nigel Farage
World.content:
Britain’s head of counter-terrorism policing Vicki Evans said the force had “been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time,” adding: “The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the counter-terrorism policing network.”

Kerry is set to appear at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday.

In August, the counter-terrorism force reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack against Farage’s home.

“I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family,” said British Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.”

A Reform official told the BBC: “This is exactly why Nigel needed £5m to protect his security for life.”

Farage is facing a parliamentary watchdog probe into a £5m gift from a billionaire donor before he became an MP in 2024, previously claiming he needed the money to ensure his security.

World.title: Wie Russland die NATO provoziert. Mit Carlo Masala
World.content:
Eine Drohne mit Sprengstoff an einer ukrainischen Frachtmaschine in Leipzig, Explosionen in Munitionsfabriken und Sabotage auf See. Russland intensiviert seine hybride Kriegsführung mitten in Europa und testet gezielt die roten Linien der NATO. Doch was passiert, wenn ein solcher Anschlag auf deutschem Boden tatsächlich gelingt und den Bündnisfall auslöst? Darüber spricht Gordon Repinski in dieser Folge mit Carlo Masala, Professor für Internationale Politik, Universität der Bundeswehr München.

Das Ziel des Kremls ist es, Panik zu schüren und die westliche Unterstützung für die Ukraine zu brechen. Im Gespräch analysiert Carlo, warum Putin gerade jetzt risikofreudiger wird und weshalb Friedrich Merz in der deutschen Debatte als entscheidender Schutzwall für weitere Hilfen gilt. Ein Wegbrechen dieser Unterstützung hätte fatale finanzielle und militärische Folgen für den gesamten Kontinent.

Gleichzeitig wächst der Druck auf Kiew massiv. Die Episode beleuchtet, wie eine mögliche Rückkehr von Trump ins Weiße Haus die Ukraine zu schmerzhaften Deals zwingen könnte und warum das europäische Superwahljahr 2027 Moskau eine beispiellose Chance bietet, die politische Landschaft endgültig zu seinen Gunsten zu drehen.

World.title: Latvian PM faces bittersweet victory in election backdropped by Russia
World.content:
His center-right partners, New Unity, are struggling to cross the 5% electoral threshold, which would be a floundering performance for a party that has been home to many Latvian prime ministers, including current European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis.

But for the party’s prime ministerial candidate and ex-Finance Minister Arvils Ašeradens, the low polling numbers are simply the “political pendulum which shifts from one way to the other,” he told POLITICO in Riga last month.

During the last election in 2022, New Unity was the major beneficiary of a rally-round-the-flag moment as Russia had just launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in 2026, voters seem frustrated with Latvia’s high inflation, the ongoing uncertainty surrounding national airline airBaltic and instrumentalized migration orchestrated by Russia and Belarus.

The prime minister may need to open talks with Ainārs Šlesers, a right-wing veteran of Latvian politics. | Robert Hegedus/EPA

Kulbergs’ other coalition partner, the agrarian Union of Greens and Farmers (known as ZZS), is also polling below the threshold. And if neither party manages to scrape by, it might force Kulbergs to work with the controversial businessman Šlesers, who carefully advocated expanding trade with Russia.

Kulbergs has dismissed this possibility — “as it is given now: no,” he told POLITICO in early September — because he does not trust the people Šlesers has surrounded himself with. Just weeks earlier, however, he had been less definitive, telling POLITICO in July: “I have to see what chess pieces I will get … to make a coalition.”

Šlesers has been a central figure in Latvian politics for decades, most notably as a local “oligarch” who, via family holdings, exerts influence over the Port of Riga. The capital’s harbor has seen its largely Russian and Belarusian hinterland slowly carved off by EU sanctions. And after Kulbergs slapped 300% tariffs on transited Russian grain this month , Šlesers told Latvian national TV such transit should be allowed, though he supports Ukraine’s EU accession.

World.title: ‘Maxi merde’: French presidential campaign rattled by a week of chaos
World.content:
Though that individual, who was granted anonymity to candidly discuss the current situation, was only referring to the increasingly violent demonstrations outside secondary schools and the government’s slow-footed response to them, it’s a sentiment likely shared by French voters after a week of particularly bleak headlines.

If there are political winners, it’s not immediately clear who they are. Establishment candidates and moderate voices are still struggling to seize the narrative from far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen and her surging far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon — both of whom want to fundamentally reshape France and its relationship with Europe.

A survey by pollster Odoxa this week found that the French disapprove of the government’s handling of the student school protests, but they also disapprove of Mélenchon and his far-left party France Unbowed’s involvement.

Mélenchon’s allies have joined demonstrators outside schools, saying they were there to show support and protect minors from confrontations with police. But the government and France Unbowed’s political opponents accuse them of fanning the flames of violence — allegations they deny.

“There’s a battle over the narrative” between the political extremes, a Socialist Party adviser said.

Whatever the case, the week’s crises are showing just how nasty the campaign can get with two populist candidates unafraid to stoke partisan divisions leading the polls.

World.title: Ukraine to step up oil attacks as Russia hits Kyiv bridges
World.content:
As Moscow intensifies attacks on Kyiv and other cities, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vowed to hit Russian energy infrastructure.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday vowed to continue hitting Russia's oil refineries in retaliation for what he called Moscow's new strategy of targeting major Ukrainian cities for intensive air strikes.

Ukraine has accused the Kremlin of stepping up attacks on civilian targets in recent days, to force residents to leave urban areas of the country before winter.

In strikes over the past two days, Russian forces have also hit two major bridges crossing the Dnipro River in the capital, Kyiv.

What did Zelenskyy say?

In an interview with Reuters news agency, Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence agencies had uncovered details of a "new doctrine" from Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelenskyy warned.

The Ukrainian leader said that Kyiv would "respond in any way (we can) ... First of all, oil refiners: who give money to them [Russia] for this war. But we will not respond, of course, like them, on any ‌civilian objects."

Second Kyiv bridge struck

This week marks the first time Moscow has targeted the bridges across the Dnipro River connecting east and west Kyiv.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Saturday that the Northern Bridge over the river was struck by Russian forces from the air.

In a statement posted on Telegram, Klitschko said two people were injured and the road surface and trolleybus wires on the bridge were damaged.

"Traffic across the bridge from the left bank to the right bank is currently blocked," he said.

Over the past two days, Kyiv's Southern Bridge has been hit several times by a volley of strikes by Russian drones.

The attacks caused traffic chaos, with long lines of stationary cars and buses clogging major roads.

Cars were stuck in traffic jams on Friday after Russian attacks on the Southern Bridge Image: Gleb Garanich/REUTERS

A total of eight bridges connect Kyiv's western and eastern banks along the Dnipro River.

Russia urges foreign diplomats, nationals to leave Kyiv

Russia's Foreign Ministry on Saturday, meanwhile, warned foreign diplomats and nationals in Kyiv to leave the city, adding that "individuals are knowingly exposing themselves to mortal danger."

"The Armed Forces of the Russian Federation will continue to deliver massive retaliatory strikes," it said, while adding that "responsibility for any potential negative consequences rests entirely with those who ignore this warning."

In the years following its February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Russia has frequently targeted Kyiv with overnight drone attacks.

Moscow has previously denied a systematic targeting of civilians during its bombings.

Putin on a war footing: escalation on all fronts? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moldova denounces latest Russian strike on Ukraine

Moldovan President Maia Sandu condemned the latest Russian attack on Kyiv and complained about a violation of her country's airspace.

"Its war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu said in a post on X. "5 Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated our airspace and exploded on our soil."

"Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped," Sandu said.

The Moldovan Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador and urged Moscow to prevent such incidents.

Moldova is a strong supporter of Ukraine, and its airspace is frequently violated due to Russian attacks on its neighbor.

Russian forces are stationed in the Moldovan breakaway province of Transnistria, raising fears that Moldova could be the next target of invasion after Ukraine.

World.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
World.content:
The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.

The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.

The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.

What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, in northern England.

He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.

The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.

Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.

He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.

The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.

One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.

The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.

Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025] Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance

Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.

Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.

The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.

Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.

UK releases air base plot suspects To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.

UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.

Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.

The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.

Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.

Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

World.title: Spain: Massive protests after housing bills voted down
World.content:
Organizers estimated that 500,000 people turned out in the streets of Madrid to demand affordable housing. Similar protests were held in around 50 other Spanish cities.

Tens of thousands of people protested across Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing.

The protests come a day after the Spanish parliament narrowly voted down two emergency bills designed to support renters and prevent evictions.

"It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt ‌to the political parties, and not the politicians to ‌what ​the people want, and this can't go on like that," one 26-year-old protester in Madrid told the Reuters news agency.

They are the latest demonstrations in a week-long wave of actions that began in response to the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascalin, in Madrid.

Protesters demanded affordable housing Image: Javier Soriano/AFP

"What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven't seen in a long time, and energy that is showing that eight days of people's power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government," said Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organizing Saturday's protest.

Protests in dozens of cities

Police said around 70,000 people took part in the demonstration in Madrid. Organizers put the figure closer to 500,000 people.

Additional protests were held in around 50 other cities.

In the eastern city of Valencia, police used tear gas and rubber bullets against protesters.

Dozens of protesters had managed to get inside Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences — a major landmark in the city — before they were ejected by police.

Protesters filled the streets of the Spanish capital Image: Juan Barbosa/REUTERS

What's next for the Spanish government?

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's proposed emergency measures included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants. However, bills were shot down by opposition parties on Friday.

This defeat infuriated those who had been protesting against the country's increasingly unaffordable housing market all week.

"We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project," another protester in Madrid, aged 31, told the AFP news agency.

Demonstrators held signs calling for 'a right to a roof' among other slogans Image: Javier Soriano/AFP

Spanish media reported that Sanchez might call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, adding that the government would be watching Saturday's protests closely before making a decion.

Sahcnez's office declined to comment on the reports.

World.title: Greece returns remains of Czar Samuel to Bulgaria
World.content:
A warrior emperor who ruled the Bulgarian Empire in the Middle Ages, Czar Samuel is a symbol of Bulgarian national identity. But his remains have been in Greece for decades – and he is also claimed by North Macedonia.

The remains of one of Bulgaria's most important medieval rulers were set to arrive in the Bulgarian capital, Sofia, on Saturday after decades of negotiations with neighboring Greece.

Czar Samuel ruled the First Bulgarian Empire from 997 to 1014, gradually extending his authority over a swathe of the Balkans as far south as Lake Ohrid, now in North Macedonia on the border with Albania.

But Samuel's rule was also characterized by conflict with the Byzantine Empire which ultimately defeated his army at the Battle of Kleidion in 1014.

Samuel is said to have died of shock when thousands of his defeated soldiers returned home having been blinded by order of Byzantine Emperor Basil II, known as Boulgaroktonos – the "Bulgar Slayer."

The Bulgarian lands fell under Byzantine rule four years later but Czar Samuel is still considered a symbol of Bulgarian national identity today, and his remains – discovered in a Greek border area 60 years ago – are set to be received with full state honors.

They are set to be flown to Sofia aboard a military aircraft accompanied by a fighter jet escort before a 21-gun salute and a procession to the Church of St. Sophia, where the public will be able to pay respects.

Free trains to the capital are being provided for the occasion, with some 750 police on duty during the handover ceremony.

Through the ages in Sofia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bulgaria: 'Czar Samuel unites us'

"These are items that belong to both our peoples; they constitute our memory and our bond, and our compatriots and future generations deserve and must have the opportunity to pay tribute to their ancestors," said Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev at a ceremony held at Museum of Byzantine Civilization in Thessaloniki, Greece, ahead of the handover.

Bulgaria officially opened talks on the return of the remains in 2007, and they became a major issue in relations with their southern neighbor.

"If, in the past, Czar Samuel divided us, I can say that today he unites us," said Radev. "He strengthens our strategic cooperation and makes the historical relations between our states and peoples even stronger."

Greece hopes for return of Parthenon Marbles

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, speaking alongside Radev, acknowledged that the remains of Czar Samuel have "incalculable cultural and spiritual but also emotional value" for Bulgaria, adding: "The global community is re-evaluating its long-standing stance on protecting cultural heritage."

In return, Greece is set to receive 48 sentimental objects pillaged by Bulgarian troops from churches and monasteries in northern Greece during the First World War.

Some prominent Greek academics and religious leaders have criticized the exchange as inadequate on the Bulgarian side, but Mitsotakis said he hoped Saturday's ceremony would bolster Greece's international campaign to return the Parthenon Marbles, a collection of 2,500-year-old marble sculptures taken from the Acropolis in Athens and later displayed in the British Museum.

"This shift is embodied by today's initiative, which rests on the obvious principle that monuments and historical heirlooms cannot be treated as spoils of war, nor as the result of circumstances subsequent to their creation."

Greece: How the Jewish cemetery in Thessaloniki disappeared To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Czar Samuel: does North Macedonia also have a claim?

However, Bulgaria is not the only country to claim Czar Samuel, who is also celebrated with a huge statue in Skopje, the capital of North Macedonia.

"The bones return, the conflict remains! Samuel once again [contested] between Skopje and Sofia!" declared the Albanian-language newspaper Koha, while Skopje daily Sloboden Pechat called the handover another "battle over history."

In 2022, a bilateral commission recommended that Samuel be presented as the head of a state that "most contemporary historiographers consider to be the Bulgarian Empire" – territory which is now North Macedonia.

"Samuel occupies an important place in the historical narrative both in Bulgaria and in North Macedonia," Dimitar Bechev, a researcher at the Carnegie Europe think tank, told the AFP news agency.

Indeed, history has been playing a major role in the run-up to this month's Bulgarian presidential election, with incumbent President Iliana Iotova, backed by Prime Minister Radev, promoting a more neutral position between the European Union and NATO – both of which Bulgaria belongs to – and Russia.

"Radev is looking to attract the patriotic electorate," said analyst Bechev, adding that the return of the remains to Sofia "aims to underline the Bulgarian character of the Slavic population of Macedonia."

World.title: Spain: Floods leave 102-year-old woman dead in southeast
World.content:
Authorities in Spain rescued some 90 people after heavy rain sparked flooding in the town of Madrigueras. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez expressed his condolences to the family of a 102-year-old woman who died.

Floods in the Spanish southeastern town of Madrigueras have killed an 102-year-old woman, regional authorities said.

Madrigueras, which has a population of around 4,000 residents, is located near the city of Albacete in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha.

Authorities said 90 people had to be rescued due to flooding in the town.

Local Spanish media said the elderly woman was found dead in her home after the floodwaters had reached a depth of one meter (3.2 feet).

The floods in the region were caused by persistent torrential rainfall on Friday. Spanish authorities said around 140 liters of rainfall per square meter came down in Madrigueras.

The flooding in Madrigueras also damaged vehicles in the town Image: Eva Manez/REUTERS

Sanchez: Spanish government monitoring flood situation

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, in a post on X, said his government is monitoring the situation. He also expressed his regards to the family of the woman who died in the flooding in Madrigueras.

Spanish meteorological authorities said heavy rainfall is expected to continue in eastern Spain through Sunday.

The torrential rain and flooding comes after the Mediterranean country witnessed its hottest summer on record this year.

Deadly wildfires were reported in Spain's north and south in recent months due to frequent hot, dry conditions.
