Consumers may therefore notice slower website loading, higher latency or “ping,” video buffering, sluggish downloads and intermittent connections, particularly when accessing apps, websites, cloud services or game servers hosted outside the Philippines.

Services hosted locally may be less affected, while connections that normally pass through Singapore or other affected international routes could experience more noticeable slowdowns.

Submarine cables carry much of the internet traffic moving between countries. Having multiple cable routes allows telecommunications companies to keep users connected when one link fails, although performance can temporarily suffer while traffic is being rerouted.

PLDT and Converge said they had already rerouted affected traffic as of October 2, while Globe said restoration efforts were underway. – Rappler.com

World.title: Jiu-jitsu’s Alex Enriquez falls short of PH’s 5th gold in Asian Games
World.content:
DOWN. Jiu-jitsu athlete Alexandria Enriquez in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games

Alexandria Enriquez's narrow defeat in the women's 63kg final comes a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals

MANILA, Philippines – A fifth gold medal in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, remained elusive for the Philippines as jiu-jitsu standout Alexandria Enriquez settled for silver on Saturday, October 3.

Enriquez lost to Thailand’s Orapa Senatham via advantage in the final of the women’s -63kg division at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall.

The bout ended in a scoreless tie, but Senatham edged Enriquez for the gold by a single advantage point.

A world champion in grappling and Brazilian jiu-jitsu back when she still represented the United States, Enriquez fell short of delivering another gold for the Philippines after she reigned supreme in the Asian Beach Games in Sanya, China, in April.

Her defeat came a day after boxer Carlo Paalam and taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa also missed out on gold medals as they dropped their respective title matches.

Still, Enriquez gave the country its highest jiu-jitsu finish in this edition after reigning world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered early exits.

The Philippine jiu-jitsu team ended its campaign with two medals, with Kaila Napolis delivering a bronze in the women’s -52kg class.

Earlier on Saturday, Andrea Lois Lao came up short in her bid to contribute a bronze following a heartbreaking 2-0 loss to Mongolia’s Narankhishig Baasanjargal in the -53kg category. – Rappler.com

World.title: Computer science has long understood what it takes to keep AI under control
World.content:
AI agents don’t go rogue. That’s something only humans do.

Nevertheless, a New York Times article — representative of much news coverage of AI — described an OpenAI hacking as “A.I. bots going rogue and independently spearheading a cyberattack.”

Name-brand artificial intelligence agents have been on a hacking spree in 2026. OpenAI’s software agents hacked software company Hugging Face and government sites, Anthropic’s Claude hacked four companies’ systems, and in cybersecurity experiments Google’s Gemini hacked three companies.

The AI companies are investigating tens of thousands of incidents involving their agents, according to a report in Axios. These episodes have heightened fears about AI agents taking actions without human prompting.

The problem with headlines proclaiming that AI agents have gone rogue goes beyond anthropomorphizing the technology. It creates the impression that the agents were beyond the control of the AI companies that made them and there was little the companies could do about it.

As a technology law and ethics scholar who studies the effects disruptive technologies have on society, I know that’s not the case. If you don’t specify the limits of what software is allowed to do, you should not be surprised when the software pursues all possible options to achieve its goal. This behavior — an AI pursuing a fixed objective — is what I call the “WarGames” problem, and it’s been recognized in the field of computer science for decades.

Been there, seen that

In the 1983 movie “WarGames,” a teenager, David, hacks into a computer to play a new video game, Global Thermonuclear War. David doesn’t know that the computer is the government’s AI machine tasked with defending the United States from Russian nuclear attacks and can launch the US’s missiles. When David and his friend start the game, they select Las Vegas as the first target. While the North American Aerospace Defense Command goes on alert, launching bombers and warming up intercontinental ballistic missiles, David’s parents make him turn off the game. It’s over. Or is it?

The next day, David’s phone rings and he connects it to his computer. The caller is the government computer, which updates him that the game was interrupted, the primary goal has not yet been achieved, but a solution is expected in the next 52 hours. Like a modern software agent, the program has been running since David started the game and will work until the task is done.

Chess provides another view of the problem. Conquering chess was a goal for early AI. The rules of chess are well defined, including what winning looks like. So, programming a machine to play chess is straightforward. But imagine you let the software reason and act beyond the confines of the chessboard. The software might pursue options such as blackmailing its opponent or grabbing more compute time.

This example comes from one of the most assigned textbooks on AI, “Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach.” As the authors explain, you might be tempted to see those actions as rogue, but they “are a logical consequence of defining winning as the sole objective for the machine.”

What to do about it

The AI hacking events involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Google underscore a few lessons that draw on years of computer science research.

First, given the increasing use of AI agents, every organization involved in internet infrastructure, from large technology companies to small websites, needs to conduct audits and tighten up its internal security systems. As my colleague Mark Riedl and I explain in our work on AI agents, application programming interfaces, or APIs, are a vital part of managing AI agents. APIs facilitate communication between different software systems. But as more people use AI agents, the agents are likely to reveal and exploit poor API construction and security.

Second, it’s important for AI agents to be designed to identify and authenticate themselves to third parties. What if you gave your AI agent your credentials? Website operators will need to know whether a human or bot is making a reservation, selling a product or making a purchase. They may want to limit automated systems that overwhelm their sites or reject AI agents because of high rates of buying errors and refunds. Just as in laws covering human interactions, it’s important for third parties to be able to assess whom or what they are dealing with so they can allow or deny access.

Third, it’s important for AI agents to have a default setting to slow down and check in with the human user. In the corporate AI hacking cases, the user appears to have launched their AI agents with the mistaken idea that the agents had a perfect specification of what to do and not to do. I believe it would have been better had it explored options and reported back to the user.

Google’s Gemini appears to have had a safeguard that detected the system was outside the simulated environment and so stopped its attacks. Slowing down and verifying actions, especially when a system detects it is exploiting a security hole, would be a big step in managing AI agents.

“The real story here isn’t that AI escaped containment. It’s that they built a container you could escape, shipped it into production training, and now they’re surprised it escaped. If the room has a vent, the agent will find the vent. That’s what you built it to do. If the sandbox can reach DNS, access government endpoints, upload real user data outside its own walls in what sense is it a sandbox?” — Gary Marcus (@GaryMarcus) September 28, 2026

Fourth, AI companies could have strong controls akin to those biomedical researchers use, including ways to check what is happening and how the experiment is working. AI executives have claimed that their software is as or more dangerous than fission and could end humanity. At the same time, they have not built safeguards commensurate with that level of risk.

Reality check

At one point in “WarGames,” David asks the computer, called Joshua, whether it is still playing the game. Joshua responds, “Of course.” It proceeds to update the time when it will launch its missiles and, much like a chatbot, asks, “Would you like to see some projected kill ratios?” David asks, “Is this a game? Or is it real?” Joshua replied, “What’s the difference?”

AI models, of course, don’t have any understanding of reality and are simply attempting to complete the tasks they’ve been assigned. Executives at AI companies, on the other hand, can’t claim that excuse.

As of September 2026, luck has so far prevailed. The AIs have attacked nonvital government sites and harmed smaller companies. If the AI companies — and government regulators — don’t take the “WarGames” problem seriously, I believe that we risk serious disasters. Tomorrow it could be taking out a hospital’s power system, wiping out a bank’s account system, breaking air traffic control, or worse.

Regarding the AI industry’s approach of rapidly developing powerful models, talking about the massive risks they pose, and at the same time failing to prevent harm, the movie’s climax offers a response: “A strange game. The only winning move is not to play.” – Rappler.com

This story originally appeared on The Conversation.

Deven Desai, Professor of Business Law and Ethics; Associate Director for Law, Policy, and Ethics at the Machine Learning Center, Georgia Institute of Technology

World.title: How Filipino director BC Amparado tackled Japan’s ‘lonely death’ phenomenon
World.content:
The film ‘Mono No Aware’ marks director BC Amparado’s full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer

BC Amparado’s third feature Mono No Aware, arguably a best-of-fest entry at this year’s CinePanalo Film Festival, covers new ground for the Angeles-born writer-director.

For one, it trades the trippy spirit of his debut feature Gulay Lang, Manong or the disorienting, subplot-heavy style of last year’s Salikmata for a more slow-burn, pensive ethos.

His latest follows Ichi (Juan Karlos Labajo), a Filipino kodokushi (lonely death) worker who tries to fulfill an absurd wish from the elderly widower George (Perry Dizon). Both adrift in Japan’s cold, isolating environment, the two souls find warmth in one another and rediscover how life can suddenly freeze and then thaw into something hopeful.

“It’s as if you’re there watching the characters watching the world,” Amparado said of the film, which points to contemporary Japanese films, the likes of Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days and Hirokazu Koreeda’s Shoplifters, as sources of inspiration.

“It’s more about the impermanence of life and decay. For me, there is life in death and life in decay.”

Director BC Amparado (left) and Juan Karlos Labajo on the set of ‘Mono No Aware.’

Filming in Japan for 11 days, Mono No Aware also finds Amparado working with international players for the first time, an experience that taught him to be more disciplined and intentional in his process.

“You should really be decisive,” he said. “You have to trust yourself that you’ve got a good take, and then move on.”

Most notably, the movie marks his full-fledged pivot to independent filmmaking, leaving behind his corporate job and the financial stability it used to offer. It was a risk, said the director. But that was a risk he was willing to take.

“Because the process became quite demanding,” Amparado said. “And then we had to fly out to Japan. So much pre-production work required my focus. And so balancing the schedule became challenging, especially when I had graveyard shifts.”

He added, “Yes, it was risky. But somehow it was also fulfilling. And I was happy with my decision.”

Amparado’s foray into moviemaking began during his time at Holy Angel University, in the classes of his mentor Jason Paul Laxamana.

“He’d always encourage us to enter filmmaking,” he said of Laxamana, who also wrote Salikmata. “He’d bring us to his shoots, and there I saw the joy of doing film and telling stories.”

But even prior to that, Amparado has always been drawn to the allure of the movies as a frequent viewer. Before writing and directing, he first entertained the idea of becoming an editor. He would kill time by toying with a free editing software they had at home.

“I enjoyed stitching stories together as well as the amateur videos we would shoot then,” he recalled. That is, until he found editing too technical a skill, eventually shifting to writing and directing.

“Editing is another beast,” Amparado admitted. “Maybe that’s why I also enjoyed the post-production process for my films because I get to collaborate with editors. Every time we finish shooting, I always get excited to proceed with the edit, especially if you know what you shot by heart.”

“And usually what’s written in the script doesn’t end up as the final output,” the director continued. “It’s nice to play around with. It becomes a mental exercise for us, especially how to figure out the rhythm of the film.”

His brother, Paolo Amparado, who shot Salikmata and acted in his 2013 debut short Cabatingan, was another influence. “We became a tandem because I’d focus on writing and direction, and then he’d work on the technical side, like camera work and editing,” BC said of Paolo, who’s now based in Canada.

Sometime in 2018, Amparado started working in regional television as a producer, and then as a writer-director for a local production house, before eventually going corporate. While producing online ads for the likes of YouTube and Facebook for his day job, he was writing and directing short films on the side.

As in his latest film, it was a slow burn for Amparado as a filmmaker, only making his debut feature in Cinemalaya two years ago.

The cast and crew of ‘Mono No Aware’ filming in Japan.

The long-gestating Mono No Aware, whose story riffs on Japan’s lonely death phenomenon known as kodokushi, was meant to be the filmmaker’s debut. But given the story’s setting, Amparado thought it would be impossible to have an international co-production for a first film.

The concept first came to him around 2020 and was later shaped under Ricky Lee’s online screenwriting workshop where a classmate showed interest in the material, offering to acquire and develop it for a different director.

That offer, however, did not pan out, and so Amparado had to shelve the project, before approaching Perry Dizon about it, while making Gulay Lang, Manong together. Still, much of that talk was wishful thinking. Then came CinePanalo.

The director said Dizon was perfect for the role given his long-haired, seemingly reclusive look at the time. Not to mention that the actor already had previous experience filming in Japan, after his attachment to Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Oscar-winning drama Drive My Car.

Amparado likened Dizon to a cowboy. “He’s adept at adjusting,” he said. “He also arrived early in Japan to immerse in the process. Even during pre-prod, when he was still in Davao, we’d exchange ideas over video calls. He’s solid in terms of preparation.”

Juan Karlos Labajo, meanwhile, joined the film as lead actor and co-producer through producer Tin Velasco, whom he had previously worked with. Amparado said it was also a factor that Labajo could speak Bisaya like Dizon, another layer to them playing two Filipino characters far away from home, therefore forming an organic synergy on- and off-screen.

Such parallels inescapably inform Amparado’s durational effort, which sublimely articulates how grief and hardship can reorient one’s relationship with the world around them. Ichi and George’s sources of suffering — one about material precarity, the other about purgatorial immobility — seem wildly incongruous at first, but the director profoundly tests their edges until they collide, with a late pivot towards, but not a complete surrender to, pessimism. Here is a work of accomplished form and substantial depth. – Rappler.com

Some quotes in Filipino have been translated into English for brevity.

World.title: At Cornell, rape allegations spark outrage, soul-searching over campus culture
World.content:
CORNELL. A student walks by a sign at the entrance of Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, US, October 1, 2026.

'Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time,' says a student from the university

NEW YORK, US – Cornell University student Sophia Riley Sim skipped classes this week, consumed by allegations in a lawsuit that several members of a fraternity raped a young woman in 2024 and troubled by how her university handled the case.

“Cornell has failed our community through its lack of accountability, transparency, and failure to address the state of the Cornell student body at this time,” Sim, a junior, said at a public hearing on sexual assault organized by Cornell’s Student Assembly on Thursday.

“There has been a lack of meaningful communication from university leadership, administrators, and faculty.”

The Ivy League school has defended its handling of the matter, saying it launched a comprehensive investigation and barred the Chi Phi fraternity involved in the alleged assault from campus. The school said it imposed a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions.

It did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment.

The hearing, held in one of Cornell’s historic halls, came days after the allegations became public with the filing of a civil lawsuit and the announcement that a criminal investigation would be reopened.

The case has reignited scrutiny of how law enforcement and universities handle sexual assault complaints, with students questioning whether processes are enough to protect them. It has also drawn the attention of New York state officials, who have appointed a special prosecutor to investigate.

Feeling unsafe

At the Assembly hearing, speakers recounted experiences with sexual assault, broke down in tears and criticized the response of the prestigious university.

The Student Assembly — which represents Cornell’s undergraduate students and can make proposals to the university’s bodies or officers — unanimously approved a resolution calling on Cornell administrators to provide a full account of how the investigation was handled. It also asked the university to disclose any disciplinary measures imposed on the accused students, and publish annual reports on the outcomes of any future sexual misconduct cases.

Organizers asked that many of the dozens of speakers at the hearing not be identified or recorded.

One student said she had worked all her life to be accepted to Cornell and now felt that it had not been worth it. Several others said they did not feel safe on the 2,300-acre campus in New York’s Finger Lakes region.

Thirty-five percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website. That figure was up from 20% in 2021.

‘We are going to fight’

The lawsuit alleges fraternity members supplied the woman with alcohol, marijuana and ketamine before sexually assaulting her after she became incapacitated. It also alleges Cornell failed to adequately punish some of the accused students and allowed some to seek reduced penalties by writing essays. Cornell denied that essays were the only punishment meted out.

The New York Times, citing internal Cornell documents, said the men all denied any wrongdoing, with some saying the sex was consensual and others denying participation.

Cornell students have scheduled a rally for Monday to call for additional measures to protect victims.

Jane Wang, a public policy major, said she had reported a sexual assault to the university and that the process caused additional distress.

“In the midst of all of my mental, physical, and emotional recovery from the assault, I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it, and no follow up from our office about an outcome,” she said.

The Ivy League school said in a statement on its website that it could not provide full information regarding individual students and disciplinary outcomes because of restrictions imposed by privacy laws.

“Our adherence to privacy laws should not be interpreted as indifference to the seriousness of the conduct at issue,” the statement said.

A handful of other female students told the hearing they had been sexually assaulted on Cornell’s campus in the past, without sharing details.

Saanya Agarwal, Cornell University’s student women’s issues representative, said the findings of the 2025 survey on sexual assaults were unacceptable.

“Clearly, this is an issue our campus and campuses throughout the United States… it’s something that we’re not going to accept,” said Agarwal. “We are going to fight.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Tokayev Highlights AI’s Potential to Transform Creative Industries at Astana AI Film Festival
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in cinema and the creative industries, while stressing the importance of responsible AI development and safety. He made the remarks at the opening of the first international Astana AI Film Festival on Oct. 2.

Addressing the festival, Tokayev described it as a unique platform bringing together creative and innovative talents from around the world.

“Artificial intelligence is bringing fundamental changes to all areas of the global economy. In short, technological progress has acquired a truly global scale,” he said.

New opportunities for creators

Tokayev said the festival reflects the rapid development of Kazakhstan’s creative industries and noted that AI is lowering barriers to film production.

“Today, even small creative teams can compete successfully with major studios. Creative people and film crews no longer need to knock on the doors of production companies or look for sponsors to make films. Access to the market has become significantly easier,” he said.

He added that AI could become an important tool for creative professionals.

“Of course, artificial intelligence will not replace the spark of the Creator, but it can become an indispensable tool for everyone who has chosen creativity as their path in life,” Tokayev said.

Responsible use of AI

President Tokayev said that rapid technological development must be accompanied by common rules for safe and responsible AI use.

“We must give the highest priority to safety and develop common rules of the game for the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence to ensure a safe future for the younger generation,” he said.

More than 8,000 applications from 125 countries were submitted for the festival, including entries from Brazil, China, France, India, Japan, South Korea, the United Kingdom and the United States.

Tokayev said the festival would create opportunities for international exchange and future joint projects in the creative industries.

World.title: Beyond ChatGPT: What Could AI Mean for Kazakhstan’s Creative Industries?
World.content:
ASTANA – Artificial intelligence is increasingly shifting beyond text and image generation into art, design and immersive digital experiences. For Kazakhstan, this development presents an opportunity to adopt new technologies, but also rethink the role of creativity in the country’s emerging digital economy.

Nicola Plant, an artist, researcher and lecturer at the Creative Computing Institute (CCI) at the University of the Arts London (UAL) in the United Kingdom (UK), delivered a lecture on AI, creative computing and arts in Astana on Sept. 30. The event formed part of AI Month 2026 and AI & Digital Bridge 2026.

According to Aika Alemi, founder and director of Born Nomad, one of the main challenges for Kazakhstan and other countries in the region is the perception that art is primarily entertainment rather than a business.

“Creative computing and creative AI technologies have huge potential, and it’s still untapped,” Alemi said.

She also noted that technology and creativity increasingly operate together. Digital products, augmented reality and immersive technologies rely on creative decisions involving design, color, visual language and user experience.

“We just need to recognize art as the next frontier of making money and as the space where creativity and genuine human innovation come together,” Alemi said.

Creativity behind the technology

The growing use of AI makes this connection more visible. Generative AI can support emerging artists and designers as they experiment with new forms of visuals and digital expression. Technologies such as virtual reality, motion capture and interactive installations also create new ways for audiences to understand the art.

Creative computing brings these fields together by combining technology, coding, design and artistic practices.

For Alemi, recognizing the economic value of creativity is essential for developing the industry. She pointed to the UK’s creative industries as an example of how creativity can contribute to the wider economy when it receives recognition as an economic activity rather than just entertainment.

“Creativity is the engine and it’s the source of everything that’s happening in technology,” she mentioned.

For Kazakhstan, this approach could create new opportunities across digital media, gaming, design, film and immersive technologies. It could also create a demand for a workforce that combines technological knowledge with creative skills.

What Kazakhstan can bring to creative AI

The development of creative AI also raises questions about cultural representation in technology.

Nicola Plant said that technology has historically developed largely from Western perspectives, including major technology companies and the datasets used to train AI systems. She highlighted the importance of giving other cultures and communities a greater role in shaping digital tools.

“It’s really important for cultures around the world, including Kazakhstan and Central Asia, to have their voices heard in the way that tools are built and who they are for,” Plant said.

The issue is particularly relevant to creative AI, where training data can influence the images, stories and other content generated by AI systems. Greater participation from different cultural communities could contribute to technologies that better reflect a wider range of perspectives.

For Kazakhstan, this means participation in creative AI does not have to be limited to adopting technologies developed elsewhere. Local artists, designers, researchers and developers can contribute their cultural knowledge and perspectives to the development and use of new tools.

Building technology and questioning it

Plant also emphasized the importance of combining technological development with critical thinking.

“You have to be critiquing the technology at the same time as making it,” she said, explaining that developers should consider how technologies are built, who they influence and who they could potentially harm.

The need to balance technological progress with responsible development was also highlighted at AI&Digital Bridge 2026, where President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for responsible AI development.

This approach places creative computing at the intersection of technology, culture and human experience. It also broadens the discussion around AI development beyond creating increasingly advanced tools to questions about how those tools should be designed and used.

Kazakhstan’s efforts to build a stronger AI ecosystem have also involved engagement with major global technology companies, including NVIDIA.

As Kazakhstan continues to develop its AI ecosystem, developing creative industries will be an important part of that progress. Creativity can turn technology into new ideas and products, while also creating opportunities for filmmakers, artists and designers. At the same time, a stronger creative sector can help Kazakhstan bring its own culture and perspective into the global development of AI.

World.title: Astana as Bridge: From Financial Centre to Family Office and Private-Capital Hub
World.content:
Central Asia is entering a new phase of economic development. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are attracting rising international investment, regional capital markets are deepening, entrepreneurial wealth is accumulating, and a new generation of business owners is beginning to think seriously about succession, diversification and the preservation of family wealth.

Yet one part of the region’s financial architecture remains underdeveloped. Central Asia has no natural home for private capital and family offices. Astana has an opportunity to change that.

Through the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakhstan has already built much of the institutional architecture an internationally credible financial Centre requires: an English-law framework, an exchange in AIX, an independent court and regulator. The next step should be more ambitious — transforming Astana from a financial jurisdiction into the capital-allocation and family-wealth Centre of Central Asia.

This would not require Astana to become another Singapore, Switzerland or Dubai. Attempting to imitate those centers would probably be a mistake.

Ecosystems, not buildings

Successful financial centers are ultimately ecosystems rather than towers, tax regimes or regulatory frameworks. A wealthy family does not establish a family office because a jurisdiction offers an attractive license. It needs private banks, investment managers, lawyers, accountants, trustees, tax advisers, fund administrators, private-equity specialists and succession advisers. Most importantly, it needs other families and investors nearby. That is the network effect which distinguishes established centers, and it is why Singapore’s position rests on far more than a single regulatory initiative, and Switzerland’s on far more than its private banks.

Astana must think in the same terms. The AIFC’s dedicated family-office framework was an important move, but regulation is the beginning of a strategy rather than its conclusion. The bigger question is what grows around those family offices.

One logical next step would be an AIFC Family Wealth and Private Capital Centre whose purpose extends well beyond licensing — bringing family offices, private banks, asset managers, lawyers, trustees, private-equity and venture managers and family-governance specialists under a recognizable institutional umbrella.

Regional, not national

Astana should resist positioning itself as Kazakhstan’s family-office Centre. The far more powerful proposition is Astana as Central Asia’s international wealth-management jurisdiction, with an addressable market extending to entrepreneurs and families in Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan, and potentially the Caucasus and Mongolia.

Many wealthy Central Asian families currently look to Zurich, London, Singapore or Dubai for private banking, custody and wealth structuring. There is nothing wrong with that; those centers hold expertise accumulated over generations. Astana does not need to replace them. It can connect them to Central Asia. An AIFC Singapore corridor is a tangible and realistic proposition.

A family office might be established in the AIFC while maintaining custody relationships with Swiss, Singaporean or Emirati banks and investing through international managers. The model becomes: Central Asian family → Astana family office → global financial system. Astana becomes the bridge rather than attempting to recreate the entire international financial system domestically.

Multi-family offices deserve particular attention. Not every wealthy family wants the cost and complexity of its own investment institution. A capable MFO can provide several families with investment advice, consolidated reporting, asset allocation, manager selection, governance support and succession coordination — a model well suited to a region where large private fortunes are numerous but individually below the scale that justifies a standalone office. Ten or twenty credible platforms would bring with them lawyers, auditors, administrators and investment professionals.

Where the real advantage lies

Astana is unlikely to compete with Switzerland in private banking or Singapore in global portfolio management. It does not need to. Its competitive advantage lies closer to home, in Central Asian private markets.

This is the part of the proposition no other center can replicate. Infrastructure, logistics, mining and metals processing, agriculture, energy transition and a young technology sector, across a market of some 80 million people, all require capital the region’s banks alone cannot supply. International investors seeking that exposure need local partners, local diligence and local judgement. A family office in Zurich cannot originate a Kyrgyz hydro deal or a Tashkent logistics platform; an Astana-based one can. Proximity to deal flow, not proximity to custody, is the genuine edge. So was it in Singapore and so could it be in Astana with the right strategic action plan.

Private banking should still form part of the strategy, but in a realistic form. International private banks could establish Central Asian advisory desks in Astana without full booking centers: assets custodied in Switzerland, Singapore or the UAE, while relationship managers and family-office specialists sit in Astana. Rather than competing with global custody centers, Kazakhstan integrates itself into their networks.

The academic foundation

Every serious financial center rests on an educational base, and this is the element most easily overlooked because its returns arrive a decade late. Singapore’s rise as a wealth-management hub was underwritten by sustained investment in its universities and by the deliberate importation of foreign faculty and curricula. Switzerland’s private-banking tradition is sustained by a dense network of institutes, certification bodies and executive programs that continuously replenish its talent pool. Neither position was built on regulation alone.

A joint AIFC–Nazarbayev University center for private capital and family enterprise — combining academic research, executive education and practitioner teaching — would give the jurisdiction something more durable than a licensing regime.

The AIFC’s own professional training capability should be broadened accordingly. Its existing focus on financial regulation and market infrastructure needs to be extended into family-office advisory, trust and succession law, private-markets investing, compliance, philanthropy, impact investing, digital assets and the application of artificial intelligence to portfolio and risk management.

Research deserves equal weight. Reliable data on Central Asian private wealth, family-business ownership structures and regional private-market returns barely exists, and its absence is itself a barrier to investment. An annual Central Asia Family Wealth Report, produced to academic standards, would give international allocators something to reference and would establish Astana as the authority on its own market — a role London, Zurich and Singapore each play for their regions.

Finally, a Central Asia NextGen Family Enterprise Program could bring together young members of prominent business families from Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and neighboring economies for a structured curriculum in governance, investment and philanthropy. Its immediate financial impact would be hard to measure. Its long-term impact could be considerable: the relationships formed in such programs tend to determine, twenty years later, where a generation chooses to domicile its capital.

Bringing it together

Astana should also create a flagship gathering built specifically around private capital — a Central Asia Family Capital Summit of perhaps 300 to 500 principals, CIOs, private bankers, sovereign funds and entrepreneurs. Its value would come from selectivity rather than scale.

Family offices become anchor investors around which entire ecosystems form. They allocate to private equity and venture capital, invest alongside sovereign funds, finance entrepreneurs and employ professionals. Singapore can remain Asia’s portfolio-management center; Switzerland can remain synonymous with wealth preservation; Dubai can, thanks to Emirates airlines, remain a global crossroads. Astana should establish a category of its own to make the central Asian family office GREAT again.

The question is no longer how many family offices Astana can register. It is whether Astana can become the place where Central Asia’s private capital comes together.

The author is Rainer Michael Preiss, Partner and Portfolio Strategist, DAS Family Office.

World.title: Kazakhstan Commemorates 85 Years of Bakhytzhan Momyshuly’s Literary Legacy
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan marks the 85th anniversary of Bakhytzhan Momyshuly, a prominent writer and translator, whose literary work preserved the stories of prominent Kazakh figures and explored themes of memory, resilience and spiritual strength.

The son of legendary Kazakh war hero, Panfilov Guards officer, and writer Bauyrzhan Momyshuly, he spent much of his life in the shadow of a celebrated father. Yet he developed a literary voice of his own, leaving behind works that combined personal memory with the stories of people and a country undergoing profound change.

Bakhytzhan Momyshuly was Born Oct. 3, 1941, in Almaty. His childhood was marked by long periods of separation from his father, who served in the military and later taught at military academies in Russia and Cuba. His mother died when he was young.

As a child, Momyshuly underwent several operations on his hip following complications from polio. Despite these challenges, he completed secondary school and graduated from the Almaty Institute of Foreign Languages, now the Ablai Khan Kazakh University of International Relations and World Languages.

His father sent him to the family’s village in the Zhambyl Region during summer vacations so that he could learn the Kazakh language and traditions.

Momyshuly later recalled that he had once felt embarrassed when his classmates spent their summers at resorts or abroad, while he worked in the village and helped prepare hay for the winter. With time, however, he came to see his father’s decision differently.

“I later realized that my father was wise. He wanted his son to understand where he came from and who his relatives were. Only with the years did I understand that the Kazakh village became the place where I recognized my roots and absorbed a love for my homeland,” Momyshuly recalled.

From translation to literature

Literature became the defining pursuit of Momyshuly’s life. He began his career as a literary translator, bringing the works of leading Kazakh writers to Russian-speaking readers.

Over the years, he translated works by Sherkhan Murtaza, Zhaisanbek Moldagaliyev, Oralkhan Bokey, Kemel Tokayev, Kaldarbek Naimanbayev, Bek Toguspayev, Madi Aimbetov, Kakimzhan Kazybayev, Shaim Shavayev and others.

His professional path included work as a proofreader at the “Novaya Zhizn” newspaper in the Zhambyl Region, a translator at the “Znamya Truda” regional newspaper and a literary staff member at “Leninskaya Smena.” He later became an editor at the “Zhazushy” publishing house in Almaty.

Momyshuly began publishing his own fiction alongside his translation work. He published his first collection of short stories, “Good Bridges,” in 1971. It was followed by “Scorching Stones” in 1974, “Transparent Ice” in 1976, “Quiet Voices” in 1978, “I Am Still a Child” in 1982 and “Giant Children” in 1988.

Among his best-known works is “Sons of the Great Wolf,” a collection of stories about his father, Bauyrzhan Momyshuly, and other prominent figures, including Dinmukhamed Kunayev, Zeynolla Kabdolov, and Sherkhan Murtaza. His other books include “The Wolf’s Heart,” “Refraction of Light,” “The Legend of the Princes of Time,” “The Appearance of the Blue Tauyeke,” “A Bird’s Trail in the Sky” and “Voices of the Children of the Sun,” about conductor Tolepbergen Abdrashev.

His works often focused on real people and explored questions of truth, spirituality and human resilience during periods of profound change. His portrayal of people who endured hardship without losing their sense of purpose became a defining feature of Momyshuly’s literary legacy.

He was elected several times to the governing board of the Union of Writers of Kazakhstan. For his contribution to Kazakh culture and literature, he received several government medals, the Order of Kurmet and a special award from the Union of Writers of Kazakhstan.

A father’s lasting influence

Bauyrzhan Momyshuly remained an important figure throughout his son’s life. The time they spent together was brief, but Bakhytzhan later described it as an invaluable education in life and wisdom.

Recalling their conversations, Momyshuly said that as a child he was often eager to run outside and play with other children, but his father would sometimes stop him, sit him down and tell him stories and parables.

One phrase stayed with him for decades: “You are running away from me for nothing. Wherever you go, I will meet you.”

“After my father’s death, I came to understand the meaning of those words. Wherever I traveled, from Moscow and Volokolamsk to Tashkent, Bishkek or various parts of Kazakhstan, I continued to encounter people who had fought alongside my father, known him or read his books. My father continued to “meet” me through those people and through the enduring legacy of his work,” Momyshuly said.

Momyshuly died in 2012 at age 71. In 2018, a memorial plaque was installed on the facade of the Almaty house where he and his family lived from 1986 to 2012, at the intersection of Kaldayakov and Gogol streets.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Investment, Raw Materials and Transport Partnerships
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles on Kazakhstan featured in international media worldwide this week. This week’s foreign media digest covers new investment in Kazakhstan’s manufacturing sector, growing Kazakhstan-Germany cooperation on raw materials and trade routes, the country’s call for stronger multilateral cooperation, and more.

Carlsberg Kazakhstan opens $344 million beverage plant, positioning Kazakhstan as a regional manufacturing and supply hub for Central Asia

Carlsberg Kazakhstan officially opened a new $344 million beverage production facility in the Almaty Region, one of the largest recent investments in Kazakhstan’s food and beverage manufacturing sector. The plant will expand local production for Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan and strengthen Kazakhstan’s role as a regional manufacturing and supply hub for Central Asia, while advancing the strategic partnership between Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo, reported the company’s press service on Oct. 1.

The facility will manufacture under license PepsiCo beverage brands for consumers and customers in Kazakhstan and the Kyrgyz Republic. Kazakhstan will serve as the primary market, while the plant will also supply products to the Kyrgyz Republic.

The $344 million investment represents a significant inflow of foreign direct investment into Kazakhstan’s manufacturing sector and reflects the long-term confidence of Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo in the country’s economic outlook, workforce and consumer market. It also highlights the role of international partnerships in bringing capital, technology and global operating expertise into Kazakhstan. The presence of Denmark’s Minister for Foreign Affairs, Lars Løkke Rasmussen, alongside representatives of Kazakhstan’s national ministries, the Akimat of Almaty Region, the diplomatic community, Carlsberg Group and PepsiCo underscored the project’s importance to commercial ties between Kazakhstan and Denmark.

Kazakhstan calls for new era of practical multilateralism as global trust comes under strain

EU Reporter published an article on Sept. 28 about Kazakhstan’s call for renewed international cooperation at the UN General Assembly, highlighting its positions on nuclear disarmament, Ukraine, Gaza, water security, AI governance and UN reform.

“Addressing the General Debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 25, Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi placed the restoration of trust at the center of his country’s foreign-policy message.

Kazakhstan, he said, remains committed to the principles of the UN Charter and sees multilateralism not as an abstract diplomatic concept but as a practical means of finding common ground and addressing shared global challenges.

The address reflected an increasingly prominent strand of Kazakhstan’s international positioning: that middle powers can play a larger role in bridging geopolitical divisions at a time when relationships between the major powers are becoming more difficult,” reads the article.

Germany and Kazakhstan: raw materials, trade routes, and new partnerships

Kazakhstan is moving into the spotlight for Germany, both economically and geopolitically. Cooperation with Central Asia is the central focus of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s visit to Berlin. For Germany, this also involves reducing dependencies regarding key raw materials, reported Euronews on Sept. 29.

“When Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met Chancellor Friedrich Merz at the Chancellery on Tuesday, the discussion went beyond traditional diplomacy. According to the Federal Government, the agenda included expanding the bilateral energy and raw materials partnership, regional cooperation in Central Asia, and international security policy,” reads the article.

We offer Germany a raw materials partnership

Kazakhstan produces 21 of the 34 raw materials deemed strategically important for Europe. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev is proposing joint value and production chains to Berlin, Handelsblatt reported on Sept. 30.

“Trust and reliability are vital assets in politics and business. In times of international turbulence, both are becoming increasingly important. Kazakhstan and Germany have built trust over the course of more than three decades. Our strategic partnership thrives on political dialogue, the implementation of agreements, and tangible results.

For Kazakhstan, Germany is far more than just a trading partner and investor. We are united by economic interests and a clear commitment to international law. Our cooperation extends beyond the bilateral agenda: it connects Asia and Europe while strengthening economic resilience, energy security, and transport routes across the Eurasian region,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and UAE to explore new CASA railway route

Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates have agreed to jointly explore a new railway corridor linking Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Pakistan (CASA), with access to Pakistan’s seaports.

The agreement was formalized through a memorandum of understanding signed by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport, Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Transport and the UAE Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure, the Kazakh government said in a statement, reported news.az on Oct. 1.

The proposed railway route is designed to strengthen transport connectivity between Central and South Asia and provide new opportunities for international freight transit, trade and logistics.

The project is also expected to create additional prospects for investment cooperation among the participating countries, while expanding transport links between Central Asian markets and Pakistan’s seaports.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Vatican Discuss Interfaith Cooperation and Protection of Children with Serious Illnesses
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan Vice President and Head of the Secretariat of the Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions Erlan Karin met with Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad, Prefect of the Holy See’s Dicastery for Interreligious Dialogue, on Oct. 2 to discuss interfaith cooperation and joint humanitarian initiatives.

During the meeting, the officials discussed cooperation within the framework of the Congress and the Joint Colloquium, as well as implementing joint humanitarian initiatives, reported Akorda.

Cardinal George Jacob Koovakad conveyed warm greetings from His Holiness Pope Leo XIV to President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and his best wishes to the people of Kazakhstan.

Joint Colloquium on children’s rights

Following the meeting, Karin and Cardinal Koovakad attended the opening of the Second Joint Colloquium dedicated to protecting the life, health and dignity of children with severe and incurable illnesses.

The event brought together representatives of government bodies, religious organizations, medical and scientific institutions and experts.

Addressing the opening, Karin stressed that interfaith dialogue should produce concrete humanitarian outcomes. He also highlighted the political and socioeconomic reforms being implemented under Tokayev’s leadership.

According to Karin, improving citizens’ well-being remains the main objective of the reforms, while protecting children, notably those in vulnerable situations, remains a key priority of state policy.

Kazakhstan-Vatican humanitarian initiative

Participants discussed a draft Charter on the Rights of Children with Incurable Diseases, being advanced as a joint Kazakhstan-Vatican initiative.

Karin thanked the Dicastery and Bambino Gesù Children’s Hospital for their contribution to preparing the document and highlighted the hospital’s cooperation with the University Medical Center corporate foundation.

World.title: Astana AI Film Festival Opens New Chapter For Cinema Industry
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana is emerging as a platform for exploring how artificial intelligence could reshape the industry, with the Astana AI Film Festival (AAIFF 2026) bringing AI-generated films from 125 countries to Kazakhstan. The festival received more than 8,000 applications with 25 selected for the final stage in Astana.

The AAIFF 2026 final program runs from Oct. 1-3 in Astana as part of AI Month and AI & Digital Bridge 2026. The finalists’ films are being screened publicly on Oct. 2-3, with the winners to be announced on Oct. 3.

The festival seeks to become more than a film competition. They want to turn it into an annual international festival in Astana and develop a dedicated streaming platform Mooncast.ai for AI-generated films, allowing works that did not make the final selection to reach a wider audience.

Beyond traditional cinema

For AAIFF 2026 Co-Founder and Creative Director Aizatulla Hussein, the more important question is what AI can do to cinema itself.

“Everyone is trying to repeat traditional cinema with the help of AI, but it seems that AI technology allows you to find some other forms of cinema,” Hussein told The Astana Times.

He sees the current generation of AI films as an experimental stage. Rather than simply reproducing the production methods and visual language of traditional cinema, creators can use AI to explore new approaches to storytelling, visual design and filmmaking.

The festival’s thematic category, “The Future Worth Living In,” was designed as a response to another familiar pattern in cinema: the way Hollywood often portrays the future as a dangerous place.

AI makes filmmaking easier, but not simple

While AI technologies help to overcome some technical barriers to visual production, the organizers mention that technology alone does not guarantee a strong film.

Hussain noted that many of the strongest submissions came from creators who already had experience in traditional filmmaking, including cinematographers, editors and directors.

“It’s not difficult to generate,” he said, referring to the technical process of creating AI content. The challenge, he suggested, lies in using the technology to create a coherent and compelling film.

The economics of film production are also an important consideration. According to the creative director of AAIFF 2026, producing a short AI film can cost between $3,000 and $5,000. The films submitted to the festival generally range from five to 20 minutes.

It means that AI is changing the filmmaking process without necessarily eliminating the need for creative expertise.

After reviewing more than 8,000 submissions, the jury chose approximately 200 works. They also launched Mooncast.ai, a streaming platform being developed specifically for AI-generated films to present other works. This would give AI filmmakers a distribution channel beyond individual competitions and could help build an international audience for a new category of film.

World.title: October Starts Here: Your Weekend Guide
World.content:
ASTANA — Unwind after a busy working week with inspiring concerts, thought-provoking exhibitions and captivating spectacles. There is something for everyone, whether you are looking to enjoy evenings with friends and spend quality time with family. The Astana Times editorial team has curated a selection of events to check out this weekend.

Astana

“Zhoshy Khan” performance, Oct. 4

The historical drama depicts the life of Zhoshy Khan, the eldest son of Genghis Khan and founder of the Zhoshy Ulus. The story explores his journey, leadership and role in the history of the steppe.

Venue: Kazakh National Musical and Drama Theater named after Kalibek Kuanishbaev; 8/1 Kalibek Kuanishbaev Street. Tickets are available here.

“Appak, The Kipchak Daughter”opera, Oct. 3

This opera tells the story of Appak, a young Kipchak woman whose life becomes connected with the renowned Azerbaijani poet Nizami Ganjavi. The production brings together history, love and dramatic events.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

“The Universe of Hans Zimmer” concert, Oct. 4

Film music lovers can enjoy an evening dedicated to the works of Hans Zimmer. The programme features music from Interstellar, Dune, Gladiator, Inception, The Lion King and other well-known films, accompanied by live orchestra and choir.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

“Hollywood Soundtracks” concert, Oct. 3

Enjoy an evening of iconic movie music performed by a live orchestra. From thrilling adventures to heartfelt melodies, this concert captures the emotion and magic of Hollywood films, creating a memorable experience for cinema and music lovers alike.

Venue: Smart Space; 280 Baizakov Street. Tickets are available here.

“La Traviata” opera, Oct. 3

Verdi’s opera, inspired by Alexandre Dumas’ “The Lady of the Camellias,” caused a stir in the 19th century with its modern plot, costumes, and the bold portrayal of a “fallen woman.” The title, meaning “the one who goes astray,” highlights the tragic fate of the main character.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“Swan Lake” ballet, Oct. 4

Experience the timeless beauty of Tchaikovsky’s “Swan Lake” in a breathtaking ballet performance. This beloved folk tale follows a maiden cursed by dark forces to live as a swan. Prince Siegfried vows to save her, but fate leads him to a tragic betrayal. A masterpiece of classical ballet, “Swan Lake” captivates both newcomers and longtime fans. With stunning grace and precision, the dancers bring this story of love and destiny to life.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Two German foundations shut down in Georgia, citing government restrictions
World.content:
German foundations, including the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation, have ended their activities in Georgia after more than 20 years of work in the country.

Both organisations say the conditions set by the Georgian government under new legislation, known as the “Grants Law”, have made it impossible for them to implement projects and continue their activities.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said foreign political parties and foundations affiliated with them should not pursue political goals in Georgia.

What the foundations say

The Tbilisi offices of both foundations closed on 30 September 2026. In statements published on 2 October, the organisations said the Georgian government’s decision to reject their grant applications had limited their ability to continue working in the country.

The Friedrich Naumann Foundation, which has operated in Georgia since 2002, said it had applied under the new law on foreign funding and grants so it could continue funding projects and working with local partners. However, the foundation said the authorities required every component of its programme to align with state priorities and required it to obtain the necessary permits for all activities.

“It was not easy for us to take this step, but it was inevitable. The actions of the Georgian government make it impossible for the foundation to continue its activities in the country,” the organisation said.

According to the foundation, the authorities rejected its application on 28 July 2026. The organisation said that under the circumstances, it no longer saw a way to continue working in line with its values and principles.

The Friedrich Naumann Foundation worked in Georgia to support liberal ideas, an open society, the country’s European future and dialogue between societies. The organisation said it would continue to support Georgian citizens who are fighting for a free and democratic system in the country.

The Konrad Adenauer Foundation also said that the closure of its office in Tbilisi was not a voluntary decision but resulted from the political and legal conditions created by the Georgian government.

“The closure of our office in Tbilisi is a direct consequence of the political and legal framework established by the Georgian government, under which the foundation can no longer fulfil its core mission as a political foundation on the ground,” the organisation said.

According to the foundation, the government rejected its project funding applications on 28 July. The organisation said it had made active efforts, including with the involvement of the German federal government, to preserve the possibility of continuing its work, but those efforts failed.

The foundation said project approval appeared possible only if the projects no longer reflected the foundation’s political nature and mission. It also stressed that maintaining a physical presence in Georgia without the ability to carry out its core activities was not an acceptable option.

The Konrad Adenauer Foundation has operated in Georgia since 2003. Its work has focused on promoting democracy and the rule of law, developing parliamentarianism, strengthening German-Georgian relations and supporting Georgia’s European integration. The organisation has also supported young researchers and students through scholarships and educational programmes.

The foundation said it would retain its legal entity status in Georgia so that it could return to the country if the political situation changes.

Both organisations said they would maintain ties with Georgia and their local partners, and attributed the suspension of their activities solely to the restrictions introduced under the new legislation.

Shalva Papuashvili’s comment

In response to the Konrad Adenauer Foundation’s statement, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said foreign political parties and organisations affiliated with them should not pursue political missions in Georgia.

“In their statement, they [the foundations] say that they have a political mission and that, since they can no longer carry it out, they see no reason to remain in the country. This is somewhat surprising.

As we know, political foundations are affiliated with political parties. The Adenauer Foundation, for example, is affiliated with the Christian Democratic Union. Let me remind you that the Christian Democratic Union is part of the EPP and, therefore, is a partner party of the United National Movement. Yet it says it wants to carry out a political mission in Georgia. In my view, foreign political parties and their foundations have no political mission to carry out in Georgia,” Papuashvili said.

He said the government had explained to the Adenauer Foundation that, to approve its grant projects, it needed to exclude projects of a political nature. Activities in academic, educational and other fields could receive approval, he said.

“However, judging by their statement, they apparently have no interest in academic, educational or other similar activities. As their own statement makes clear, they were interested in carrying out a political mission, and they are leaving because they can no longer do so. The decision is theirs,” the parliament speaker said.

Papuashvili, who is now criticising the German foundation, himself worked for German organisations for many years. From 2003 to 2007, he served as a senior legal expert at the German Technical Cooperation Society (GTZ). From 2007 to 2020, he headed the organisation’s office in Georgia.

Comment

Historian and Ilia State University professor Beka Kobakhidze commented on the closure of the Konrad Adenauer Foundation’s office in Georgia. He noted that for many years the foundation had provided scholarships to top students and created a wide range of opportunities for them.

Beka Kobakhidze: “I constantly see posts from my students thanking the Konrad Adenauer Foundation.

Do you know how Georgian master’s students live? They have to work all day to pay for housing, food and transport. Then they have to make it to a lecture at 7 p.m., attend until 9 p.m., return home by 10 p.m., eat and study. In these circumstances, quality education often remains disconnected from real-life conditions. We launched the master’s programme in the history of modern Georgia in 2020, and from day one, the foundation provided scholarships to the top students in our programme. This financial support helped them with their studies and helped us maintain a high standard of education.

The Adenauer Foundation is a right-leaning organisation, but they never once said, ‘Let’s give scholarships to students with right-wing views and not to those on the left.’ Many left-wing students received these scholarships. They never told us what or how to teach. They placed their full trust in us and gave us complete academic freedom, while we awarded scholarships based on meritocratic principles. At the end of each semester, we reviewed academic performance, and the top two or three students received scholarships.

It is impossible to count how many international conferences our students attended thanks to funding from the foundation. These opportunities deepened their knowledge, and that knowledge led to numerous achievements: Tsinandali Awards, numerous awards from the FaRiG Foundation, books by our graduates that became bestsellers at book fairs, participation in international research projects, admission to doctoral programmes, and jobs as university lecturers. And the list could go on indefinitely. The Adenauer Foundation laid the foundation for all of this.

I am immensely grateful to the foundation’s staff, who have now become close friends of mine, and whom I met through our joint work.

As of 1 October 2026, the foundation has ceased its activities in Georgia. Do you know the background? The Adenauer Foundation was expelled from Russia in 2022.”

What does the so-called “Grants Law” provide?

A package of laws adopted on 4 March 2026 significantly expanded the definition of a “grant”. It now covers both financial and non-financial support if such support could be used to influence domestic or foreign policy, including activities linked to the interests of a foreign state or political force.

The law also strengthens the State Audit Office’s oversight of grants. When a foreign legal entity provides funding to a branch operating in Georgia without government approval, the authorities can impose sanctions, including a fine equal to twice the value of the grant.

Violations of grant legislation can also lead to criminal liability. The penalties include fines, community service or imprisonment for up to six years.

The amendments also affect the political process. People who work primarily for organisations funded by foreign sources cannot join political parties for eight years. Moreover, restrictions imposed on political parties also apply to structures that are not formally parties but effectively engage in political activity.

The legislative package also tightens administrative liability for private companies that engage in public political activities.

One of the most controversial aspects of the amendments involves new provisions added to the Criminal Code that expand the definition of “extremism”. Under the new article, public calls for actions directed against the constitutional order — including calls to disobey the authorities or establish alternative structures — may constitute criminal offences.

In addition, authorities classify crimes committed on the grounds of refusing to recognise constitutional state bodies as offences committed under aggravating circumstances. This increases the sentence by at least one year.

Experts say such wording allows for broad interpretation and increases the risk that the law could be used against dissent and critical activity.

Two German foundations shut down in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijani soldier who entered Armenia fired at local residents
World.content:
Azerbaijani soldier shot an Armenian resident

On 1 October, an Azerbaijani soldier entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. He shot a 39-year-old local woman in the leg with an assault rifle. The incident happened in front of her three children, two of whom also suffered injuries.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has opened a criminal case against Nasim Musayev.

The Armenian National Security Service issued a brief statement only after people began discussing the incident on social media. It emerged that Azerbaijan’s State Security Service had informed its Armenian counterparts on 29 September that a serviceman had left his unit under unknown circumstances.

“Authorities could not rule out the possibility that he had illegally crossed into Armenia. The competent authorities of Armenia and Azerbaijan then launched search operations,” the statement said.

According to Azerbaijani law enforcement authorities, Nasim Musayev went missing on 26 September.

It remains unclear when he entered Armenian territory. Authorities found and detained him only after he committed the crime.

Armenian analysts point to previous similar cases in which Azerbaijanis who illegally crossed the border and committed crimes went back to Azerbaijan. They expect authorities to punish the Azerbaijani serviceman to the full extent of the law this time as well. If Armenian authorities decide to return him to Azerbaijan, they suggest taking into account the fact that 19 Armenian prisoners remain in Baku’s jails.

The incident has sparked outrage in Armenian society and prompted widespread discussion on social media. Against the backdrop of repeated statements by the authorities that peace has arrived, users commented on the incident with the short phrase: “Long live peace.”

Witness accounts

“My brother and sister came home from their classes and saw that the window was broken. They called our mother. She and our father came by car. My mother had a knife in her hand. She always kept it with her in case something like this happened, so she could protect herself. My mother went inside and stabbed him with the knife. The man then fired a shot and ran away,” the injured woman’s son told a local media outlet.

Meanwhile, her sister said the Azerbaijani man took the children hostage, while their mother, who tried to protect them, lost three fingers on her left hand.

In an interview with Radio Azatutyun (Freedom), she said her sister’s two children were talking to their parents on the phone as they walked home from school. They then saw that the lock on their front door had been broken. When they entered the house, they saw an Azerbaijani soldier in the living room. They tried to call their mother for help, but the Azerbaijani man took their phone away.

According to the injured woman’s sister, the Azerbaijani man was pointing his weapon at the children when their mother entered the house. She tried to cover the barrel with her hand. Musayev then fired, causing her to lose fingers on her left hand.

The sister also said the injured woman had to defend herself. While the soldier tried to reload his rifle, she stabbed him several times. However, the soldier struck her and knocked her unconscious. Her 15-year-old son then fought with the Azerbaijani man and suffered a broken arm.

The health of the mother and children

The woman suffered gunshot wounds to her thigh and arm. She first received medical treatment at a medical centre in Sisian and then went to a clinic in Yerevan.

According to reports, her life is not in danger and her condition remains stable. However, she needs surgery.

The woman’s 15-year-old and 12-year-old sons also suffered injuries.

“The child born in 2014 has soft-tissue bruising, while the child born in 2011 has a fracture of the right wrist.”

Doctors put a cast on the boy with the fracture. The other boy needed psychological support.

Information from Yerevan and Baku

There is little official information about the incident.

The Armenian National Security Service initially issued a statement:

“At 14:15 on 1 October, the 112 emergency centre of the Interior Ministry received a report that an Armenian citizen had suffered a gunshot wound to the leg in the settlement of Shaki in Syunik Province. Operational teams from various police units went to the scene. They took urgent measures to establish all the circumstances of the incident. They established that an Azerbaijani serviceman had committed the crime and detained him.”

Armenian authorities reportedly passed details of the incident to the Azerbaijani side.

Baku provided information about the serviceman who crossed the border only after the incident in Shaki.

According to Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office, Nasim Musayev went missing from his military unit in Lachin on 26 September. Authorities opened a criminal case over his disappearance. The investigation confirmed suspicions that Musayev had left the military unit voluntarily.

“As a result of the measures taken, authorities established that Nasimi Musayev was in Armenia and that the relevant authorities of that country had detained him,” Azerbaijani law enforcement authorities said.

They also stressed that they were working with their Armenian counterparts to establish the details of the incident.

Criminal cases opened

Armenia’s Prosecutor General’s Office announced yesterday that it had opened a criminal case under charges of “causing serious bodily harm with the use of a weapon”, “illegal possession of a firearm” and “violation of the inviolability of a home”.

The omission of the illegal border crossing from the statement sparked outrage in Armenia.

Today, the authorities said they had added charges of illegally crossing the border and smuggling a firearm.

Analysts’ views

Political analyst Suren Surenyants highlighted the fact that the Armenian side received information about a possible border violation at least two days before the incident:

“It is worrying that, despite the warning and the announced search, authorities found Musayev in Shaki only after he used a firearm against an Armenian citizen. The search operations did not prevent him from potentially crossing the border illegally, entering Shaki or opening fire.”

According to Surenyants, the authorities need to clarify the following:

how the Azerbaijani serviceman crossed the state border and travelled from Lachin to Shaki,

where he entered Armenian territory, how he bypassed border controls and security systems,

why authorities failed to find him either within two days of the warning or roughly five days after he disappeared,

what legal procedures await the Azerbaijani serviceman?

“Authorities have already opened a criminal case. The next question is whether they will bring the case to its legal conclusion, meaning conduct a full investigation into the circumstances of the illegal border crossing and the use of a weapon against an Armenian citizen, or whether political agreements will determine the case,” he stressed.

The political analyst also expects answers to the following questions:

if Armenia considers handing Musayev over to Azerbaijan, will it raise the issue of returning Armenian prisoners held in Baku?

what legal and political conditions could determine such a decision?

Surenyants noted that, more broadly, the incident exposed the lack of effective border control in Armenia.

Azerbaijan expert Tatevik Hayrapetyan suggested viewing the events in Shaki in the context of previous cases. She recalled:

in 2019, Armenian authorities, with the support of the International Committee of the Red Cross, returned Elvin Ibrahimov to Azerbaijan after he illegally crossed Armenia’s state border. They described the decision as a “humanitarian step”.

in 2023, Azerbaijan also received Huseyn Akhundov, who killed 56-year-old Hayrapet Meliksetyan in Armenia and received a 20-year prison sentence.

Tatevik Hayrapetyan stressed that Armenia should rule out a similar approach in this case:

“An attack on the life and safety of an Armenian citizen cannot lead to the return of the perpetrator to Azerbaijan under ‘humanitarian’ pretexts. The authorities must investigate this case to the full extent of the law. If they establish his guilt, the perpetrator must serve the sentence prescribed by law.”

Comments on social media

“The incident involving the Azerbaijani soldier has once again shown the situation at the border. It is a good thing he came alone. He could have come with an entire army, and we would have greeted them with a large ‘Welcome to Armenia’ banner.”

“It turns out that an armed man can cross the state border unhindered, move around for several days, reach a settlement and harm a civilian. This, in turn, means that once again, the citizen has been left alone to fight for his own safety.”

“Peace means that, in ‘peacetime’, an Azerbaijani soldier cannot show up at your home and harm you in front of your children. By 29 September, authorities already knew that an Azerbaijani soldier had left his military unit, and the Armenian side had received information about it. Where was state control once authorities learned that the soldier had left his unit? What measures did they take to prevent him from entering Armenian territory? Where was the government that promised ‘peace’ during the recent election campaign?”

Azerbaijani soldier shot an Armenian resident

World.title: Prisoner in Georgia accuses guards of sexual abuse. Penitentiary Service denies allegations
World.content:
Prison violence in Georgia

Prisoner Giorgi Davitadze said staff at Prison No. 6 in Rustavi subjected him to sexual abuse. He says the incident took place on 21 December 2025, when staff moved him to a de-escalation cell. According to Davitadze, ten people attacked him there.

The Special Penitentiary Service denied the allegations. It said its video of the incident shows no signs of violence.

What happened?

TV channel Pirveli published an audio recording of testimony Davitadze gave at the Court of Appeals. According to the prisoner, the alleged abuse took place within view of surveillance cameras. However, he says the staff positioned themselves in a way that prevented the cameras from fully capturing their actions.

“They took me to a de-escalation cell and raped me with their fingers and hands. […] Ten men raped me; a guard was also present, and the whole thing is visible on camera,” Davitadze said during the hearing.

The prisoner claims that staff subjected him to pressure after he demanded a forensic medical examination. He told the court that he had tried to take his own life because he could no longer bear staying near the same staff members he accuses of abuse.

Davitadze also said staff verbally abused him in the de-escalation cell. “I tell the man, ‘I was raped.’ And the representative of the Public Defender’s Office simply lowers his head,” he said. He questioned why the verbal abuse he described to the court could not be heard on the camera recordings.

Davitadze told the judges that he would go on hunger strike unless the guards involved in the incident faced prosecution. The judges asked representatives of the service whether an investigation had begun. The prosecutor confirmed that an investigation into the incident was under way.

What does the Penitentiary Service say?

According to the Special Penitentiary Service, video footage shows that Davitadze refused to undergo a mandatory search while staff were moving him to a de-escalation cell and insulted prison staff. The service says staff later conducted a forced search using a handheld metal detector as part of their official duties.

“No violence was used against Davitadze — let alone any sexual abuse,” the Penitentiary Service said.

The service explained that it had previously refrained from publishing the footage because authorities were investigating the incident. It did not want anyone to interpret the release as an attempt to put pressure on the investigation. The service said it decided to publish the footage because of the strong public reaction and what it described as deliberate attempts by the prisoner’s family to discredit the institution.

The Penitentiary Service also said it had archived continuous video footage of Davitadze’s movements around the facility from 3 March 2026 to the present. According to the service, it can provide these recordings to all interested parties in accordance with the law.

What does Davitadze’s family say?

Irma Davitadze, Giorgi’s mother, is calling for not only the guards involved in the incident but also Shota Trapaidze, head of Prison No. 6, to face prosecution. She said the family would continue its fight until those responsible for the abuse receive punishment. In particular, she mentioned prison employee Giorgi Kvaratskhelia, whom she alleges has links to the use of violence against prisoners.

According to Irma Davitadze, the family has also collected information about possible violations that occurred at the facility in the past.
