World.title: I used to think having a dog would make travel more difficult. This weekend changed that
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life I used to think having a dog would make travel more difficult. This weekend changed that Abby Seaman October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the October 4 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Before Junior, my three-year-old rescue greyhound, came into my life, escaping for a spontaneous weekend away was as easy as throwing a toothbrush and PJs into an overnight bag. Now it requires a little more planning to pin down a dog-sitter or taking the easier, though less exciting option: simply declining the invite. My perfect holiday would be to bring Junior along but, understandably, most accommodation isn’t pet-friendly, especially for a 30-kilogram greyhound. So when I get wind that Unyoked’s secluded and off-grid cabins dotted around Australia offer pet-friendly options, I can’t grab Junior and his lead quickly enough before the two of us hit the highway to the Hunter Valley, three hours north from our home in Sydney. Junior getting settled into his holiday. Abby Seaman For one last civilised hurrah before two nights in nature, we stop at Tintilla Estate in Pokolbin for a wine, meat and cheese tasting. I’m running late for my reservation, a result of my first time travelling with Junior, and am just about to start my flurry of apologies when I’m greeted with a calm “No worries” from the owner.



Sitting in the sun, looking over the rolling vineyard, with lunch and a beverage, I let go of my flustered state. I’m pleased to discover that many wineries in the Hunter Valley allow dogs outside. Even the hatted restaurant, Bistro Molines, offers a dog-friendly lunch booking. While plenty of the Unyoked tiny cabins welcome both dogs and cats, the company has also teamed up with Australian dog food company Lyka to offer the Lyka Lodge at Pokolbin, creating perhaps the most dog-friendly holiday imaginable. (For southern travellers, there is also a Victorian Lyka Lodge – in the Tarra Valley, south-east of Melbourne.) Once I arrive and park at the site, Junior and I start out on a short walk through the bush to our cabin. Anticipating the trip, I gave myself a pep talk about how I would embrace and immerse myself in nature – something that comes naturally to Junior, of course. I am greeted by a mob of kangaroos, who idle in a paddock. A wild rabbit sprints in the nearby foliage. A goanna startles Junior and me as it hisses and climbs the nearest tree. The cabin itself is built with sustainably sourced timber and powered by solar energy, and features a composting toilet. It’s furnished with cookware, a cosy bed and hot water. Just enough to disconnect from modern life, but to enjoy a comfortable stay.



For the pup guest, it includes a large bed, hygiene wipes and spray, a dog bowl, and much-appreciated dental treats. There is also an extra-long dog lead to allow Junior to explore safely. Escape to nature in style. Nikita Brown In addition, the cabin includes a guide to starting a campfire. Junior and I wander around our surrounding area, picking up sticks and kindling, ready to pretend we are in an episode of Alone Australia. By nightfall, I am so excited to cook dinner (grilled corn and jacket potatoes) over the campfire that I almost forget to look up at the clear night sky full of stars. The next day I wake to the early sunrise and a chorus of birds. I take my time preparing coffee. I grind the coffee beans with the provided hand grinder and meditatively watch the moka pot boil over.



After I use the provided yoga mat to stretch outside, Junior wakes from his nap in the sun to join me in an impressive downward dog. Related Article Sunday Life ‘You’ll see someone famous’: Visit this bar for one of the last old-school NYC experiences We take a walk, bird-watching along the way – an activity I love but rarely find the time for, or the variety of birds, in the city. Back at our tiny home, we dedicate some more time towards rest. Junior sprawls out on a picnic blanket and naps in the sun, I intermittently read and doze in the hammock. It turns out I’m pretty good at doing nothing. I find myself spending time just sitting and thinking, not of my to-do lists and what to achieve next, but simply contemplating. “Why don’t I make time to do this more?” is one thought that floats by often.



By the evening, the bird song has quietened. To fill the silence, I pop on one of the provided CDs and find myself dancing while preparing dinner. At least I’m so remote that no one can see me, besides the judgement-free eyes of Junior. Later, he and I snuggle by the fire, roasting marshmallows and watching the stars. I enjoy witnessing him get in touch with his wild side. The whole experience would be great without Junior, but bringing him with me makes it special. Before checking out on our last morning, I soak up every last drop of relaxation. I do some yoga outdoors, we bird-watch and I make one last hearty meal and slowly brewed coffee, while dancing to the CD. The cabin has worked its magic and massaged the knots of stress out of my mind. As I walk back into the real world, I vow to carry some part of this calmness I’ve found with me. With ideas like, “Once I get back, I’m going to slow down and savour my time.” Realistically, I know it probably won’t last. But at least I know the cabin will be there for an easy, spur-of-the-moment getaway in nature – with my best mate, Junior.



The writer travelled as a guest of Lyka Pet Food and Unyoked. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.

World.title: Forget the men, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles carry the true love story of this film
World.content:
Daisy Edgar Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood in the new film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility.

The two actors are the perfect pick to play sisters in this latest Austen reboot.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the October 4 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

A decade before anyone put them in bonnets, Daisy Edgar-Jones met Esmé Creed-Miles on the 2017 Yorkshire set of coming-of-age drama Pond Life. “I was so blown away by her,” says Edgar-Jones, who was then 19, of her co-star, then 17. “[She] has this energy that is so compelling. She’s a wonderfully intelligent and sort of wild person, in the best way.” The teenagers became fast friends and “had a really great summer of watching Love Island and shooting this indie film”. Creed-Miles’ first impression of her co-star is equally vivid: “Daisy was unbelievably kind and talented. She put me at ease and I could tell I had a friend in her.” Admittedly, “it would be hard not to get on with Daisy. She’s just one of the loveliest people.” Almost a decade on, the women are reunited on a much grander stage: Georgia Oakley’s gorgeous adaptation of Jane Austen’s 1811 debut novel, Sense and Sensibility, in which they star as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood. “To already have that shorthand with Esmé and to feel a sort of sisterly feeling, made it so seamless,” says Edgar-Jones. An Austen adaptation is a world away from a small budget indie, but this is no polite costume drama either. It’s a kaleidoscope of undone hair, mud, rage and running. “I was really trying to get into what it might have felt like to live in Devon 200 years ago,” Oakley has said of her film’s unbridled aesthetic. “Steering away from this preconceived idea we have about Austen, that everything takes place in a stuffy drawing room.” When Edgar-Jones, 28, appears on our video call, it’s 11am in London. She’s just off a call with Australian writer Tony McNamara about Mosquito, their upcoming comedy series. What does a Gucci, Boucheron and Estée Lauder brand ambassador wear when working from home? As it turns out, a striped rugby jumper, no discernible make-up and “sports shorts” from a morning workout: “It’s not my best look!”



A few days later, Creed-Miles, 26, is similarly casual when she Zooms in just after 1pm. “I woke up quite recently,” she says, wandering around her London home, earbuds in, breaking off to answer the door: “I think it’s some food.” Daisy Edgar-Jones: “What Austen does so well is explore the variety of love we can experience in a life.” Charlotte Hadden for Focus Features Seeing the pair like this – using tech, in athleisure wear, waiting on deliveries – is faintly surreal after seeing them as the Dashwoods, physically and emotionally entwined as they braid hair, share a bed and absorb each other’s heartbreaks. With apologies to Edward Ferrars (George MacKay) and Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum), they’re the heart of the film and its true love story. “I’m really glad that you say that because I remember that being such a clear piece of direction that Georgia, our director, wanted to follow,” says Edgar-Jones. Growing up an only child, she “had to outsource that sisterly or that familial sibling bond to friends”, and found it here. “It’s just a really lovely thing that the love story is the two women and how much they gift each other.” To Oakley, the Dashwoods “represent these two opposing forces that a lot of women have within themselves that are always at war”. For Austen-era women with few ways to support themselves and little control over inheritance, says Creed-Miles, “the bond of motherhood or sisterhood becomes more prescient”. “It’s just a really lovely thing that the love story is the two women and how much they gift each other.” DAISY EDGAR-JONES In Austen’s world, marriage was survival – do it or sink. So in 2026, when women have careers, best friends and their own front-door keys, what is romantic love actually for? “It’s a great question, and I think it’s one we’re always asking,” says Edgar-Jones.



In a relationship with photographer Ben Seed for nearly four years, Edgar-Jones says she “loves love” and that modern romance is “for friendship and companionship and support”. But her longer answer is pure Elinor: “What Austen does so well is explore the variety of love we can experience in a life – be it platonic, familial, romantic – and how valuable all of those are. The same exists today. It’s so magic to cultivate love in all those different areas of your life if you can.” Asked about the same topic, Creed-Miles admits defeat – “Oh gosh. Literally, that is just too big a question for me”. There is romance in her life, though, in the form of an engagement to musician Daisy Maybe – yes, another Daisy. “I love going for a walk with my fiancée,” she says. “We take our dog to the park. We might cook some nice food and watch a bit of telly and chill out. Very simple.” The successor to Kate Winslet’s Marianne, Creed-Miles has never seen the 1995 adaptation of Sense and Sensibility. Charlotte Hadden for Focus Features In real life, which of the pair is sense and which is sensibility? Edgar-Jones says she is “probably a mixture, honestly”, adding “I don’t fall in love very easily” while admitting to being “a massive romantic”. Creed-Miles, gloriously vulnerable and untamed as Marianne, leans “more towards sensibility, internally. I definitely experience that sort of crushing depth of feeling.” “Perhaps the thing I love most in the world is a good bit of hardcore yearning.” DAISY EDGAR-JONES Marianne is the kind of woman Creed-Miles always wanted to be, someone “outgoing and with a passion for life who took risks”, whereas she describes herself as “quite reclusive”. That introversion is something she’s “constantly reconciling” with her other day job as singer and guitarist in UK duo Cusk.



Edgar-Jones is a devotee of Ang Lee’s 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility, describing Emma Thompson’s Elinor as “one of the most beautiful performances in cinema”. The successor to Kate Winslet’s Marianne, Creed-Miles has never seen the 31-year-old film, but says the new incarnation will “hopefully do [Winslet] and Emma and Ang Lee proud”. The storyline, of course, is awash with yearning: Elinor and Edward for each other, Colonel Brandon for Marianne, Marianne for Willoughby, mothers and relatives for weddings. It’s a mode Edgar-Jones perfected as another Marianne, opposite Paul Mescal’s Connell in the 2020 smash TV series Normal People, which made her a household name and garnered her Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. Does she ever wish we’d forget Normal People? “Oh no, I’d be so sad if that happened,” she says. “I love those characters so much, and I love that show. I mean, perhaps the thing I love most in the world is a good bit of hardcore yearning, and I do think Sense and Sensibility and Normal People really tick that box.” Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood. MacKay’s Edward also extends a streak she copped to in Elle last year: “I have worked with basically all of the internet’s boyfriends,” she said, citing Mescal, Sebastian Stan and Jacob Elordi. “Just Timothée Chalamet and Austin Butler left!” Born in London to Wendy, a film editor, and Philip Edgar-Jones, a television executive, Daisy acted in school plays before studying at the National Youth Theatre. Teenage TV roles in Cold Feet and Silent Witness led to Normal People, then Where the Crawdads Sing, Under the Banner of Heaven and Twisters. The daughter of actors Samantha Morton and Charlie Creed-Miles, Esmé made her showbiz debut at seven as a tiny Shirley Temple impersonator in Harmony Korine’s 2007 film Mister Lonely, before moving on to three seasons of snapping necks as the title assassin in Amazon’s Hanna and a role in Kristen Stewart’s 2025 directorial debut, The Chronology of Water.



Both women talk glowingly of the fun and shared knowledge on Sense and Sensibility’s female-led set: director Oakley, writer Diana Reid, a cast including Fiona Shaw (Killing Eve, Andor) and Caitríona Balfe (Outlander). Were gossip and tips swapped around the catering table? “It was wonderful to learn from Fiona and Caitríona, but I think less to do with the industry and more just to do with their attitude towards life and storytelling,” says Creed-Miles. “Even if it was like a squeeze of the hand or a moment of eye contact, to feel like you were held in those spaces was really precious.” The shared experience extended to the costumes. Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles raided each other’s on-set wardrobes, just like real sisters, and covet each other’s actual things. Edgar-Jones– whose off-duty staples are jeans, a “really good” white T-shirt and a “woolly jumper” – loves her friend’s vintage loafers. What would Creed-Miles steal in return? “Daisy is the chicest,” she says. “Probably one of her really cool coats.” Related Article Pop culture Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions The day we speak, Edgar-Jones is heading to a pub to see Creed-Miles’ band, although Esmé says that Daisy, a fan of Sarah J. Maas fantasy novels and personalised stationery, is the better after-dark girl. Edgar-Jones laughs at that. A DJ, she runs through what makes a great party – “the lighting has to be dark” – while on the decks “I’m still obsessed with Charli XCX. But then, I love a bit of Motown.” The film’s PR tagline is, “No one knows your heart like a sister.” Creed-Miles says it’s true, adding, “Daisy is family to me. That kind of sisterhood is really important in this world and in this job. I’m very grateful.” Marriage plots come and go. This is the love match that stuck.

World.title: A ski town that’s not like most others – it has a soul
World.content:
InspirationSki holidays A ski town that’s not like most others – it has a soul Jim Darby October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

You can thank Lord Revelstoke for all the puns and the bumper stickers – “get Stoked”, “feel the Stoke”, and even “ride the Stoke chair”. His Lordship arranged the finance to get the railway through here in the late 1800s and the town beneath the mighty Selkirk and Monashee mountain ranges in Canada’s British Columbia was named after him as a tribute. Nat Segal skiing fresh snow at Revelstoke, with the Columbia River valley below. Ryan Collins A century or so on, Revelstoke has grown somewhat, and there are no signs of the peerage, for here you have all the attributes of a mountain town – full of youth and energy and shops and services dedicated to outdoor pursuits. In summer, it’ll be buzzing with hikers and mountain bikers and all sorts of water lovers on the lakes and the Columbia River that runs right alongside. In winter, you’ll find skiers and snowboarders hopping aboard one of the dozen or so heli-skiing operations to get their thrills in the hills or making the short trip up the road to the Revelstoke Mountain Resort.



The Resort itself is a work in progress, as far as its base area goes – there are hotels and apartments established and under construction, cafes and bars for the hungry and thirsty, and excellent ski/board retail and rental outlets. 



“My first time skiing at Revelstoke Mountain Resort was in 2013 when I was competing on the Freeride World Tour. I just remember having my mind blown, like I’d never skied trees like that or found pillow lines [mounds of snow covering logs or rocks] like that in bounds”, Segal says. Australian Nat Segal on her new home mountain. Ryan Collins She returned several times and used it as a location for the feature-length documentary she made with her sister Anna – Finding the Line. “So I had some connections through that and a few friends who had moved here, and I moved to Revelstoke in 2018”. By now, she knows the mountain well. The main drag, as she calls it, is the gondola, with some long blue (intermediate-level) groomed runs “if it’s a little busier, I’ll just do laps on the gondola, just fast. It’s the best place to get your legs going because they’re such long runs. When my parents come to visit me and I do it with them, we have to stop all the time and I’m just like ‘oh come on you two, you haven’t done your training’.” The Stoke Chair gives access to some of the mountain’s bigger bowls – North Bowl and Greely Bowl and if you don’t mind a hike you can head up to the sub-peak area below Mackenzie Peak. “There’s amazing access all through there. A lot of the areas off the Stoke Chair are ungroomed, off-piste. It’s the more challenging terrain, but they’re really fun runs and it’s a great place for stepping up into harder and harder terrain.”



Then there’s the Ripper Chair, lower in elevation but offering entertaining blue and green (easiest) groomed runs and if you want to head off those runs, “there’s some tree skiing that’s not too steep but still really fun and playful. “Some people on a powder day will go straight to the Stoke Chair and other people go straight to the Ripper. It’s all to do with style. I like the steeper terrain, I like a little bit more open terrain, whereas I have friends that all they want to do is ski the trees.” One of the “Art Alleries” – street art in downtown Revelstoke. Rob Buchanan Another measure of the area relates to the company you’ll keep. Revelstoke has the highest concentration of Association of Canadian Mountain Guides members in the country (you’ll see the ACMG status with their signature). Many work as heli-ski or cat-ski guides and backcountry ski touring guides. It also has a healthy community. “One of the reasons I moved to Revelstoke and I’m staying, is the community. I live in the downtown area, just a few blocks from the main street. And it feels so lovely – so much art and culture and some amazing nonprofits.



“If you stick around for a season you can be really involved in the town, but even if you’re just there for a visit, there’s always stuff going on. A classic is going to the Grizzlies [ice] hockey games. There are local kids playing and you have people who have lived there all their lives to people who have been for a week all cheering for the same team.” Revelstoke town at night. Tom Poole “From my house downtown to the resort parking lot is seven minutes if I time it. And there are buses and shuttles, so if you’re staying at one or the other you can easily get between the two. “You can stay at the resort and get that resort feeling, but then if you want to go downtown and have a walk around a cozy town, you can do that as well. There are lots of options for accommodation in the town and the resort. Sutton Place Hotel – a stroll away from the lifts at Revelstoke Mountain Resort. Royce Sihlis



“One thing I really appreciate is that there isn’t a divide, there are lots of residents living in the areas where tourists stay, but at the same time, the tourist accommodation isn’t crowding out the town, the town still has soul.” Given its deep-in-the-mountains location, outside winter, Revelstoke still draws in the visitors and has plenty to entertain the locals. Related Article Ski holidays If you wanted to create the ultimate ski resort, this place would be the template That might be hiking or mountain biking, or spending time on the river or lakes. Those waterways are mountain-fed though. “It’s funny, as someone who loves the water and grew up by the beach, it doesn’t replace the beach, but Canadian lakes are lovely in their own right. So there’s a whole experience out there. But the water is freezing!



“Later in the summer it does warm up, so at the end of September it’s just like March in southern Australia. But yeah, early season, you’re not staying in the water very long,” Segal says. THE DETAILS STAY + SKI

Two choices in location and then many choices for accommodation. Stay at the resort base, at the likes of the Sutton Place Hotel (suttonplace.com rooms from $C469/$470 a night in winter), and you can wander out the door and straight on to the lifts. Stay in town, a few minutes’ from the skiing, and you get all the accommodation, cafes, bars and shops of Revelstoke township. The lift pass is part of the Ikon and Mountain Collective networks, which will suit some season pass holders from Mount Buller and Thredbo. See revelstokemountainresort.com FLY + DRIVE

Air New Zealand (airnewzealand.com.au) flies daily to Vancouver where there are onward connecting flights to Kelowna (about an hour in the air). Revelstoke is about a two-and-a-half hour drive from Kelowna, with hire cars and regular shuttle services available. A tip in winter is to come via Kelowna, rather than Calgary on the Alberta side, as snow is more likely to interrupt access if you’re coming in from Alberta. The writer flew to Canada as a guest of Air New Zealand and visited Revelstoke as a guest of Destination British Columbia (supernaturalbc.com) and Revelstoke Mountain Resort.

World.title: The lonely boy with the sad eyes finally got to come back to Australia
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The tale of the lonely boy left at a Sydney orphanage broke the hearts of a nation. Described as a war child of mixed race with “sad eyes”, Geoffrey Joiner was the result of a wartime romance between an Australian woman and an African-American man who met at a Sydney nightclub. Joiner was born in Sydney on the day after his father, Trennon, a US Navy sailor, was shipped home in 1944. Three years later the boy was surrendered to Dalwood Children’s Home at Seaforth on Sydney’s northern beaches by his mother, Jean Aughey. The Daily Telegraph report on the eve of Geoffrey Joiner’s fifth birthday in 1949. The Daily Telegraph Known as the world’s loneliest child, or the lonely boy, Geoffrey Joiner was left at Dalwood Children’s Home. After a story about him being the loneliest boy appeared in the Daily Telegraph in 1949, Geoffrey Joiner was showered with visitors, birthday gifts and an offer from a philanthropist E. J. Hallstrom to pay for him to be reunited with his father Trennon in the US. The Daily Telegraph Joiner had no other home and was stateless. He was not the only one.



“There are potentially thousands of children [like Joiner] born of war who have been neglected by the United States and Australia,” said historian Dr Victoria Grieves Williams, who developed an Australian Research Council project looking into such cases. “We have almost 40 of the children and their families in the project, and every story is different.” Most were love stories. “People fell in love and wanted to marry,” Grieves Williams said. “Many were bitterly disappointed by the two racially segregating regimes [Australia and the US] not allowing them to marry and form families for their children.” Like Joiner, many were never issued a passport or any papers. The story of five-year-old Geoffrey Joiner’s abandonment, his loneliness and the generosity of the public and a prominent philanthropist and trustee of Taronga Park Zoo, Sir E. J. Hallstrom, who funded Joiner’s reunion with his father Trennon in the US, made gripping news. Geoffrey Joiner as a baby with his mother, Jean Aughey. Aughey sent this photo to the boy’s grandmother in the United States; prospective war brides were encouraged to correspond with family overseas. But the military usually didn’t action requests by mixed-race couples to marry, said expert Victoria Grieves Williams. Geoffrey Joiner jnr. Like a real-life soap opera, it prompted daily coverage by newspapers to quench readers’ interest in the boy’s fate.



By March, the five-year-old was reunited with the father he had never met. Joiner never made it back to Australia before he died, aged 79, in Ohio in 2023, and did not ever see his mother or his older sister Betty again. This year, though, his son, Geoffrey Joiner jnr, of Virginia Beach, US, brought his late father’s ashes back to Australia. Before his father died Joiner jnr asked: “Would you like for me to take you back to Australia and dump your ashes somewhere? And he was like … ‘That’ll be the best thing that could ever happen. That way I’ll be back to where I started from’.” Joiner’s remains were spread at Dalwood, no longer a children’s home, and at Aughey’s grave. His family sprinkled more ashes at Taronga Zoo, where Hallstrom’s archives are held. A long-serving director and trustee of the zoo, Hallstrom made his fortune selling Silent Knight refrigerators. He wrote a blank cheque to cover the costs of sending Joiner to live with his father in the United States. The Joiner family visited Taronga Zoo in early 2026 to scatter the ashes of Geoffrey Joiner snr. Geoffrey Joiner jnr is in the middle. Geoffrey Joiner jnr Hallstrom’s philanthropy also included bringing three boatloads of animals from Africa, South America and Papua New Guinea after the war to Australia, which he had bought and donated to the zoo.



In correspondence, Hallstrom marvelled that Joiner had grown to more than two metres tall. The boy may have remained at Dalwood for his entire childhood if it wasn’t for a report by The Daily Telegraph on the eve of his fifth birthday in 1949, and headlines describing him as “the loneliest boy in the world”. “Geoffrey never has a visitor, and nobody contributes to his support … he gets all dressed up and sits waiting for someone to come see him, but no one ever calls,” the report said. It included a plea from Trennon Joiner, writing from Ohio. “Won’t you please send my son to me? Why should he suffer for what was wrong?” The next day the boy with no visitors had crowds of them, and a mountain of toys. Soon after, Hallstrom gave him the blank cheque to get him home. Later in life Geoffrey Joiner wanted to return to Australia, but he had been scared that if he left the US he would not be able to come back. And when the boy arrived in the United States he was detained until the paperwork for his entry was complete. He was not issued with a passport.



Joiner jnr said his father never recovered from his experience in Australia. A fear of abandonment had haunted Joiner snr’s life, making him insecure in relationships and unsure of his citizenship. In an undated letter, he writes to his half-sister Betty in Australia, apologising for not being in touch: “I had no way of corresponding with mother and you.” He writes that he doesn’t know how they were separated, and adds, “please don’t let it happen again”. “He didn’t really know if he had proper citizenship in the United States, and he had been living under the radar his entire life,” Joiner jnr said. “The biggest question we all have is why Jean didn’t come. Sometimes I ask myself if it was the military, or if she had a change of heart. Maybe my Aunt Betty wasn’t allowed to come and she didn’t want to leave her behind. Or perhaps some paperwork was required for her because from that point on it’s where [Hallstrom] steps in.”

World.title: Barnyard punks in Orange, empty stages in Byron Bay: The NSW towns where live music thrives or dies
World.content:
17-year-old Lachlan Munro at Orange’s The Gig. His schoolmates helped spike his hair before classes started at 8am.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In showground barns usually reserved for cattle on the outskirts of Orange in western NSW, Mitch Colton awaits hordes of hardcore punk and metal fans ahead of his inaugural two-day music festival, The Gig. Speaking to the Herald under a corrugated iron roof two hours before the scheduled start time, Colton appears unbothered but is apprehensive. “Two weeks ago, the ticket sales were awful,” the co-organiser and seasoned event manager says. “Tickets are getting better now.” “I was talking to the guy that owns Mojos, which is a really famous live music venue in Fremantle, and he’s like, ‘Yeah, we do 80 per cent of our tickets on the day now’.” Dozens of punters as young as 12, clad in leather garments, with spiked hair and face piercings, stream in throughout the first frosty Friday night. “Even if it’s not packed out, as long as it’s a good turnout and there’s a good crowd [that’s a success],” Colton says. Teens at the front barricade of Orange’s The Gig festival. Audrey Richardson Colton had hoped for 500 patrons. Instead, about 190 came through. The following Saturday night, 250 did. “Obviously, we’d like it to be a commercial success, but the reality is, as long as it feels good – because the joke of the sign is that nothing ever happens in Orange,” he says, referencing the festival’s poster, which in the spirit of punk declares just that.



Live music scenes across the state are evolving. Musicians are struggling to get stage time in the Northern Rivers’ once-bustling scene, while the Central West is remaking the model and Newcastle is emerging as a hotspot. Meanwhile, in Sydney, venues are shutting as punters’ behaviour changes amid the cost of living crisis and the decline of alcohol consumption. Over the years, the regions have nurtured some big names. Singer-songwriter Shannon Noll was born in Orange, while Lismore delivered Grinspoon and Skunkhour. Country stars Keith Urban, Lee Kernaghan, James Blundell and Beccy Cole got golden tickets at Tamworth’s annual country music festival. Co-organiser of The Gig Mitch Colton t-minus two hours from when gates open. Audrey Richardson The Gig’s poster. Audrey Richardson Byron Bay has cradled Parcels, Skegss, Parkway Drive, Tones and I and Pete Murray and Newcastle claims the likes of Silverchair, The Screaming Jets, Morgan Evans and Catherine Britt. Colton’s festival is one of the increasing number of independently organised cultural events in NSW’s regions. On the festival’s first night, pub-rock Orange-born band Where’s Jimmy performs an electric set. The high-school mates moved to Newcastle for better opportunities after exhausting the “same two pubs” in Orange soon after forming in 2020 amid the pandemic. Now, they regularly book gigs in Newcastle, occasionally in Sydney and are fresh off a European tour.



“It’s special for our first show back to be at home,” the band’s bassist James Pansini says. On stage, lead singer Hugh Westcott squirms erratically and jumps around barefoot, before launching into an acrobatic midair split. In the band’s music video for the song KICK IN THE HEAD, he takes it further, running barefoot around a barn with animal faeces strewn across the straw ground. Since the band relocated, Orange and the rest of the state’s Central West towns have embraced an experimental attitude towards their live music landscape, says Sophie Jones, the region’s Music NSW coordinator. “People are wanting to step away from the pubs and clubs where there are pokies,” Jones says. Orange’s Badlands Brewery’s ticketed gigs include acts such as Alex Lloyd, Meg Washington, Josh Pike and The Whitlams. But the most exciting event, says Jones, is the “little blues festival in the car park” the venue runs. Lead singer of Where’s Jimmy, Hugh Westcott, in a brief moment of tranquility. Audrey Richardson “It’s so cool to see these smaller venues doing these non-council-run little one-day festivals,” she says. “My band’s been playing together for 12 years now, and we started here in Bathurst, and there was nowhere for us.



“Now it’s taken this kind of turn where a lot of people are really wanting to come to Bathurst and play at venues like Reckless, The Victoria and Keystone … There’s still a challenge of getting people along to ticketed original shows, but it’s definitely got better in the last 10 years.” Beyond towns and in the outback, music scenes are also pushing boundaries. In Lightning Ridge, musicians perform, record and collaborate out of a “tinny”, or a performance space modelled on the housing in the typical 1950s Aboriginal “tin camp” and designed by First Nations musician Warren Mason. “He’s got a permanent one set up at [venue] Hungry Spirit ... but he takes the tinnies all around and, oh man, it’s so cool! And all original music,” Jones says. “Warren’s toured all across the outback and then around the bottom of Victoria, like Mildura.” Teens at the all-ages Orange festival, The Gig. Audrey Richardson Newcastle’s talent pool and hunger for gigs has never been higher, Joab Eastley, that city’s coordinator for Music NSW, says. “I feel like we’ve punched above our weight for quite a while here in Newcastle,” he says. “Every time you go somewhere like Big Sound and Music Conference, or get out to another city, everyone’s like, ‘Wow, what’s going on in Newcastle?’ Or everyone’s got a story of, ‘I saw this band from Newcastle in Brisbane the other week, and they blew my socks off.’ It’s a very common line.” Eastley says it’s natural there are more opportunities in a bigger city like Newcastle for acts such as Where’s Jimmy than in other regional towns. But, as with Orange and Lightning Ridge, venues and event organisers are experimenting with how to deliver gigs.



“A lot of our bigger festivals have seemed to have gone by the wayside; that was sort of post-COVID,” he says. “Instead, it’s more like boutiquey-niche things are what’s happening. Claire O’Brien, who’s an amazing DJ from Newcastle, Mulubinba, puts on a thing called Ode events, which are raves in all different unique places, and they absolutely slap.” As the NSW government expands its music and nightlife agenda through its $150 million hospitality nightlife reforms and new live music laws, funding and policy ideas are being fed into the regions. Tamworth has become the first regional town to trial Labor’s “special entertainment precinct” scheme that allows councils to set more relaxed planning rules in a designated nightlife area. But some regions in NSW are still struggling. In the Northern Rivers, Byron Bay has become a victim of its own success: creatives are being priced out of the bohemian capital, says Music NSW Northern Rivers coordinator Niño Haggith. Meanwhile, its music events – Falls Festival, Splendour in the Grass and more recently, Bluesfest – have been cancelled. “I was the general manager of a local festival, Mullumbimby Music Festival, and we also had the Bellingen Winter Music Festival down in the Mid North Coast, and we froze those purely because of COVID, and [they] haven’t come back yet,” Haggith says, adding the region has also suffered from a spate of natural disasters, including the 2022 floods.

World.title: Two solo travellers hit a cruise together. Will it be smooth sailing?
World.content:
InspirationEurope Two solo travellers hit a cruise together. Will it be smooth sailing? Rob McFarland and Julie Miller October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What’s it like cruising with a mate? Does it offer the ultimate flexibility, letting you both do your own thing, or is it a frustrating endeavour of endless negotiation and compromise? As long-time friends and committed solo travellers, we decide to put it to the test, boarding the Sun Princess for an action-packed seven-day cruise from Barcelona to Rome. Rob McFarland and Julie Miller about to embark the Sun Princess as co-cruisers. Rob McFarland We’ve travelled together before, but on land. How will we fare at sea? Will we stay the course or are we fairweather friends?



He says ... 



Things have certainly gotten bigger, but they’ve also gotten easier. The Princess app is a lifesaver. It lets you book shore excursions, reserve specialty restaurants and order food and drinks from almost anywhere on the ship. There’s also a handy route-finder that shows you the best way to get from A to B. Equally ingenious is the personalised Medallion, which charges purchases to your onboard account and even unlocks your cabin door as you approach. Premium Deluxe room with a balcony. If there’s a downside to travelling with a friend of the opposite sex, it’s that room sharing can be a bit, well, awkward – which is why we opt for separate cabins. We know it’s not how most friends would travel and, in hindsight, we could have made it work (the cabins are certainly spacious enough), but it saves Julie from having to endure my habit of taking long showers and me from her thunderous snoring. One of the great advantages of travelling with a mate is that there’s less pressure to do everything together. So while Julie often starts her day at the gym, I opt for some gentle stretches in the fitness studio or head out early to watch us glide into port.



When it comes to shore excursions, neither Julie or I have been to Portofino, so we book the same tour out of Genoa – a fabulous trip that also visits the pretty coastal towns of Rapallo and Santa Margherita. Portofino is the rock star, though: an impossibly photogenic huddle of pastel-coloured mansions surrounding a superyacht-studded harbour. In Marseille, while Julie heads to the wetlands of the Camargue, I join an unexpectedly intrepid e-bike tour of France’s oldest city. Port cities aren’t always renowned for their beauty, but Marseille is much prettier than I expected, particularly when viewed from Notre-Dame de la Garde, the striking Byzantine basilica on top of the city’s highest hill (thank you e-bike). The old port of Marseille with the Basilica of Notre Dame de la Garde on the hill beyond. iStock High on both our wish lists is Cinque Terre, the string of five UNESCO World Heritage-listed fishing villages that tumble down the Ligurian coastline near La Spezia. I spend hours researching the perfect strategy, devising an itinerary that allows us to see all five using a mixture of trains and hiking paths, finishing with a sunset ride along the coast. And then, the day before we arrive, Italy’s rail workers go on strike.



Plan B is a more strenuous hike from Monterosso to Vernazza in 30-degree heat, which Julie wisely decides to abandon halfway through. I push on, safe in the knowledge that she’ll be much happier enjoying an Aperol Spritz overlooking Monterosso’s picturesque harbour. Another potential pitfall of travelling with a mate is that you can be less inclined to socialise with other passengers. We combat this by attending an informal singles and solo travellers meet-up on the first night, where we meet Sharon from Brisbane, who has already spent two weeks onboard and is a mine of valuable information. Wake View Terrace is a less-visited spot at the aft of the ship with a stunning infinity pool. We learn about the best place to have breakfast (the promenade outside the Eatery buffet) and the secret lift to the Wake View Terrace, a less-visited spot at the aft of the ship with a stunning infinity pool. Over the course of the week, we meet every combination you can imagine, from solos and couples to multi-generational families and large groups of friends. It’s hard to think of another travel style that so effectively caters to such a disparate range of ages and interests.



Despite my best efforts, we don’t have time to sample everything. But there are numerous highlights, including a fun-filled night in the specialty Umai Teppanyaki restaurant, where I need four attempts to catch a piece of omelette in my mouth. Julie, of course, nails it first time. Spellbound is another standout – a theatrical magic show accessed via an anonymous black door. Staged in an atmospheric Victorian-style parlour, it includes some genuinely astonishing close-up card tricks by members of Hollywood’s Magic Castle. Umai Teppanyaki is one of the many restaurants on board. Finally, the candlelit concerts in The Dome – a striking glass venue near the bow – are intimate and evocative, even if the acoustics aren’t perfect. A cruise may just be the ideal holiday to take with a friend, but choosing the right companion still matters. There aren’t many people who would put up with my over-ambitious scheduling, penchant for multiple desserts or insistence on moving tables for the best view (three times in one restaurant). If you’re lucky enough to have a Julie in your life, consider a cruise. You’ll have a ball.



She says ... As the Sun Princess pulls into the French port of Marseille, I watch in fascination from my balcony as the ship is masterfully manoeuvred alongside the wharf. Suddenly my phone pings – it’s my travel hubby Rob, texting me from another deck. “Did you watch the ship come in? Amazing bit of parallel parking!” Rob McFarland and Julie Miller: shared experiences elevate the mundane into something memorable. Rob McFarland and Julie Miller We may not be in the same physical space, but this shared experience has elevated the mundane into something memorable. And on a cruise, these snapshots become so much more vivid when created with a friend. Rob and I are both currently single, creatures of habit and comfortable with our own company. But when the opportunity arises for us to spend a week together cruising from Barcelona to Rome on the Sun Princess, I jump at the opportunity. I mean, the Med – what’s not to love?



Not to mention travelling with “spreadsheet guy” means I can pack away my brain, with Rob pre-planning every second of the week down to coffee breaks on shore. Having spent the past 36 years parenting and grandparenting, I’m more than happy to relinquish control over such boring details, tagging in his lanky wake like an obedient puppy. This week’s itinerary – one leg of a three-week round trip through the Mediterranean – is unusual in that it stops at a different port every day, with no days at sea. And that’s quite the whirlwind, with a lot of exploring and three different languages to contend with. Corsica’s rugged coastline. Getty Images On the Spanish island of Mallorca, we venture into the town of Palma independently. An impromptu attendance at Sunday mass in the impressive Cathedral of Santa Maria is an unexpected highlight. Meanwhile, the blue waters of the Mediterranean beckon in Corsica, best known as the birthplace of Napoleon, while our shore excursion to Genoa, a beautiful city with flamboyant Baroque architecture and cobbled laneways, includes lunch at Zefferino, which has been serving handmade pasta since 1939.



On the French Riviera, Rob and I go our separate ways: Rob cycles the streets of Marseille (my idea of hell in the midday heat!) while I admire flamingos and herons at a bird sanctuary in the moody Camargue, famed for its cowboys, black bulls and beautiful white horses. Between shore visits, there’s a lot to squeeze in onboard, with very little time. We only manage one group fitness class, a video tai chi session under The Dome (Rob earnest, me inept); we spend as much time as possible in Lotus Spa’s luxurious thermal and hydrotherapy suite, well worth the additional expenditure if used daily. A traditional ranch with a herd of bulls in the Camargue, France. iStock For research purposes, we also while away an afternoon in the Sanctuary Club, a pool and bar exclusively for passengers staying in Sanctuary Collection suites. Less rowdy than the other pools, with a dedicated menu and waiter service, this proves a welcome taste of the high life, epitomised by a glass of champagne magically appearing upon the ring of a bell. Perhaps as backup, should my company prove too tedious, social butterfly Rob is keen to meet other solo travellers, dragging me to a singles get-together on the night of embarkation. Interestingly, Rob is the only male in the mix, perhaps an indication that women are, in general, more adventurous and prepared to take on the challenges of travelling alone.



Having said that, I’m not a fan of the tedious “table for one”, an unavoidable malady of our profession; I welcome the opportunity to dine with a friend, with eight specialty restaurants available to passengers who’ve purchased the Premier Package. The irony of the artistic-inspired dining experience that is Love by Britto – and its heart-shaped dishes – is not lost on us as the only non-couple in the restaurant. Did Rob mention I caught a flicked egg the first time at teppanyaki, humiliating him into a feeble fourth attempt after his first three failures? Belly laughs like this just don’t happen when you’re travelling alone. Concerts are held in The Dome, a striking glass venue near the ship’s bow. Several of Sun Princess’ entertainment venues, such as The Dome and Princess Live, are quite intimate; we learn early in the cruise to plan accordingly or endure standing through a performance. Mind you, sit too close to the stage and you risk audience participation, as we discover at the end of the Viva La Musica stage show, when we’re dragged onto the dance floor with energetic and co-ordinated cast members. And spare a thought for a young American lad named Stone, whose unconventional name makes him the unrelenting butt of jokes from British comedian Liam Withnail during a highly entertaining late-night comedy show.



Related Article Cruises My first time on a big ship taught me a big lesson From high-flying aerial performances to white-themed dance parties and singalongs at O’Malley’s Irish Pub, there’s no rest for the wicked on this cruise, despite my feeble efforts at escaping for an early night. With the intense shore itinerary and more onboard bars and restaurants than we can possibly conquer, I need a holiday by the end of the week. But while this journey was, as I’m constantly reminding my friends, “work”, I honestly haven’t had so much fun in ages. And that’s all down to the company I’ve kept, with life at sea all the more enticing with my favourite first mate. THE DETAILS Princess Cruises’ seven-day Western Mediterranean with Italy cruise from Barcelona to Rome from $2010 a person, twin share in an interior cabin. Add-on Premier Package (unlimited drinks, speciality dining, Wi-Fi, reserved theatre seating, shore excursion credits and room service) costs $134 a day. See princess.com



FIVE MORE MEDITERRANEAN SURPRISES The Cathedral of Santa Maria of Palma, commonly referred to as La Seu, in Palma, Mallorca. iStock Palma, Mallorca

An ornate riot of pinnacles and flying buttresses, Palma’s 13th-century Gothic cathedral, commonly referred to as La Seu, took 400 years to build and was extensively remodelled by Antoni Gaudi in the early 1900s. Admire its colourful frescoes and stunning stained-glass windows on a self-guided visit, or stay for the atmospheric Sunday mass. Marseille, France

It’s no surprise that France’s oldest city has more than 30 museums, but two stand out. Housed in a striking lattice-clad cube, Mucem’s eclectic collection (spanning everything from Neolithic art to tarot cards) explores Mediterranean history and culture. Next door, Cosquer Mediterranee offers a theme-park-style journey through a faithful recreation of an underwater cave adorned with prehistoric paintings. Genoa, Italy

Often overlooked in favour of shore excursions to Milan or Portofino, Italy’s largest port is an intriguing mix of narrow medieval alleyways and grand boulevards lined with 16th-century palaces. Don’t leave without trying its signature culinary exports: freshly baked focaccia and creamy pesto Genovese.



Ajaccio, Corsica

Corsica’s capital is much more than just a tribute to its most famous son, Napoleon Bonaparte. The city also boasts lovely beaches, an impressive 15th-century Genoese fortress and a lively daily market perfect for stocking up on local cheeses, cured meats and honey. La Spezia, Italy

While it’s hard to compete with nearby Cinque Terre, La Spezia is a coastal gem in its own right. Stroll along the palm-lined seafront promenade, sample a traditional farinata (savoury chickpea pancake) and explore the city’s rich maritime history at the Naval Museum. FIVE CRUISE ACTIVITIES THAT ARE BETTER WITH A FRIEND Sailaway drinks

It’s all hands on deck – holding cocktails – as the Sun Princess makes its afternoon departures from its Mediterranean ports, tooting its signature Love Boat-themed horn. Grab a seat at the Wake View Terrace (by the infinity pool) to watch dreamy cities disappear into the sunset, celebrating the moment with obligatory selfies. Dance classes

While no partner is required for Sun Princess’ free salsa, Zumba or line dancing classes, there’s nothing more amusing than watching a friend floundering under the instructions.



Dining

Let’s face it, dining alone can be a drag, particularly on a ship with such a wealth of options. Make sure your chosen restaurant satisfies dietary requirements (for instance, Julie is vegetarian, so we don’t try The Butcher’s Block) and choose at least one dessert to share. Unless you’re Rob, who orders the entire sweets menu. Silent disco

While you dance to your own beat in a silent disco, the event is all the more hilarious as you watch friends wallow in their own musical universe. Spellbound

In the first collaboration with LA’s Magic Castle, Spellbound elevates old-fashioned magic shows, with mind-blowing card tricks that will keep you and your friend pondering “but how?” for hours after. The writers were guests of Princess Cruises.

Italy

Spain

Cruises After abandoning a sensible career in IT, Rob McFarland now divides his time between Sydney, the US and Europe. He’s won seven writing awards, including Australian Travel Writer of the Year, and offers writing courses for tourism operators, PR professionals and aspiring travel writers. While not averse to a 5-star hotel, his most memorable travels include scaling the mountain behind Machu Picchu and rafting Patagonia’s Futaleufu River. Follow his travels on Instagram @mctraveller. Connect via email Julie Miller scrapes a living writing about the things she loves: travel, riding horses and drinking cocktails on tropical beaches. Between airports, she lives in a rural retreat just beyond Sydney.

World.title: How Elizabeth Hurley views the safety-pin dress that made her famous 32 years ago
World.content:
LifestyleFashionSunday Life How Elizabeth Hurley views the safety-pin dress that made her famous 32 years ago Caroline Leaper October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the October 4 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Many celebrities, when asked whether they enjoy dressing for the red carpet, will feign shyness. They’ll tell you that the flashbulb parades are just a part of the job that has to be done, and that being all dolled up for a premiere is something one must tolerate while playing the part of a “serious actor”. Not Elizabeth Hurley. She embraces the showmanship wholeheartedly. She does the glitter and the bodycon, the plunge neckline and the thigh-high split, whether she’s at Elton John’s peak-Hollywood Oscars party (she’s a patron of the Elton John Aids Foundation) or graciously accepting an unexpected award in a German spa town. Elizabeth Hurley: “You can wear the most beautiful dress in the world, but if it doesn’t fit properly, you’ll never feel your best.” Ellen von Unwerth/Trunk Archive/Snapper “I’ve always found it much easier to dress for the red carpet than for everyday life,” she admits. “I find black-tie events easy-peasy, but smart-casual surprisingly tricky.” Now 61, Hurley’s approach to glamorous dressing has, on paper, hardly changed since she arrived in showbusiness in the 1990s, starring in films such as Austin Powers and Mad Dogs and Englishmen, and upstaging her then-partner Hugh Grant when she wore a sliver of a Versace gown held together by gold safety pins at the Four Weddings and a Funeral premiere.



There have been some subtle tweaks along the way. “I engage in the art of eliminating what I don’t like and highlighting what I do,” she says of her approach to finding the right gown for her figure. “Fit always comes first. You can wear the most beautiful dress in the world, but if it doesn’t fit properly, you’ll never feel your best. I’m not bad at altering things myself, but I also have a good alterationist and I’m forever having clothes nipped and tucked.” “I certainly wasn’t thinking about creating a fashion moment; I just wore what I could get my hands on.” ELIZABETH HURLEY Her safety-pin dress of 1994 is still regarded as seminal, effectively unclasping a trend for “naked dressing” that has since been reworked time and again by stars such as Kim Kardashian and Beyoncé. Hurley is their pin-up; she’s still cited as a reference on designer mood boards some 30 years later. “It’s very flattering because, at the time, I certainly wasn’t thinking about creating a fashion moment; I just wore what I could get my hands on,” she insists. The dress was a last-minute borrow, handed over by a publicist in a white plastic bag. And it wasn’t the only outfit she wore in the 1990s to have a major impact, resulting in her being featured on front pages around the world.



“I remember in the ’90s wearing a lace Emanuel Ungaro dress that was completely see-through, with large knickers underneath,” she says. “It was about 30 years ahead of its time and I think it was viewed back then as eye-poppingly risqué. But by today’s standards, it would be very tame. Ditto my Versace safety-pin dress; it was considered extremely shocking and special 30 years ago; I doubt anyone would turn a hair if it were debuted today.” Hurley didn’t use the services of a professional stylist back then, but has collaborated with several in the years since. “Through the ’90s and 2000s, I was sent all my red-carpet looks directly from brands such as Versace, Gucci and Fendi, with whom I still have wonderful relationships,” she explains. Freddie Leiba sourced some of her favourite looks for films, while another New York-based stylist, Ann Caruso, still puts together the “vast pink wardrobes” she wears for all of her breast cancer fundraising activities. She adds, “Mike Adler, who I work with in the UK, also pulls great looks for me, including the magnificent Celia Kritharioti dress I wore to the Vanity Fair Oscars party last year.” Her village is well versed in what she likes to wear at those events. But what about for the “everyday”? “Valentino, who sadly passed away earlier this year, used to always tell me that everything had to look ‘easy’,” she says. “Never looking like you tried too hard. Mix new with old. Mix Zara with Hermès. The object was to not look like a ‘lady who lunched’.”



Her friend Joan Collins, 93, is another glamorous guiding influence. “I call her ‘mommy dearest’,” says Hurley. “Joan is exactly the same in private as she is in public – incredibly energetic, extremely funny, and gorgeously stylish.” These teachings have led Hurley to shop in a mix of places, including dresses from Versace, Zhivago and Roberto Cavalli and resort wear from Charo Ruiz Ibiza and her own brand, Elizabeth Hurley Beach. Hurley wore ‘that dress’ back in 1994. But it looks “very tame” by today’s standards. Dave Benett/Getty Images Two recent advertising campaigns for Canadian label Joseph Ribkoff have helped her address a self-acknowledged missing link: polished daywear. “The clothes are elegant, flattering and incredibly easy to wear,” she says. “They make you feel put together without looking as though you’ve tried too hard. “Everything was also very comfortable, which is my be-all and end-all. I can’t abide anything that digs in anywhere.”



This is another new diktat from a woman who has previously admitted to tolerating boning so sharp it made her bleed. Hurley’s wardrobe at her home, a Georgian mansion in Herefordshire, UK, is “messy”, she admits, “[but] I know where everything is”. Splitting her time between there and Nashville, the home of her partner of two years, country singer Billy Ray Cyrus, might lead to the illusion that she’s living out of a suitcase. Related Article Sunday Life ‘Of course I make an effort with how I look’: Elizabeth Hurley at 58 “Most people think my closet looks like I’ve been burgled,” she jokes. “I’m a perfect candidate for a hoarding show as I loathe throwing anything out. I’ve kept pretty much everything I’ve ever worn, except my Versace safety-pin dress, which is in the Metropolitan Museum [of Art, in New York]. “I have way too much and it’s overflowing. I often do a swoop and put things in boxes, but frequently burrow through them and out it all comes again. I exhaust myself with my messiness.”



To see Hurley in the Herefordshire countryside is perhaps the closest one could get to seeing her truly “off-duty”. She loves being outdoors – anyone who follows her on Instagram will have seen her as a particularly girly farmer, lambing in pigtails and pink lip gloss. “I would hardly describe it as a style,” she says, “as I’m usually covered in mud, with twigs sticking out of my hair. I spend my entire time gardening and am covered in cuts and bruises. Ancient jeans, thick socks and wellingtons are the order of most days.” This activity, she says, is also the key to her confidence. “I never go to the gym. I much prefer being active in ways I enjoy – walking, gardening and just keeping busy. For me, it’s less about how I look and more about feeling healthy and energetic.” That, in turn, makes her feel better in those dresses. “When you feel good, you naturally carry yourself with more confidence, and I think that’s reflected in how you dress.” Liz’s style tips Revisit old favourites Over lockdown, I did a biblical sorting session and have since reworn some of my favourite pieces – like a Versace [dress] I first wore to the 1997 Met Gala to a big party in India in March. Take care of treasures I feel nostalgic towards some of my couture evening dresses; they are exquisite and still in perfect condition. Be bold at events Colour certainly comes into it; for events I usually like a bright colour or white. Stand tall Posture is everything. I infuriate my friends by poking them in the shoulders and telling them to sit up straight. Don’t buy if you don’t have to I borrow diamonds for big events, but they go back the next day. I’d rather spend my money on trees for my house in Herefordshire. Borrow from the boys I steal from my son – trackies and hoodies, mostly. I think it really annoys him. World.title: I used to think having a dog would make travel more difficult. This weekend changed that
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsSunday Life I used to think having a dog would make travel more difficult. This weekend changed that Abby Seaman October 4, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the October 4 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

Before Junior, my three-year-old rescue greyhound, came into my life, escaping for a spontaneous weekend away was as easy as throwing a toothbrush and PJs into an overnight bag. Now it requires a little more planning to pin down a dog-sitter or taking the easier, though less exciting option: simply declining the invite. My perfect holiday would be to bring Junior along but, understandably, most accommodation isn’t pet-friendly, especially for a 30-kilogram greyhound. So when I get wind that Unyoked’s secluded and off-grid cabins dotted around Australia offer pet-friendly options, I can’t grab Junior and his lead quickly enough before the two of us hit the highway to the Hunter Valley, three hours north from our home in Sydney. Junior getting settled into his holiday. Abby Seaman For one last civilised hurrah before two nights in nature, we stop at Tintilla Estate in Pokolbin for a wine, meat and cheese tasting. I’m running late for my reservation, a result of my first time travelling with Junior, and am just about to start my flurry of apologies when I’m greeted with a calm “No worries” from the owner.



Sitting in the sun, looking over the rolling vineyard, with lunch and a beverage, I let go of my flustered state. I’m pleased to discover that many wineries in the Hunter Valley allow dogs outside. Even the hatted restaurant, Bistro Molines, offers a dog-friendly lunch booking. While plenty of the Unyoked tiny cabins welcome both dogs and cats, the company has also teamed up with Australian dog food company Lyka to offer the Lyka Lodge at Pokolbin, creating perhaps the most dog-friendly holiday imaginable. (For southern travellers, there is also a Victorian Lyka Lodge – in the Tarra Valley, south-east of Melbourne.) Once I arrive and park at the site, Junior and I start out on a short walk through the bush to our cabin. Anticipating the trip, I gave myself a pep talk about how I would embrace and immerse myself in nature – something that comes naturally to Junior, of course. I am greeted by a mob of kangaroos, who idle in a paddock. A wild rabbit sprints in the nearby foliage. A goanna startles Junior and me as it hisses and climbs the nearest tree. The cabin itself is built with sustainably sourced timber and powered by solar energy, and features a composting toilet. It’s furnished with cookware, a cosy bed and hot water. Just enough to disconnect from modern life, but to enjoy a comfortable stay.



For the pup guest, it includes a large bed, hygiene wipes and spray, a dog bowl, and much-appreciated dental treats. There is also an extra-long dog lead to allow Junior to explore safely. Escape to nature in style. Nikita Brown In addition, the cabin includes a guide to starting a campfire. Junior and I wander around our surrounding area, picking up sticks and kindling, ready to pretend we are in an episode of Alone Australia. By nightfall, I am so excited to cook dinner (grilled corn and jacket potatoes) over the campfire that I almost forget to look up at the clear night sky full of stars. The next day I wake to the early sunrise and a chorus of birds. I take my time preparing coffee. I grind the coffee beans with the provided hand grinder and meditatively watch the moka pot boil over.



After I use the provided yoga mat to stretch outside, Junior wakes from his nap in the sun to join me in an impressive downward dog. Related Article Sunday Life ‘You’ll see someone famous’: Visit this bar for one of the last old-school NYC experiences We take a walk, bird-watching along the way – an activity I love but rarely find the time for, or the variety of birds, in the city. Back at our tiny home, we dedicate some more time towards rest. Junior sprawls out on a picnic blanket and naps in the sun, I intermittently read and doze in the hammock. It turns out I’m pretty good at doing nothing. I find myself spending time just sitting and thinking, not of my to-do lists and what to achieve next, but simply contemplating. “Why don’t I make time to do this more?” is one thought that floats by often.



By the evening, the bird song has quietened. To fill the silence, I pop on one of the provided CDs and find myself dancing while preparing dinner. At least I’m so remote that no one can see me, besides the judgement-free eyes of Junior. Later, he and I snuggle by the fire, roasting marshmallows and watching the stars. I enjoy witnessing him get in touch with his wild side. The whole experience would be great without Junior, but bringing him with me makes it special. Before checking out on our last morning, I soak up every last drop of relaxation. I do some yoga outdoors, we bird-watch and I make one last hearty meal and slowly brewed coffee, while dancing to the CD. The cabin has worked its magic and massaged the knots of stress out of my mind. As I walk back into the real world, I vow to carry some part of this calmness I’ve found with me. With ideas like, “Once I get back, I’m going to slow down and savour my time.” Realistically, I know it probably won’t last. But at least I know the cabin will be there for an easy, spur-of-the-moment getaway in nature – with my best mate, Junior.



The writer travelled as a guest of Lyka Pet Food and Unyoked. Get the best of Sunday Life magazine delivered to your inbox every Sunday morning.
