World.title: Forget the men, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles carry the true love story of this film
World.content:
Daisy Edgar Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles star as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood in the new film adaptation of Sense and Sensibility.

The two actors are the perfect pick to play sisters in this latest Austen reboot.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This story is part of the October 4 edition of Sunday Life. See all stories .

A decade before anyone put them in bonnets, Daisy Edgar-Jones met Esmé Creed-Miles on the 2017 Yorkshire set of coming-of-age drama Pond Life. “I was so blown away by her,” says Edgar-Jones, who was then 19, of her co-star, then 17. “[She] has this energy that is so compelling. She’s a wonderfully intelligent and sort of wild person, in the best way.” The teenagers became fast friends and “had a really great summer of watching Love Island and shooting this indie film”. Creed-Miles’ first impression of her co-star is equally vivid: “Daisy was unbelievably kind and talented. She put me at ease and I could tell I had a friend in her.” Admittedly, “it would be hard not to get on with Daisy. She’s just one of the loveliest people.” Almost a decade on, the women are reunited on a much grander stage: Georgia Oakley’s gorgeous adaptation of Jane Austen’s 1811 debut novel, Sense and Sensibility, in which they star as sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood. “To already have that shorthand with Esmé and to feel a sort of sisterly feeling, made it so seamless,” says Edgar-Jones. An Austen adaptation is a world away from a small budget indie, but this is no polite costume drama either. It’s a kaleidoscope of undone hair, mud, rage and running. “I was really trying to get into what it might have felt like to live in Devon 200 years ago,” Oakley has said of her film’s unbridled aesthetic. “Steering away from this preconceived idea we have about Austen, that everything takes place in a stuffy drawing room.” When Edgar-Jones, 28, appears on our video call, it’s 11am in London. She’s just off a call with Australian writer Tony McNamara about Mosquito, their upcoming comedy series. What does a Gucci, Boucheron and Estée Lauder brand ambassador wear when working from home? As it turns out, a striped rugby jumper, no discernible make-up and “sports shorts” from a morning workout: “It’s not my best look!”



A few days later, Creed-Miles, 26, is similarly casual when she Zooms in just after 1pm. “I woke up quite recently,” she says, wandering around her London home, earbuds in, breaking off to answer the door: “I think it’s some food.” Daisy Edgar-Jones: “What Austen does so well is explore the variety of love we can experience in a life.” Charlotte Hadden for Focus Features Seeing the pair like this – using tech, in athleisure wear, waiting on deliveries – is faintly surreal after seeing them as the Dashwoods, physically and emotionally entwined as they braid hair, share a bed and absorb each other’s heartbreaks. With apologies to Edward Ferrars (George MacKay) and Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum), they’re the heart of the film and its true love story. “I’m really glad that you say that because I remember that being such a clear piece of direction that Georgia, our director, wanted to follow,” says Edgar-Jones. Growing up an only child, she “had to outsource that sisterly or that familial sibling bond to friends”, and found it here. “It’s just a really lovely thing that the love story is the two women and how much they gift each other.” To Oakley, the Dashwoods “represent these two opposing forces that a lot of women have within themselves that are always at war”. For Austen-era women with few ways to support themselves and little control over inheritance, says Creed-Miles, “the bond of motherhood or sisterhood becomes more prescient”. “It’s just a really lovely thing that the love story is the two women and how much they gift each other.” DAISY EDGAR-JONES In Austen’s world, marriage was survival – do it or sink. So in 2026, when women have careers, best friends and their own front-door keys, what is romantic love actually for? “It’s a great question, and I think it’s one we’re always asking,” says Edgar-Jones.



In a relationship with photographer Ben Seed for nearly four years, Edgar-Jones says she “loves love” and that modern romance is “for friendship and companionship and support”. But her longer answer is pure Elinor: “What Austen does so well is explore the variety of love we can experience in a life – be it platonic, familial, romantic – and how valuable all of those are. The same exists today. It’s so magic to cultivate love in all those different areas of your life if you can.” Asked about the same topic, Creed-Miles admits defeat – “Oh gosh. Literally, that is just too big a question for me”. There is romance in her life, though, in the form of an engagement to musician Daisy Maybe – yes, another Daisy. “I love going for a walk with my fiancée,” she says. “We take our dog to the park. We might cook some nice food and watch a bit of telly and chill out. Very simple.” The successor to Kate Winslet’s Marianne, Creed-Miles has never seen the 1995 adaptation of Sense and Sensibility. Charlotte Hadden for Focus Features In real life, which of the pair is sense and which is sensibility? Edgar-Jones says she is “probably a mixture, honestly”, adding “I don’t fall in love very easily” while admitting to being “a massive romantic”. Creed-Miles, gloriously vulnerable and untamed as Marianne, leans “more towards sensibility, internally. I definitely experience that sort of crushing depth of feeling.” “Perhaps the thing I love most in the world is a good bit of hardcore yearning.” DAISY EDGAR-JONES Marianne is the kind of woman Creed-Miles always wanted to be, someone “outgoing and with a passion for life who took risks”, whereas she describes herself as “quite reclusive”. That introversion is something she’s “constantly reconciling” with her other day job as singer and guitarist in UK duo Cusk.



Edgar-Jones is a devotee of Ang Lee’s 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility, describing Emma Thompson’s Elinor as “one of the most beautiful performances in cinema”. The successor to Kate Winslet’s Marianne, Creed-Miles has never seen the 31-year-old film, but says the new incarnation will “hopefully do [Winslet] and Emma and Ang Lee proud”. The storyline, of course, is awash with yearning: Elinor and Edward for each other, Colonel Brandon for Marianne, Marianne for Willoughby, mothers and relatives for weddings. It’s a mode Edgar-Jones perfected as another Marianne, opposite Paul Mescal’s Connell in the 2020 smash TV series Normal People, which made her a household name and garnered her Golden Globe and BAFTA nominations. Does she ever wish we’d forget Normal People? “Oh no, I’d be so sad if that happened,” she says. “I love those characters so much, and I love that show. I mean, perhaps the thing I love most in the world is a good bit of hardcore yearning, and I do think Sense and Sensibility and Normal People really tick that box.” Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood and Creed-Miles as Marianne Dashwood. MacKay’s Edward also extends a streak she copped to in Elle last year: “I have worked with basically all of the internet’s boyfriends,” she said, citing Mescal, Sebastian Stan and Jacob Elordi. “Just Timothée Chalamet and Austin Butler left!” Born in London to Wendy, a film editor, and Philip Edgar-Jones, a television executive, Daisy acted in school plays before studying at the National Youth Theatre. Teenage TV roles in Cold Feet and Silent Witness led to Normal People, then Where the Crawdads Sing, Under the Banner of Heaven and Twisters. The daughter of actors Samantha Morton and Charlie Creed-Miles, Esmé made her showbiz debut at seven as a tiny Shirley Temple impersonator in Harmony Korine’s 2007 film Mister Lonely, before moving on to three seasons of snapping necks as the title assassin in Amazon’s Hanna and a role in Kristen Stewart’s 2025 directorial debut, The Chronology of Water.



Both women talk glowingly of the fun and shared knowledge on Sense and Sensibility’s female-led set: director Oakley, writer Diana Reid, a cast including Fiona Shaw (Killing Eve, Andor) and Caitríona Balfe (Outlander). Were gossip and tips swapped around the catering table? “It was wonderful to learn from Fiona and Caitríona, but I think less to do with the industry and more just to do with their attitude towards life and storytelling,” says Creed-Miles. “Even if it was like a squeeze of the hand or a moment of eye contact, to feel like you were held in those spaces was really precious.” The shared experience extended to the costumes. Edgar-Jones and Creed-Miles raided each other’s on-set wardrobes, just like real sisters, and covet each other’s actual things. Edgar-Jones– whose off-duty staples are jeans, a “really good” white T-shirt and a “woolly jumper” – loves her friend’s vintage loafers. What would Creed-Miles steal in return? “Daisy is the chicest,” she says. “Probably one of her really cool coats.” Related Article Pop culture Should I keep waiting for Mr Darcy? Jane Austen answers your most pressing questions The day we speak, Edgar-Jones is heading to a pub to see Creed-Miles’ band, although Esmé says that Daisy, a fan of Sarah J. Maas fantasy novels and personalised stationery, is the better after-dark girl. Edgar-Jones laughs at that. A DJ, she runs through what makes a great party – “the lighting has to be dark” – while on the decks “I’m still obsessed with Charli XCX. But then, I love a bit of Motown.” The film’s PR tagline is, “No one knows your heart like a sister.” Creed-Miles says it’s true, adding, “Daisy is family to me. That kind of sisterhood is really important in this world and in this job. I’m very grateful.” Marriage plots come and go. This is the love match that stuck.

World.title: Whistleblowers offer to aid Education Ministry probe
World.content:
Education Ministry whistleblowers, who contacted RNZ in the past week, plan to add their voices to an investigation by the Office of the Ombudsman.

The investigation was announced after publication of a video showing a ministry manager asking staff not to mention contact with the Education Minister's office in writing.

Nine people with inside knowledge of different parts of the ministry subsequently contacted RNZ to corroborate claims that ministry managers routinely asked staff not to write down sensitive information, least it be discovered through the Official Information Act.

Some were from the ministry's curriculum centre, which was the subject of a negative report about workplace culture published last week.

Others said that a culture of secrecy and avoidance of written records was common in other parts of the organisation.

The Education Ministry said the comments made in the leaked video did not meet its expectations, but it would not comment on claims made by the people who contacted RNZ.

It initially said it was investigating whether there was a wider problem, but told RNZ it had dropped plans for an internal inquiry in light of the Ombudsman's investigation.

Three of the sources confirmed they would contact the Ombudsman to make a protected disclosure and others said they were likely to do so.

A 10th person - former ministry staff member Claire Coleman - told RNZ she had already offered to participate in the Ombudsman's investigation.

This week, Chief Ombudsman John Allen said he had formally notified the ministry of the investigation.

"I will be looking at various practices, including whether the ministry's curriculum centre staff have either deliberately failed to make records or have been told not to do so," he said.

Chief Ombudsman John Allen Supplied

"My investigation will concentrate on administrative conduct, and whether the Ministry has met its legal obligations under the Official Information Act and the Public Records Act.

"I will not be considering any substantive advice or decision making relating to the curriculum itself."

Coleman, who has been a strong critic of the government's approach to the curriculum rewrite, said she hoped the Ombudsman "might get to the truth of things".

"I hope we can hold some people responsible and any future processes are transparent."

Coleman also hoped the Ombudsman's work might lead to a wider inquiry into the curriculum rewrite.

"There were far too many things that were done in a secretive and unethical way," she said. "Too many financial interests that have no business in that space."

Coleman previously claimed work on the curriculum was heavily politicised and several of the ministry insiders who contacted RNZ made similar allegations.

One source told RNZ the new curriculums felt like a step back in time.

"It felt like I was taken right back to the 80s of 'we don't let brown people have any rights' and 'we're going to whitewash everything,' and 'we're going to make sure that this is back to how things should be'," they said.

They said the curriculum was too directive of what teachers must teach.

"Some of the prescribed nature is needed, in order to be consistent and to make sure that children have all got equity wherever they are," they said. "I get that, but not to the extreme this is.

"New Zealand is innovative, creative... yet we're just throwing it all down the tubes."

Another source said schools could teach the new curriculums with resources left over from 20 years ago.

"It misses how young people learn today and it misses what's important for young people today," she said. "It's such a missed opportunity for what a good curriculum could look like.

"It's devastating, actually."

Another source said: "I think the public deserve to know, in no uncertain terms, that the quality of primary and secondary education in this country is being directly compromised and coloured by the government's ideological position, that the people responsible are consciously aware of it and that the minister, ministry and related parties have taken steps to circumvent proper protocol, and intentionally obscure the truth about how they have been operating."

Minister of Education Erica Standford RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Foreign influence

Several of the nine whistleblowers said the Australian firm Learning First had a major hand in draft curriculums and some ministry staff were flown to Melbourne to work with the company.

One said the primary school maths curriculum was completely rewritten by Learning First and other learning areas were heavily influenced by the company.

"The general feeling amongst internal staff was that the work being produced by Learning First was bad and unnecessary," they said. "There was a lot of confusion about why they were involved at all."

Another said Learning First wrote a lot of curriculum content, but ministry staff were told not to imply or say that the ministry was not the author of the curriculum.

"Learning First replaced everything we had done," they said.

They also said Learning First's understanding of the Treaty of Waitangi was "completely wrong".

A third source said Learning First provided a lot of content for some curriculums, but not for others, and ministry staff rewrote much of it.

"A lot of it was wrong, literally wrong," they said.

However, Learning First chief executive Ben Jensen denied the allegations.

He said the claim Learning First wrote most of the content for several curriculum drafts was not true.

"We did lots of research, benchmarking, provided advice and so on, but this is just completely false," he said.

Jensen said his company did not write the revised version of the maths curriculum

"We provided comparisons with other systems and made suggestions," he said. "We do a lot of work on how to sequence foundational learning in maths and what this means for the curriculum, but as above, we were not even doing this work when the draft was written.

"A lot of the feedback we provided was rejected by the ministry, so the idea that we wrote most of it is simply not true.

"When we finished, a lot of writing was still taking place, so just don't know how people can say it was mainly written by us."

Jensen said he was not aware of Learning First content being rewritten due to errors, and the company was up front about not having expertise on local knowledge and history, such as the treaty.

The Education Ministry also defended the process, and said it was responsible for all final content and decisions.

"Characterisations of the curriculum process based on individual recollections or particular examples do not necessarily reflect the full context of how curriculum content was developed, reviewed, and finalised," it said.

"The ministry develops and writes the curriculum, drawing on input from teachers, subject matter experts, stakeholders and external advisers throughout the process.

"As previously outlined publicly, including during the Education and Workforce Select Committee scrutiny examination, external advisers may contribute specialist expertise and international perspectives.

"For example, ministry officials have previously explained that Learning First helped identify relevant international curriculum content, while the curriculum itself was written by the ministry."

123RF

No written records

The Ombudsman's investigation was sparked by a video showing a principal seconded to the ministry to lead work on the secondary school curriculum, warning staff not to mention in writing feedback from the Education Minister's office.

The source of that video said they were outraged by the attempt to circumvent the proper processes for recording and providing information.

"These rigorous processes are put in there exactly to serve the children and to serve the schools, and us bypassing them is not okay," they said.

They said they heard similar requests almost once a month.

Other sources who contacted RNZ shared similar stories.

"Verbal instructions were given for changes that were controversial and come directly from the minister's office," one ministry insider told RNZ.

Another source said the comments made by the ministry manager in the leaked video were not an isolated case.

"This was a routine and extensive problem before she was seconded," they said. "The problem did not walk in the door with her."

Another ministry insider told RNZ: "We have been told many times not to write things down."

As RNZ reported last week, a person present at a ministry-run curriculum hui said ministry staff were present to take notes and one of those staffers revealed that they had been told to be very careful about what they wrote down.

"The things that they weren't writing down were pretty obviously things that they didn't want to be recorded as part of the feedback we were giving," she said.

She said, later at the same hui, a ministry manager instructed their staff to stop recording what was being said, because it was beyond the scope of the meeting and because it could be discovered through the OIA.

An established culture

Several sources told RNZ they witnessed repeated attempts to keep information off the record prior to the change of government in late 2023, but it became worse after the election.

One said ministry managers would respond to complaints or potentially critical queries with face-to-face meetings, a tactic that appeared aimed at avoiding a written email response.

"The whole 'have meetings, keep things off paper' is deliberate," they said.

The source said there were frequent meetings where nothing was written down.

"It didn't feel like there was any integrity."

A separate source said they commonly heard "that you shouldn't write things down, because they would then be OIA-able" prior to the 2023 election.

"Recording discussions and notes was sometimes discouraged, with people encouraged to have conversations instead," they told RNZ.

Another source said, prior to the change in government, reminders about the OIA and putting things in writing were light in tone and emphasis, but after the election, the term "OIA-able" was frequently used and, in 2024 meetings, became the preferred mode of communication.

Banned words

A learning lesson from a book for teaching te reo Māori. RNZ / Te Aniwa Hurihanganui

Most of the sources told RNZ they were told to remove Māori words from curriculum documents or noticed that others had done so.

They said the word "Aotearoa" was used as a synonym for or alongside New Zealand in original curriculum drafts, but was later removed.

"This instruction was never written down and, in some cases, senior staff made the changes themselves, rather than relay this change to the writing teams," one source said.

Another said Aotearoa New Zealand was the blanket term used in the curriculum, often shortened to ANZ, but proofreaders and editors were told to replace it with New Zealand.

One source said the push to remove Māori words began before the new coalition government had even taken office, with some managers indicating they wanted to make the change because "it was in the pipeline".

Two other sources said some English words were also apparently unwelcome, with instructions to remove words including "culture", "identity", and "wellbeing".

The Education Ministry had previously denied that it sought to remove Māori language from the curriculum.

Bullying and fear

The source of the video said ministry staff were being asked to behave dishonestly.

"We're public servants and we're being bullied, which I would say strongly, we are being bullied," they said. "The majority of people in the ministry are under a toxic environment."

They said nobody felt safe to complain.

"If you speak up and ask a professional, polite question of 'is this okay?', you very quickly have your fixed-term contract ended," they said.

Another ministry insider said staff felt they had to comply with government demands or lose their jobs.

"There was a lot of fear within the ministry that our jobs were now at risk, due to the change in government, and this contributed to what I experienced as an overall feeling that we had to say yes to everything and not question whether proper process was being followed," they said.

World.title: Cost of fixing storm-damaged Whangārei roads balloons to more than $23m
World.content:
The cost of fixing storm damage inflicted on Whangārei district roads earlier this year has risen to more than $23 million - of which almost $11m has been spent clearing one giant landslide.

The almost week-long January storm cut off coastal settlements at Ōakura and Whangaruru, swept away a bridge approach, damaged dozens of homes and destroyed others, and triggered a huge number of slips on the coastal road between Whangārei and Russell.

One section of road at Helena Bay Hill was only re-opened on Friday, after an eight-month effort to remove almost 100,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and trees.

Further storms in March and April added more damage.

A report prepared for Whangārei District Council said the initial estimate for repairing storm-damaged roads was $16.5m, but that had now increased to $23.2m.

The report, by transportation manager Greg Monteith, sought councillors' approval for the extra $6.7m.

The NZ Transport Agency was expected to contribute $16m, leaving Whangārei ratepayers to pick up the remaining $7.2m.

The $23.2m total included $10.9m for emergency works at the massive Helena Bay Hill slip on Russell Road, the main connection between Whangārei and coastal communities at Ōakura and Whangaruru.

Almost $11 million has been spent repairing Russell Road, in the Whangārei District, after a massive slip on 21 January. Supplied / Ngātiwai Trust Board

The council previously described the slip repair as one of the biggest and most complex projects it had ever undertaken.

About 93,000 cubic metres of soil, boulders and downed trees had to removed - reduced from the initial estimate of 110,000 cubic metres - and the 35m-high slip face had to be stabilised.

The cost of fixing the slip had previously been put at $7.5m.

The council would fund its share of the extra costs by borrowing, to avoid major delays or cuts to existing roading projects.

The report stated the original cost estimate for the Helena Bay Hill slip was based on a completion date of mid-2026.

Since then, however, persistent wet weather, difficult ground conditions, giant basalt boulders, fill site constraints and further slip movement had delayed work and increased costs.

Some boulders were so big, they could not be broken up, even with a 50-tonne breaker, and instead required blasting or a specialist rock-breaking crew.

The report stated there had also been delays due to health and safety issues, such as near-misses involving trucks and local residents, and unauthorised entry into exclusion areas.

Aerial view of the cleared slip on Russell Road’s Helena Bay Hill. Supplied / Whangārei District Council

Once the slip had settled, which was expected to take about a year, more funding would be needed to repair the road below the slip and along the 2km route to the clean-fill site.

The estimated road rehabilitation cost was $2.3m.

During the road closure, the Whangārei District Council operated a convoy, via steep, narrow and unsealed Kaiikanui Road, to allow continued access from the south.

Piloted convoys left every 35-40 minutes from 6.30am to 6.30pm, seven days a week.

The cost of operating the Kaiikanui Road detour was put at $2.1m.

According to claims recorded by the Insurance Council, the total nationwide cost of the January storm, was $75.9m.

More than 5000 claims were lodged including $54.5m for damage to homes, $13.7m to commercial property and $4.6m for vehicles.

According to the Insurance Council, the most costly event of the past decade in terms of insurance claims was the 2023 Anniversary Weekend storm, which totalled $1.98 billion nationwide.

World.title: Green Party announces plan for passenger rail between major NZ cities
World.content:
The Green Party says it will connect the country with intercity passenger rail services, if elected.

The party has announced plans to introduce an overnight rail service between Auckland and Wellington, passenger rail between Christchurch and Dunedin, and to extend the Te Huia train route to Tauranga.

"Where public transport has been invested in, it's well used, saving people time and money every day. But for a lot of New Zealand, public transport options remain expensive and infrequent, especially when travelling long distances," Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said.

"We want to connect our cities and our country with alternative ways to travel that will save people money, connect our communities and give New Zealanders real transport choices."

"Aotearoa was once connected by a reliable passenger rail system, with fast, frequent services linking communities across the country. But the privatisation of the rail network led to the sale of our assets for private profit and was returned to the people in disarray.

"Now, our aging rail infrastructure is suffering from a generation of underinvestment, leaving the rail network in a state of decline with cancellations, delays and bus replacements.

"We should restore these systems so we can have an efficient, comfortable and affordable alternative to experience our country."

Green Party co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick Tess Brunton / RNZ

Green Party transport spokesperson Julie Anne Genter said the tracks were already there, so should be used.

"Restoring commuter rail will give smaller regions and towns the benefits of more travellers stopping at their town stations, creating more economic opportunities and connecting them to main centres and other towns."

There were compelling reasons to back the services the party had set out, she said.

"The train journey from Auckland to Wellington is long, which makes it perfect for an overnight service. All that is needed is new, comfortable sleeper trains and operating funding.

"Extending Te Huia to Tauranga would connect one of NZ's fastest-growing regions. All it needs is some station, tunnel and track upgrades to give the region an affordable alternative to driving.

"With KiwiRail already undertaking significant work on the Christchurch to Dunedin track, extending it to passenger rail would only take building stations and some upgrades, making better use of existing rail infrastructure," she added.

Peters: 'Our job is to make sure it's viable'

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters was not opposed to the idea of a sleeper train between Auckland and Wellington.

Peters, who has been the Minister for Rail in the coalition government, said his party did not rule out any idea - it just made sure "we can stand it up practically first".

"There's nothing new about the idea, that's been around for over 100 years," he said.

Regional rail had operated in the past but had ended up shut down, he said.

"That's the point. Our job is to make sure it's viable.

"I'm not saying I'm opposed to supporting anything until I've done the work on it, done the analysis, because the Greens will announce 1000 announcements, but as for the business case, they wouldn't know what the expression means."

Rail was run down when he came back into office in 2023, he said.

"We turned this around for the second time.

"But at least we've got an acceptance in the business community at last that rail is critical for our future."

Luxon says proposal won't work

National leader Christopher Luxon did not want taxpayer funding going into a "white elephant" that was not commercially viable.

"Where it makes sense that's really good but you need a concentration of population to make passenger rail work.

"Of course we're very committed to our 17 roads of national significance and we make no apology for that."

World.title: One injured after air gun fired at Hamilton bus stop
World.content:
An air gun was reportedly fired at a Hamilton bus stop on Saturday.

Police said they received a call just before 3pm that the gun had been fired at a member of the public at a bus stop on Masters Avenue, near Hillcrest Park.

They said one person sustained moderate injuries and were transported for medical treatment.

Police said 4-5 suspects were described to be in a small orange car, with one occupant having long hair.

World.title: Sir Sam Neill's legacy lives on in Two Paddocks' next harverst
World.content: "Sam bought it and he kept a whole lot of those botanicals and did a whole lot of planting himself, lots of shelter belts. His one comment was when he bought the farm, there were no indigenous trees, there were no native trees here. And there were no tuis, no bellbirds, and no songbirds. So he sort of felt that another part of his legacy was sort of the thousands of native plantings that he's done here. And it's brought back the tuis and the bellbirds and the songbirds. So he was really, really delighted about that.

World.title: Mystery man a 'hero' after saving 89-year-old from burning home
World.content:
A mystery man has been hailed as a "hero", after he entered a burning building to save an 89-year-old from a housefire in Gisborne.

The fire on Aberdeen Road was reported to emergency services about 1am Saturday.

Detective Senior Sergeant John Love said police understood the man was driving past the burning home, saw the fire and pulled over.

"He then entered the burning building and pulled the occupant to safety through a window.

"However, he left the scene, before emergency services were able to speak with him."

Love said police were now looking for the man to thank him for "his quick thinking and courageous actions".

The occupant of the burning home was taken to hospital for further assessment and observation.

Love encouraged anyone with information that could help identify the man to contact Police on 105, quoting file number P067820889.

World.title: Tragic deaths mourned by Auckland councillors
World.content:
Auckland councillors are lamenting after several tragic deaths this week.

A 33-year-old man has been charged with murder after a man died on a residential street in Glen Innes on Thursday afternoon.

Three family members were also found dead at a Papatoetoe home on Thursday evening.

Manukau Ward Councillor Lotu Fuli said one of the victims, a man found on the front porch of the home, had young children.

"It's a man who is well-known in the community and helps out in the community.

"What I've heard from our community and people who live nearby is that it has come as a complete surprise to their neighbours and everybody who knew the family. The family is a quiet family. Everyone is quite shocked because of that."

RNZ / Felix Walton

Fuli believed the victims' extended family were being supported.

She said there was no threat to the wider community and people should still feel safe.

"I know there's a bit of uncertainty out there, but as far as we're aware, there's no ongoing threat and no wider issue for our Papatoetoe community and neighbourhood.

"Hopefully people are feeling okay, and for those neighbours who did see what happened and are experiencing grief and loss, I hope they are able to get some help, some counselling, to help them through it as well. I know it will be a very difficult time for everybody involved."

RNZ / Felix Walton

Fellow Manukau Councillor Alf Filipaina said he planned to pay his respects when possible.

"I've heard that they [the victims] are community people and well liked in the community."

The former police officer said his thoughts were with the families, first responders, and communities affected by both tragedies this week.

"I know what impact it has when you see something of that nature. Please seek professional advice to get you through. I've found that if you take that offer and take it early, it helps you process what you've seen.

"My plea to the community is to stay strong and stand together."

'Huge effects' on the workforce

Police Association President Steve Watt said police around the country dealt with four suspected homicides in one week - with investigations also underway in

Buller and Christchurch.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406082423112

He said that would put the workforce under pressure.

"Homicides are extremely intensive and resource driven operations and there's no doubt that having multiple homicides at the same time will draw on a number of police investigations in order to deal with it."

Watt said the investigations had "huge effects" on the workforce, who were driven to get a result and deliver justice for family members and friends.

World.title: Saints hit rock bottom, Essendon, Suns, Port claim AFLW victories
World.content:
St Kilda have kicked just a single point, the club's lowest ever score in an AFLW match, as the Western Bulldogs scored a 30-point victory in Ballarat.

Incredibly, the Saints only managed the behind in the final 90 seconds of the game in a horror afternoon for the winless club.

The Bulldogs were barely better in tough conditions in Ballarat, with sideways rain and winds limiting the hosts to just three goals 13 on a day were accuracy in front of goal suffered.

Rylie Wilcox, Sarah Hartwig and Cleo Buttifant scored the goals for the Bulldogs, while Isabelle Pritchard (35 disposals, six clearances) was outstanding in the testing, cold conditions.

For the Saints, only Ashleigh Richards's point spared the cellar dwellers the ignominy of a bagel.

Earlier, star midfielder Madison Prespakis steered battling Essendon to an eight-point comeback victory over GWS for its first win of the season.

Essendon recorded its first win of the 2026 AFLW season. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

The Giants got out to a game-high 25-point lead at the start of the third quarter and appeared on track for a second win of the season, before Prespakis kicked into overdrive and the Bombers lifted their pressure.

The star on-baller racked up 13 disposals, six contested possessions, three clearances and a goal in the third term to put Essendon on her back and inspire a terrific 6.7 (43) to 5.5 (35) comeback at Henson Park on Saturday afternoon.

"Genuinely just so proud of the resilience of the group," skipper Bonnie Toogood told Fox Sports.

"And it's been a challenging season, I suppose, and the persistence through adversity, particularly today.

"The first half wasn't what we were planning on, but to come out in the third like we did and just big moments by individuals — bloody inspiring."

The victory relieves some pressure on Bombers coach Natalie Wood and leaves St Kilda as the league's only winless team.

It was a devastating loss for Cam Bernasconi's Giants, who kicked five of the first six goals then only scored one point in a second half where they were completely overwhelmed by Essendon's manic pressure.

Madison Prespakis was sensational, with 13 disposals, six contested possessions, three clearances and a goal as the Bombers came from behind. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Essendon had trailed by just four points at the final change when star forward Toogood gave the Bombers a massive rev-up at the huddle.

"I'm passionate and emotional all the time — it could be the Italian in me," Toogood said.

"They were on the back foot … I was like, 'We've got 'em — lean into that, we've got them, our football is working.'"

Essendon hit the front when it went from end to end and Daria Bannister tumbled home a long-range goal.

Then Emily Gough kicked a terrific checkside from a forward-50 stoppage that sealed victory.

Prespakis finished with a mammoth 35 disposals and five clearances, and she was well supported by Maddi Gay (21 disposals) and Georgia Gee (15), along with ruck Steph Wales (20 disposals, 14 hitouts, eight clearances).

Later, the Gold Coast Suns finally secured their first victory over the Brisbane Lions, winning a fiery Q-Clash by 20 points in Brisbane.

Havana Harris kicked two as the Suns won their first Q-Clash. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Meara Girvan may have cause for concern after pinning the arms of Cathy Svarc in a tackle during the first quarter, while Charlotte Mullins was penalised for high contact on Niamh McLaughlin later in the game.

The Lions led by two points at the final change but failed to kick another point as the Suns booted three in the final term to win 5.10 (40) to 3.2 (20).

Havana Harris kicked two for the Suns, who recorded their sixth win of the season to sit fourth on the ladder.

In Saturday's final fixture, Port Adelaide ended a four-match losing run by winning the Showdown against Adelaide in front of a record crowd of 5,441 fans at Alberton Oval.

Port Adelaide completed a second Showdown victory in a row at Alberton Oval. (Getty Images: Sarah Reed/AFL Photos)

The Power joined the Crows on 12 competition points thanks to a 5.6 (36) to 2.10 (22) victory.

Port (3-5) had five different goal kickers in the opening three quarters to open up a 34-7 advantage, but failed to hit the target in the fourth.

After going goalless for three terms, Caitlin Gould and Teah Charlton kicked straight for some respectability on the scoreboard for Adelaide (3-5).

AAP/ABC

World.title: FOMO and 4am wake-up call get Pallister in the ocean
World.content:
Is there anything Lani Pallister can't do?

On Friday night, Pallister wrapped up a hugely successful Australian short course championships with a fourth gold medal in the 800-metre freestyle to seal her spot in the 24-strong squad for the world championships.

Then, the 24-year-old rushed up to Queensland's Sunshine Coast to claim honours in the 1.2-kilometre Bluff to Bar ocean swim at Alexandra Headland on Saturday morning, after a 4am wake-up call.

"I'd get really bad FOMO [fear of missing out]," Pallister said when asked why she made the trip.

"It's important to give back … Alexandra Heads Surf Club helped make me the athlete I am today."

Lani Pallister won her third-straight Bluff to Bar race. (Supplied: Alexandra Headland Surf Lifesaving Club)

Pallister's dedication to her surf club cannot be doubted after she posted a story on her Instagram feed tagged at 4:38am to get her flight for an 11:20am race on the Sunshine Coast.

And the Paris Olympian made sure the early wake up was worth it, leading a stacked field from start to finish to claim a third-straight victory in the event.

Competing in a point-to-point ocean swim couldn't have been more different from the 125 tumble turns she completed in competition at the Sydney Olympic Park Aquatic Centre in the past four days.

Pallister competed in every freestyle event from 100m to 1,500m, winning gold in all but the 100m, where she finished second.

That ensured that she would be the headline act for the Dolphins squad named for the Beijing world championships from December 1-6.

The squad includes six debutants: Amelie Smith, Mark Nikolaev, Marcus Da Silva, Emily Jones, Cameron Bladen and Alex Quach.

Lani Pallister (left) and Jenna Forrester both had excellent championships. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Head Dolphins coach Rohan Taylor noted Pallister's performance as a stand-out in Sydney, with Sam Short's clean sweep of the 400m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle and Jenna Forrester's four silvers and a gold also worthy of mention.

"Those three without a doubt have been stand-outs here," Taylor said.

"But also it's been great to see the likes of Amelie Smith and Marcus Da Silva come through the ranks and shift the dial.

"Also credit to Mark Nikolaev; it's a credit to his consistency and perseverance that he has earned his Dolphin number tonight.

"The international exposure in Beijing is an opportunity to come together and build towards LA 2028 and the meet presents a great opportunity for our younger swimmers to learn from established Dolphins."

Lani Pallister won the 200, 400, 800 and 1,500m freestyle events at the Australian short course championships. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Speaking of experienced Dolphins, Cam McEvoy is also set to join the Aussie team in Beijing, despite not competing at the national championships this week.

World Aquatics is offering wildcard spots for the world championships to any to any swimmer who finishes on the podium of an individual final during the the World Cup series.

The 32-year-old long course world record holder duly set a new national short course record of 20.22 for the 50m freestyle to win gold on the opening night of the 2026 World Cup series in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Friday.

Pallister will now head for an altitude training camp in Flagstaff, USA, before the world championships, which represents her ninth Australian Dolphins selection.

"Off to altitude in a couple of weeks' time, and then just pretty much getting back into full training, knuckling down and targeting world champs," Pallister said during the short course titles.

"I didn't really anticipate fast swimming this week. I was actually pretty shocked with the 200 being plus 0.2, so [I'm] pretty happy."

Dolphins World Championships squad

Iona Anderson, Ben Armbruster, Cameron Bladen*, Brittany Castelluzzo, Josh Collett, Isaac Cooper, Marcus Da Silva*, Jenna Forrester, Max Giuliani, Emily Jones*, Tara Kinder, Mark Nikolaev*, Lani Pallister, Alexandria Perkins, William Petric, Alex Quach*, David Schlicht, Sam Short, Amelie Smith*, Flynn Southam, Stuart Swinburn, Matt Temple, Olivia Wunsch, Josh Yong.

*debut Dolphins squad

World.title: Roosters met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger days before Bondi attack
World.content:
On December 9, 2025, a group of Sydney Roosters players met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger and other leaders in the Eastern Suburbs Jewish community.

It was a Tuesday in the off-season for the rugby league club, months away from a ball being kicked or a tackle made.

They are a club on occasion tagged as well-oiled, representing the richest postcodes in Australia and lacking deep community ties.

But here were the Roosters, including Hugo Savala, Cody Ramsay and Billy Smith, eating kosher food, learning of Jewish customs at the Chabad of Bondi and walking along the beachfront and Bondi Pavilion.

Days later, metres away from that pavilion, the most devastating terror attack in Australian history occurred.

One of the 15 people killed in the mass shooting at Bondi Beach was Eli Schlanger.

Ten months on, and the Roosters are on the eve of a grand final against a Newcastle side almost universally cast as Sunday evening's community-minded underdog — but Easts' involvement and then support of their community during its darkest hour offers a glimpse into a story far more complex.

Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, Rabbi Shchlanger's father-in-law, was also on hand to meet with the players at the Chabad of Bondi Synagogue.

"They came to the synagogue, and they had a run-down of the different meanings and symbolisms," Rabbi Ulman told ABC Sport.

"And I remember they were very curious and very interested to understand everything that was going on."

The Roosters observed a minute's silence for the victims of the attack before their first home game of the season. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Roosters CEO Joe Kelly, also present on the day, said the players took an immediate liking to Rabbi Schlanger — something that came as no surprise to Rabbi Ulman.

"Eli was a person who could connect with anybody," Rabbi Ulman said.

It was a "very happy occasion", according to co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Alex Ryvchin, who was also present.

"The Roosters came, they were incredibly charming, engaged, very articulate, very knowledgeable already about the Jewish community in this area," Mr Ryvchin told ABC Sport.

"And just really thirsting for more knowledge and understanding of Jewish customs and traditions … really left a very positive impression on everybody they met."

Billy Smith was one of the players to meet with Rabbi Schlanger. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings)

But the players also ended the day with a greater understanding of some of the darkness experienced by the community in the 12 months prior.

While walking down the promenade at Bondi Beach, Ryvchin explained to them how the uptick in antisemitic incidents had impacted the local community.

"They had a very high level of awareness already in terms of the fire bombings that were happening here routinely," Mr Ryvchin said.

"They were concerned about it, but at that point it was still probably abstract for them."

The events of December 14 were deeply impactful for the Roosters, as they were for the entire country.

And for those players who had broken bread with Rabbi Schlanger earlier that week, Joe Kelly said he could feel the enormity of their grief and shock.

"[It had] a real impact on those players, and on the wider club," Mr Kelly said.

"The fact that it was only five days, it was really close to home for us, and I know that that was felt more broadly across the community as well as across the country."

Joe Kelly says the terror attack hit particularly "close to home". (ABC News: Scott Preston)

Rabbi Ulman, who spoke at Rabbi Schlanger's funeral at the very synagogue that had hosted the Roosters barely a week earlier, could understand their grief.

"When we see something that happens in the world that is wrong, we are affected by it, and we automatically feel how wrong this is," Rabbi Ulman said.

"But when it happens to somebody that we know, it affects us so much more because it's close to home.

"They saw Eli, they connected with him, and five days later, you know, what happened, happened."

Away on a training trip on the day of the attack, the Roosters players gathered to pay their respects on Bondi Beach as soon as they could, before hosting an open training session on the sand in January.

The Tricolours also had Summer, sister of the youngest victim, Matilda, toss the coin and deliver the ball ahead of the Roosters' first home game of the new year.

Mr Kelly said the organisation "got around the community as much as we possibly could" — while Rabbi Ulman said the reaction of the club, especially from those players he met at the synagogue just days before the attack, said a lot.

"That just shows you that they are good people. Because any good person would be deeply affected by what happened," he said.

World.title: Brisbane 2032 emblems leaked by official YouTube channel
World.content:
The emblems for the Brisbane 2032 Olympics and Paralympics have been accidentally leaked by the Games' official YouTube channel, ruining its own grand unveiling.

Pieces of the emblem had been revealed during a Queensland tour over the past week, with the full picture slated to come together on Monday.

But the cockatoo-inspired emblem was entirely revealed last night in a preview image for an "Emblem Explainer" video set to go live on Monday morning.

Pieces of the emblem had been revealed during a Queensland tour over the past week. (ABC News: Dominic Cansdale)

An explanation of the emblem was also visible in the video's description.

"The Brisbane 2032 emblems are inspired by the spirited cockatoo — a symbol of Australia's unique wildlife and playful heart! The cockatoo's crest is a living torch, reminiscent of the iconic Olympic and Paralympic flame," the description reportedly read.

"Shaped like Queensland, with its eye on Brisbane, the emblem is a universal symbol to unite Brisbane, Australia and the world in 2032."

The image has subsequently been removed from YouTube.

Olympics Minister Tim Mander said he was "excited" about the emblem's unveiling. (ABC News)

Olympics Minister Tim Mander told the Today show he was "excited" the emblem was "finally out".

"The emblem is something that will make us known around the world with regard to the Games in 2032," he said.

"We just want to celebrate it."

Mr Mander would not comment when questioned if the leak was planned.

"Obviously there were people so enthusiastic about looking for the emblem that they'd been scanning the internet," he said.

"It's appeared for a short time, and it's out there."

Brisbane 2032 chief marketing officer Brent Hill said the reaction to the emblem has been positive. (ABC News: Dominic Cansdale)

Brisbane 2032 chief marketing officer Brent Hill said the leak had generated "incredible" publicity for the Games.

"If we had our time over, maybe there's different ways that we could have done it," Mr Hill said.

"The overarching piece from our side is still the fact that we wanted people to guess, we wanted the clues to be out there, and now it's out there.

"The reaction to it has been really positive."

Opposition leader Steven Miles welcomed the cockatoo-inspired emblems, but said Brisbane 2032 organisers should own up to the blunder.

"No doubt there will be a lot of questions asked about how this mistake was made so that they can avoid it again in the future," he said.

"I know there was a lot of interest though, so Queenslanders will be excited that they got to see it sooner than they were meant to."

The emblem unveiling tour is set to continue in Brisbane this weekend after stops in Cairns, Townsville, Rockhampton and the Sunshine Coast last week.

There will be a community unveiling of the emblem on Monday night in Brisbane.

World.title: Cats notch seventh-straight AFLW win as Scheer fires against Richmond
World.content:
Forward Chloe Scheer has continued her rise from the depths of injury despair, powering Geelong to the summit of the AFLW ladder with a 34-point win over Richmond.

After underlining their premiership credentials with a rousing 36-point defeat of Hawthorn last Thursday, the Cats snared their seventh straight victory at Princes Park on Friday to leap above defending premiers North Melbourne.

Scheer dazzled in the 7.12 (54) to 3.2 (20) win, kicking three majors in blustery conditions to go equal top of the league's goal-scoring charts with Hawthorn's Aine McDonagh (18 goals).

Her glittering form comes despite the 26-year-old missing the entire 2024 and 2025 seasons with foot and knee injuries, respectively.

Co-captain Nina Morrison (26 disposals, seven tackles, one goal) was also prolific, while forward Mikayla Bowen was busy with 20 disposals and seven tackles.

But it wasn't a smooth-sailing victory as Richmond employed unrelenting pressure until midway through the second quarter when the Cats sprang into life.

It was a stunning team goal finished off by forward Jacqueline Parry that started the visitors' onslaught as they piled on five of the next six majors while the Tigers' wheels fell off.

Richmond missed out on a chance to spring into the top eight.

Midfielder Ellie McKenzie (20 disposals, six tackles) was a shining light, but the Tigers will hope forward Laura McClelland recovers quickly after she left the field with a shoulder injury.

The home team put the foot on the throttle early, scoring the first goal through forward Olivia Wolmarans, although Scheer slotted a settling major to help the visitors lead by two points at quarter-time.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

The Tigers hit back when forward Gabby Seymour pounced on Wolmarans' handball before Parry secured a crucial score.

Minutes later, Morrison thumped the ball through the centre sticks, but Ana Mulholland snagged her first AFLW goal to close the deficit.

Forward Jasmin Stewart kicked a major after the siren to help the visitors extend their advantage to 27-20 at the main break.

The Cats flew out of the gates after half-time, dominating the inside 50 count and ballooning their lead by 29 points at three-quarter time.

Richmond was kept scoreless in the final term as the visitors cruised to victory.

AAP

World.title: Tedesco and Ponga went through different worlds to meet in NRL grand final
World.content:
Sunday's NRL grand final between the Roosters and Newcastle is a land of contrasts and nowhere is more apparent than the difference between the two fullbacks and captains, James Tedesco and Kalyn Ponga.

Their position, status and ability is about all the two have in common and right from the start the two have walked very different paths to Stadium Australia.

Ponga has been in the papers since he was 15, his first highlights went viral when he was only 17, his first NRL game was a sudden-death semi-final and his first touch was a scorching linebreak that announced a new prince was born.

Once he joined Newcastle in 2018 and finished as the Dally M runner up in his first full season in first grade, his talent was so blinding he never had to prove himself — belief was in his ability was assured.

The world was his, because everyone in rugby league was so eager to give it to him.

For the 33-year old Tedesco, things were different. The Camden product was a good junior, but far from a great one. Just making first grade was far from a guarantee.

Eventually, he didn't just run down those who were ahead of him, he raced right past them and by the time he made his NRL debut for Wests Tigers in Round 1 of the 2012 season he'd shown himself to be a player of the future.

But that future would have to wait. Where Ponga's debut was covered in chrome, Tedesco's became the hardest day of his young life when he blew his knee out 30 minutes in and was stretchered off Leichhardt Oval in tears.

It kicked off a series of injury troubles and it wasn't until three seasons later that Tedesco managed to shrug them off and become an every-week first grader.

During those years, the naysayers rose up and once again Tedesco outlasted them. He is a player of enormous internal motivation — for him, improvement is less of a journey to be better than a compulsion that defines him and he has put a saddle on that beast and ridden it to greatness.

Tedesco suffered a serious knee injury in his NRL debut. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The doubt of others is the whip he uses to flog it, like he did when time seemed to come for him as he lost his New South Wales and Australian spots two years ago.

He was old enough to go quietly into that good night without shame, and after a career of magnificent achievement the game was prepared to move on only Tedesco would not let it.

"In 2024 and 2025 when I wasn't playing Origin or Test footy, people were doubting me a bit and I got some drive from that," said Tedesco.

Tedesco defies time en route to record Dally M triumph Roosters fullback James Tedesco held off the challenge of players over a decade his junior to defy time and claim his second Dally M player of the year award.

"I've been used to that — growing up I was told I wasn't going to make it when I wasn't picked in teams, when I had injuries at the start of my career people told me my body wouldn't last.

"Those external things do motivate me, but the internal one is still the biggest. That'll always be there for me and when it isn't I'll realise it's time to finish."

It had been so long since he was counted out but Tedesco still fought like a demon to prove himself one more time as he claimed last year's Dally M medal and returned to Origin this season.

It has given him a second life but it's still not enough. He is not satisfied and doubts he ever will be.

"I'll never be happy with my game. I always want to improve and learn and get better," said Tedesco.

"That's a part of me, that's been ingrained in me since I was a kid. It's got me to where I am today."

At 33, Tedesco is still one of the best players in the competition. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

Tedesco has been in that place for many years and that is where Ponga now strides towards.

Right from those first days in Newcastle his raw star power, through no fault of his own, quickly made him bigger than the club he played for.

The adulation continued to flow like a river as the highlights and the Fox League spots stacked up as personal success came naturally to Ponga, but in terms of team success there were many lean winters.

The 29-year old didn't play in a final until 2020, didn't win one until 2023 and in the last three weeks the Knights have more finals victories than the rest of Ponga's time with the club combined.

Ponga has carried the weight of expectations his entire career. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

What seemed like a pre-destined journey to the top has not always been smooth. But if Ponga could speak to his younger self he wouldn't ask him to change because if he did it might not have brought him to where he is right now.

"He'd have wanted it earlier, he was impatient. But it makes it sweeter, to go through those tough times — the adversity, injuries, bad years," said Ponga.

"All the emotion came out when Sandon (Smith) took that intercept. But I wouldn't trade any of it because I'm grateful to be here now.

"There was a lot of tension. I think everyone was riding that last minute with us. The relief — nine years I've been here and I've always dreamt of being in this position and it came true with that intercept."

Emotion has been the driving force of Newcastle's run to the grand final. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Ponga's uncontainable passion as a leader has been vibrant and bustling and it's come through in his football, which has perhaps been better but has never been tougher.

He has not scored a try or set one up in this finals series even as he's been outstanding in all three matches, with his running game, defence and leadership coming to the fore.

"When you grow up, you mature — or you'd hope so. The environment I'm in has changed, it allows me to be the best version of myself and it allows me to be myself," said Ponga.

"There's no pressure on me to be someone I'm not, as a player or a person. Justin (Holbrook) has done that and this playing group has done that."

The raw and bleeding edge Ponga has showed is a far cry from his younger days, when sometimes he could be a little too relaxed for his own good.

It helped him carry the weight of a city, a club and a game that expected so much of him, but other times it came to the surface in ways that did not befit a player of his stature — most notably when he said a strawberry thickshake lifted his spirits after coach Nathan Brown was sacked in 2019.

"Off the field, early in his career, he'd probably admit he was a bit lackadaisical. He was cruisy, he'd kick back," said Bradman Best, who first played alongside him that season.

"Now he holds everyone accountable, he drives standards. He's having an impact on other people.

"He's found that balance between staying calm and firing up."

Ponga has led from the front to take Newcastle to the brink of a premiership. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

Young prop Cody Hopwood, who was just 11 years old when Ponga first came to town and knows him only as he is now, puts it best.

"He doesn't try and overdo the role, he doesn't try to be someone he's not," said Hopwood.

"He's Kalyn Ponga and that's enough."

The Roosters always expect to be in grand finals so on some level they knew they could be here but the Knights have known it as well, as long ago as the old days of about three weeks ago.

Plenty said they'd never get anywhere, but now we know that they knew better and while Ponga has envisioned lifting the premiership trophy plenty of times before it's only in the last two weeks that it's come into sharper focus.

Newcastle rises as one ahead of grand final Ahead of their first grand final in a generation, Newcastle is ready to hold the Knights closer to their hearts than ever before as team and city show why they are one.

"You do it nearly every day because it gives you a purpose. It's why you wake up and train so hard, it's why you dedicate yourself to this, it's why you put your body through things you shouldn't," said Ponga.

"But it didn't become a reality until after the Warriors, before that it was just a thought."

Ponga's love for his club and his town is palpable and that's important because it hasn't always been so.

Over the years there have been whispers of moves to Sydney — the Roosters were always meant to be in the mix, even with Tedesco — or of a possible move to rugby, plus a serious flirtation with the Dolphins when they were entering the competition.

But earlier this season he signed for another four years on a watertight contract with none of the clauses or flexibility he's had in the past.

It was a show of faith that has been rewarded and since his transformation from a great player who plays for the Knights into a great Knight and now he is Newcastle, forever and always, no matter what.

"We're in it and to see it, to feel it, it's inspiring. It's everything you ever dreamt of," said Ponga.

"I'm proud to be a part of this club. I'm proud to lead these boys. I'm proud to be a part of this community."

A grand final win will be a moment for ascension for Ponga's nine years with the club and he has moved to the edge of paradise because he has been able to fuse the internal and external motivations as Tedesco has long done.

At 33, Tedesco still holds his club's premiership fate in his hands. (Getty Images: Ayush Kumar )

For Tedesco and his Roosters it's a bit simpler. Having slayed the latest demons, he wants to take the feelings out of the grand final as best he can.

Their key is to keep this as a football game rather than a holy war, to be as calm in the face of overwhelming passion as Ponga once was.

"Just the other night I found myself thinking about the game almost too much, thinking about moments and what could happen," said Tedesco.

"I had to get away from that, because I didn't want to play too early. But it's not about the result, it's about the performance and the process.

"It's easier to say that than it is to do it, but that's something I have to instil into the boys.

"Be proud of where we are, but know the job isn't finished."

World.title: Man City appeals guilty findings of breaking EPL's financial rules
World.content:
Manchester City has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, seeking to overturn the verdict and avoid potentially severe sanctions.

The league said on Tuesday that ​City had used "sham" commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than £900 million ($1.71 billion) over nearly a decade.

City was found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the league's financial rules over nine seasons from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as three out of four charges concerning failures to cooperate with the investigation.

The club has denied wrongdoing throughout the process.

"Manchester City Football Club can confirm that at 7pm on Thursday 1st October 2026 the Club lodged its comprehensive Appeal against the opinion of the Premier League Commission, in relation to the Premier League disciplinary matter," the club said in a statement.

"The Club's firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case."

The appeal will be heard by an independent three-member appeal board appointed by the chair of the league's Judicial Panel.

"The club lodged the appeal to the Chair of the Judicial Panel," the league said in a statement.

"The independent Appeal Board hearing will remain private and confidential until publication of the outcome is permitted."

Appeal decision is final

The Premier League's rules state that an appeal hearing should be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding.

The appeal will take place in private, as did the original hearings. The board will review the commission's decision, but will not conduct a full rehearing of the case.

The board can dismiss the appeal, allow it, refer the case back to the commission for further consideration or alter any sanction or compensation order imposed.

A decision by the appeal board is final and cannot be challenged further except in limited circumstances that permit a subsequent arbitration process.

With potential sanctions including heavy fines, points deductions and other sporting penalties, and with relegation or the removal of titles also discussed as possible outcomes, the case could have consequences across the league.

City can also separately appeal against any sanctions. It remains unclear whether sanctions will be announced before the appeal is heard, and whether they would take effect immediately.

A league representative told Reuters they could not discuss the process for confidentiality reasons.

While the fate of the case remains unresolved, the season will continue, with leaders City looking for their sixth straight league win when they visit Liverpool on October 11.

Reuters

World.title: NRLW needs its own CEO, says legend Ali Brigginshaw
World.content:
In her final press conference before retirement, rugby league legend Ali Brigginshaw has called on the NRL to create a separate chief executive for the women's game.

As she prepares for a fairytale finish hoping to win back-to-back premierships with Brisbane, Brigginshaw knows the NRLW still has much growing to do.

At today's official pre-grand final press conference, the Bronco was asked to put herself at the desk of newly crowned executive chairman Peter V'landys.

"If there's someone in charge of the [women's] game, maybe someone that plays the game, not me, maybe Millie," Brigginshaw joked about her fellow retiring grand finalist, the Roosters' Millie Elliott.

"Just someone that knows the game and what we've been through.

"We try to shape our game exactly [how] the men do, but there's nothing saying we have to just follow in those footsteps.

"We can go in a different direction, we can do what we want to do and what's best for the [NRLW] players and the staff."

Ali Brigginshaw was given a guard of honour for Brisbane's last home game. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

The women's game is currently managed by the chief executive of the NRL. In contrast, the AFLW has always had its own dedicated leadership, currently headed by Laura Kane.

It was not the only major innovation suggested at today's fan event, with tributes to Brigginshaw also on the agenda.

"She will be remembered in the game for such a long time, and I really hope that they name an award after Ali," Broncos coach Scott Prince said.

The 2020 Dally M medallist has captained her state and country and now leaves behind a legacy that even her fiercest rivals admire.

"Ali's been a pioneer of our game for a very long time now, and I've been really lucky to know Ali for a number of years and play with her and experience her as a leader as well," Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly said.

Roosters captain Isabelle Kelly paid credit to the retiring Ali Brigginshaw. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

She also shared plenty of praise for her own retiring teammates Corban Baxter and Elliott, the 2022 Dally M medallist.

"[Millie] never stops; she's always putting her best foot forward. She promotes the game in such a positive and respectful light that so many young girls look up to.

"Corban, she's the most humble, beautiful human that I think has just put such a landmark on this game."

Meanwhile, the Roosters will make a last-second decision on winger Jayme Fressard as she races the clock to have her shoulder right for grand final day.

The Blues representative picked up a shoulder injury in last week's win over Canberra and did not return to the field after half-time.

A final decision will be made after the captain's run tomorrow, with coach John Strange rating Fressard a "50-50" chance of playing.

"A little niggle, a few fitness tests to still get through, but hopefully looking good," Strange said.

"I just really want to be present this week and do everything that I need to do to be the best athlete as possible."

AAP

Tech.title: Capcom is preparing for a ‘future where we create games together with AI’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.
